title: Context Window
description: 从 token 预算到长上下文质量，用同一客服案例算清容量、成本与证据位置。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  In [Model Context](/docs/context/model-context), the support assistant found an order and a refund policy. Now ask: **as chat history, tool results, and policy documents grow, how much can the model fit and how well can it use them?** An accepted request only shows it stayed within an API limit; it does not prove the answer is reliable.

  This page starts with token budgeting from [Tokenization](/docs/llm/tokenization), connects cost to attention and the KV cache from [Attention & Transformer](/docs/llm/transformer), then examines evidence position and evaluation. In interviews, calculate and diagnose rather than memorize today's model limits.

  <Note type="tip" title="2026-10-04 update: what to review">
    🆕 **New Level 4**: claimed vs effective length (RULER, NoLiMa, Context Rot), KV-cache memory math, long-context pricing tiers.

    🔁 **Review**: Level 1 (prefill/decode, KV cache) and Level 2 (lost in the middle) — Level 4 builds on both.

    ✏️ **Original text unchanged**: no factual errors found; your highlights are intact.
  </Note>

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Budget | How do input, reserved output, and a window limit fit together? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Compute | Why does more context usually cost more time and money? | 25 min |
  | 2 · Quality | What is lost in the middle, and is it universal? | 25 min |
  | 3 · Decision | When do long context and retrieval make sense, and how do you test? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Deep dive (added 2026-10) | Why is effective length shorter than the claimed window? How much memory does the KV cache take? | 30 min |

  The running example is a support assistant deciding whether order 20240915 qualifies for a refund using history, an order lookup, and policy. All token counts below are **teaching assumptions**; verify real counts with the chosen model's counting endpoint and response usage.

  ## Must know

  * Separate input tokens, generated tokens, output reserve, model window, and API limits; budget one call.
  * Distinguish long-input prefill from sequential decode; O(n²) is not an API pricing formula.
  * Explain possible long-context degradation and position effects without claiming they hold equally for all models.
  * Compare long-context and retrieval designs on answer quality, citations, latency, and cost.
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Budget the window first

  ### What does the context window limit?

  A context window is the amount of context a model can use for one generation, usually expressed in tokens. Also distinguish the **published model limit**, provider-specific input or output limits, and the maximum output configured for this request. Look up the rules for the actual model and API version; a single “128K” label is not enough.

  Assume an illustrative interface permits **16,000 tokens total** for this call:

  ```text
  Instructions and tool definitions    1,000
  Question and relevant history        2,000
  Order tool result                      500
  Refund policy passages               8,000
  ------------------------------------------
  Estimated input                     11,500
  Maximum output reserve               1,000
  Planned total                       12,500 ≤ 16,000
  Remaining margin                     3,500
  ```

  The 1,000-token reserve is a **planned maximum**, not guaranteed output. Leave room for template overhead, special tokens, multimodal inputs, and counting differences. Appending another 6,000 tokens of raw tool logs would bring the planned total to 18,500. First decide which lines actually matter to the refund decision.

  <Note type="warning" title="Do not treat window numbers as permanent">
    Windows, output limits, and billing rules vary by model, provider, and endpoint. Count before sending and reconcile response usage afterward. Gemini's [token guide](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens) distinguishes request and response counts.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why leave 3,500 tokens of margin in the example?
    2. If logs add 6,000 tokens, what would you inspect before blindly dropping old chat turns?
    3. Does “16K window” alone prove the request and output configuration are valid?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Why long input has a cost

  ### What do prefill, decode, and the KV cache do here?

  **Prefill** processes supplied input and builds state for generation. **Decode** generates one new token at a time. Self-attention lets a token use other permitted positions. In a simplified dense-attention analysis, a length-n sequence has roughly n² position pairs. Real latency also depends on architecture, FlashAttention, batching, hardware, and serving implementation; n² does not directly predict a bill.

  The **KV cache** retains previously computed keys and values during generation, avoiding recomputation of all earlier positions at each new token. Its inference-memory footprint grows with retained context. It is distinct from the cross-request prompt cache in [Caching](/docs/context/caching). [Inference](/docs/llm/inference) covers the implementation.

  In the support case, an 8,000-token policy usually costs more input processing than an 800-token relevant excerpt. Shrinking it to 800 tokens **does not automatically improve quality**: removing a refund exception can make the answer wrong. Preserve decision-critical evidence while controlling tokens.

  <Note type="tip" title="Do not equate complexity with price">
    Say: “Dense attention has a quadratic pairwise pattern in a simplified prefill view; provider latency and price require measurement.” Then name your measures: input and output tokens, time to first token, total latency, and cost.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Does longer input first affect prefill or the number of generated decode steps?
    2. What does the KV cache store, and why can long context increase its footprint?
    3. Why can't O(n²) directly calculate an API bill?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Fitting is not the same as finding

  ### What is lost in the middle, and how should we qualify it?

  In long-document experiments, some models perform worse when the same decisive evidence appears in the **middle** of the input rather than near the beginning or end. The original [Lost in the Middle study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172) tested multi-document QA and key-value retrieval. This is an empirical result for tested models and tasks, **not a universal U-shaped law for every newer model or length**.

  For the support assistant, use one decisive policy line: “Shipped orders cannot use the unshipped-order refund flow.” Place it near the front, middle, and end of otherwise identical long policy packs. Keep the question fixed. If middle placement reduces accuracy, you have evidence of **position sensitivity for this model, task, and length**. Improve retrieval and visibility, then compare orderings; do not turn one paper into “always put the answer last.”

  <Note type="warning" title="Separate hard limits from soft degradation">
    Exceeding the window is a capacity problem and may trigger rejection or truncation. A wrong answer within the window is an information-use problem. First rule out missing retrieval, stale evidence, and hard multi-hop reasoning.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. How would you vary only evidence position in a comparable test?
    2. If the model gets a 200K-token page and answers incorrectly, name three possible causes.
    3. Why is lost in the middle not a fixed law for all models?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Choosing long context and retrieval

  ### With a very large window, do we still need RAG?

  It depends on corpus size, update frequency, traceability, latency, and measured quality. A finite customer-provided contract that must be read end to end may fit directly. Frequently changing orders and policies or a large knowledge base usually call for authoritative lookups and versioned retrieval. **Long context and RAG can combine**: retrieval narrows the candidates, then the model receives enough surrounding evidence to decide.

  Compare three designs on a set of realistic support questions: A sends the whole policy; B sends retrieved passages; C retrieves and adds necessary surrounding context. For each, check live order status, correct policy citations, and the refund decision. Record input tokens, time to first token, and cost. Move decisive evidence across positions as a separate test. **Simple text recall is not the business task**; a correct decision grounded in order state and policy is.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. When might sending one whole document be simpler than a RAG pipeline?
    2. Why does a large window not remove the need to query live order state?
    3. How would you compare A, B, and C without mistaking fluency for correctness?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: effective length, KV memory, long-context pricing

  ### Why doesn't a claimed 1M window mean 1M of usable context?

  The limit only means the request won't be rejected. Long-context evals consistently show effective length is shorter: Needle in a Haystack tests literal single-point retrieval and is too easy; RULER (NVIDIA, 2024) adds multi-needle, multi-hop tracing, and aggregation, and many models claiming 32K+ hold quality far below their claimed length; NoLiMa (2025) removes literal overlap between question and needle, and performance drops much faster; Chroma's Context Rot (2025) shows degradation with length even on simple tasks, especially with similar-but-wrong distractors — exactly the "not shipped" vs "shipped" refund clauses.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "A claimed window is capacity, not quality. RULER, NoLiMa, and Context Rot all show quality falling with length once semantic matching or distractors are involved, so I measure on my task at my lengths."
  </Note>

  ### How much memory does the KV cache take?

  `bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per value`. Llama 3 70B (80 layers, GQA with 8 KV heads, 128 dims, BF16): ≈ 0.31 MB per token, so a 128K request needs ≈ 40 GB of KV cache alone. That's why long requests crowd out concurrency, why GQA matters (64 full KV heads would be 8× larger), and why KV quantization and PagedAttention exist.

  ### Why can long context cost more?

  Beyond linear token billing, some providers charge a higher rate above a length threshold (e.g. 200K) because long requests use disproportionate memory and compute. Check official pricing.

  ### How do models reach such long windows?

  Mostly RoPE with position interpolation or scaling (e.g. YaRN) plus continued long-context training. Models perform best at lengths they saw most in training — one reason effective length trails the claim.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why is Needle in a Haystack insufficient, and what does NoLiMa change?
    2. Compute the KV cache for a 32K Llama 3 70B request.
    3. Why does GQA reduce long-context memory pressure?
    4. Two ways long context costs more beyond token count?
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note type="danger" title="“A larger window always improves answers”">
    Capacity does not guarantee relevance, accuracy, or freshness. Long-context behavior varies across models; test the actual task.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  ```text
  Model Context → candidate inputs
  Context Window → capacity and actual utilization
  Construction → evidence selection
  Compression → preserving facts when history grows
  ```

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you budget input and output for one call?
  2. How do prefill, decode, and the KV cache relate to context length?
  3. How would you test lost in the middle?
  4. Does a very large window eliminate RAG?
  5. Which quality and production metrics would you compare?

  ### Added 2026-10

  1. How do claimed and effective context length differ, and how do you measure it?
  2. Estimate the KV-cache memory for a 128K request.
  3. Why do long-context requests reduce serving concurrency?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

* 2min:

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Budget the window first

  ### What does the context window limit?

  A context window is the amount of context a model can use for one generation, usually expressed in tokens. Also distinguish the

, provider-specific input or output limits, and the maximum output configured for this request. Look up the rules for the actual model and API version; a single “128K” label is not enough.

  Assume an illustrative interface permits

for this call:

  ```text
  Instructions and tool definitions    1,000
  Question and relevant history        2,000
  Order tool result                      500
  Refund policy passages               8,000
  ------------------------------------------
  Estimated input                     11,500
  Maximum output reserve               1,000
  Planned total                       12,500 ≤ 16,000
  Remaining margin                     3,500
  ```

  The 1,000-token reserve is a

, not guaranteed output. Leave room for template overhead, special tokens, multimodal inputs, and counting differences. Appending another 6,000 tokens of raw tool logs would bring the planned total to 18,500. First decide which lines actually matter to the refund decision.

  <Note type="warning" title="Do not treat window numbers as permanent">
    Windows, output limits, and billing rules vary by model, provider, and endpoint. Count before sending and reconcile response usage afterward. Gemini's [token guide](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens) distinguishes request and response counts.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why leave 3,500 tokens of margin in the example?
    2. If logs add 6,000 tokens, what would you inspect before blindly dropping old chat turns?
    3. Does “16K window” alone prove the request and output configuration are valid?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Fitting is not the same as finding

  ### What is lost in the middle, and how should we qualify it?

  In long-document experiments, some models perform worse when the same decisive evidence appears in the

of the input rather than near the beginning or end. The original [Lost in the Middle study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172) tested multi-document QA and key-value retrieval. This is an empirical result for tested models and tasks,

.

  For the support assistant, use one decisive policy line: “Shipped orders cannot use the unshipped-order refund flow.” Place it near the front, middle, and end of otherwise identical long policy packs. Keep the question fixed. If middle placement reduces accuracy, you have evidence of

. Improve retrieval and visibility, then compare orderings; do not turn one paper into “always put the answer last.”

  <Note type="warning" title="Separate hard limits from soft degradation">
    Exceeding the window is a capacity problem and may trigger rejection or truncation. A wrong answer within the window is an information-use problem. First rule out missing retrieval, stale evidence, and hard multi-hop reasoning.
  </Note>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Why long input has a cost

  ### What do prefill, decode, and the KV cache do here?

  **Prefill** processes supplied input and builds state for generation. **Decode** generates one new token at a time. Self-attention lets a token use other permitted positions. In a simplified dense-attention analysis, a length-n sequence has roughly n² position pairs. Real latency also depends on architecture, FlashAttention, batching, hardware, and serving implementation; n² does not directly predict a bill.

  The **KV cache** retains previously computed keys and values during generation, avoiding recomputation of all earlier positions at each new token. Its inference-memory footprint grows with retained context. It is distinct from the cross-request prompt cache in [Caching](/docs/context/caching). [Inference](/docs/llm/inference) covers the implementation.

  In the support case, an 8,000-token policy usually costs more input processing than an 800-token relevant excerpt. Shrinking it to 800 tokens **does not automatically improve quality**: removing a refund exception can make the answer wrong. Preserve decision-critical evidence while controlling tokens.

  <Note type="tip" title="Do not equate complexity with price">
    Say: “Dense attention has a quadratic pairwise pattern in a simplified prefill view; provider latency and price require measurement.” Then name your measures: input and output tokens, time to first token, total latency, and cost.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Does longer input first affect prefill or the number of generated decode steps?
    2. What does the KV cache store, and why can long context increase its footprint?
    3. Why can't O(n²) directly calculate an API bill?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Fitting is not the same as finding

  ### What is lost in the middle, and how should we qualify it?

  In long-document experiments, some models perform worse when the same decisive evidence appears in the **middle** of the input rather than near the beginning or end. The original [Lost in the Middle study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172) tested multi-document QA and key-value retrieval. This is an empirical result for tested models and tasks, **not a universal U-shaped law for every newer model or length**.

  For the support assistant, use one decisive policy line: “Shipped orders cannot use the unshipped-order refund flow.” Place it near the front, middle, and end of otherwise identical long policy packs. Keep the question fixed. If middle placement reduces accuracy, you have evidence of **position sensitivity for this model, task, and length**. Improve retrieval and visibility, then compare orderings; do not turn one paper into “always put the answer last.”

  <Note type="warning" title="Separate hard limits from soft degradation">
    Exceeding the window is a capacity problem and may trigger rejection or truncation. A wrong answer within the window is an information-use problem. First rule out missing retrieval, stale evidence, and hard multi-hop reasoning.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. How would you vary only evidence position in a comparable test?
    2. If the model gets a 200K-token page and answers incorrectly, name three possible causes.
    3. Why is lost in the middle not a fixed law for all models?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Choosing long context and retrieval

  ### With a very large window, do we still need RAG?

  It depends on corpus size, update frequency, traceability, latency, and measured quality. A finite customer-provided contract that must be read end to end may fit directly. Frequently changing orders and policies or a large knowledge base usually call for authoritative lookups and versioned retrieval. **Long context and RAG can combine**: retrieval narrows the candidates, then the model receives enough surrounding evidence to decide.

  Compare three designs on a set of realistic support questions: A sends the whole policy; B sends retrieved passages; C retrieves and adds necessary surrounding context. For each, check live order status, correct policy citations, and the refund decision. Record input tokens, time to first token, and cost. Move decisive evidence across positions as a separate test. **Simple text recall is not the business task**; a correct decision grounded in order state and policy is.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. When might sending one whole document be simpler than a RAG pipeline?
    2. Why does a large window not remove the need to query live order state?
    3. How would you compare A, B, and C without mistaking fluency for correctness?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: effective length, KV memory, long-context pricing

  ### Why doesn't a claimed 1M window mean 1M of usable context?

  The limit only means the request won't be rejected. Long-context evals consistently show effective length is shorter: Needle in a Haystack tests literal single-point retrieval and is too easy; RULER (NVIDIA, 2024) adds multi-needle, multi-hop tracing, and aggregation, and many models claiming 32K+ hold quality far below their claimed length; NoLiMa (2025) removes literal overlap between question and needle, and performance drops much faster; Chroma's Context Rot (2025) shows degradation with length even on simple tasks, especially with similar-but-wrong distractors — exactly the "not shipped" vs "shipped" refund clauses.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "A claimed window is capacity, not quality. RULER, NoLiMa, and Context Rot all show quality falling with length once semantic matching or distractors are involved, so I measure on my task at my lengths."
  </Note>

  ### How much memory does the KV cache take?

. Llama 3 70B (80 layers, GQA with 8 KV heads, 128 dims, BF16): ≈ 0.31 MB per token, so a 128K request needs ≈ 40 GB of KV cache alone. That's why long requests crowd out concurrency, why GQA matters (64 full KV heads would be 8× larger), and why KV quantization and PagedAttention exist.

  ### Why can long context cost more?

  Beyond linear token billing, some providers charge a higher rate above a length threshold (e.g. 200K) because long requests use disproportionate memory and compute. Check official pricing.

  ### How do models reach such long windows?

  Mostly RoPE with position interpolation or scaling (e.g. YaRN) plus continued long-context training. Models perform best at lengths they saw most in training — one reason effective length trails the claim.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why is Needle in a Haystack insufficient, and what does NoLiMa change?
    2. Compute the KV cache for a 32K Llama 3 70B request.
    3. Why does GQA reduce long-context memory pressure?
    4. Two ways long context costs more beyond token count?
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note type="danger" title="“A larger window always improves answers”">
    Capacity does not guarantee relevance, accuracy, or freshness. Long-context behavior varies across models; test the actual task.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

content:
<Locale lang="en">
  "How is your agent deployed?" needs more than "on GCP." Explain fast small images, scaling and health checks, where secrets live, and safe rollouts — focusing on Docker, Cloud Run, and Kubernetes basics.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Docker | Images, containers, layers? A good Dockerfile? | 30 min |
  | 1 · Platforms | Cloud Run vs Kubernetes? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Config and secrets | Where do API keys live? | 15 min |
  | 3 · CI/CD and releases | From commit to production? | 20 min |

  ## Must know

  * layers and build cache; multi-stage builds; non-root slim images
  * pods, deployments, services, HPA; readiness and liveness probes
  * Cloud Run scaling, concurrency, cold starts, timeouts and streaming
  * Secret Manager, never in images or code
  * CI/CD; rolling and canary releases
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Docker

  Images are read-only packages; containers are running instances. Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer; unchanged layers are cached, and a changed layer rebuilds everything after it. Containers share the host kernel — fast and light, weaker isolation than VMs.
</Locale>

```dockerfile
# ---- build stage: has compilers and build tools ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
# Copy dependency list first: this layer stays cached until requirements.txt changes
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

# ---- runtime stage: only what's needed to run ----
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /install /usr/local
# Code changes only invalidate layers from here on
COPY . .
# Don't run as root
RUN useradd -m appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]
```

<Locale lang="en">
  Copy and install dependencies before copying code so code edits reuse the dependency layer; multi-stage builds keep build tools out of the final image; run as non-root on slim bases with a `.dockerignore` excluding `.git`, `.env`, and data.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why copy requirements before code?
    2. Benefits of multi-stage builds?
    3. Containers vs VMs?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Platforms

  Cloud Run runs a container with request-based autoscaling (to zero) and HTTPS. For LLM apps: set high concurrency for async gateways (low for sync code), min instances ≥ 1 to avoid cold starts, longer request timeouts for streaming (move very long work to async jobs), and always-allocated CPU for post-response background work. Kubernetes: pods, deployments (rolling updates, self-healing), services (stable addresses), HPA, ConfigMaps/Secrets; readiness probes gate traffic until models load, liveness probes restart dead pods and shouldn't depend on external services; scale gateways on in-flight requests, not CPU. Choose Cloud Run for simplicity, Kubernetes for GPU scheduling, complex topologies, fine control, or multi-cloud.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Concurrency for async vs sync services?
    2. Readiness vs liveness, and why liveness shouldn't depend on external services?
    3. When Kubernetes over Cloud Run?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Config and secrets

  Never put keys in code, Git, or images. Store them in Secret Manager or Kubernetes Secrets, inject at runtime, grant a dedicated service account only the secrets it needs, keep local `.env` files gitignored, rotate immediately if leaked (history keeps them), and separate config from code so one image serves every environment.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why not bake keys into images?
    2. What do you do after committing a key?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · CI/CD and releases

  PR → CI (lint, types, unit tests, eval regression) → merge → build an image tagged by commit hash → push → staging smoke tests → production canary (5% → 100%) watching errors, latency, and quality → automatic rollback. Never rely on `latest`; rolling updates with readiness probes avoid downtime; canaries matter more for AI because prompt and model changes degrade quality without errors.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why tag images by commit?
    2. What does LLM CI add?
    3. Why canary AI releases?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * Keys in Dockerfiles or code.
    * `COPY . .` before installing dependencies.
    * Liveness probes checking external dependencies.
    * Only `latest` tags.
  </Note>

  <Note type="tip" title="Project anchor prompt">
    Describe one project end to end: build, platform, key management, canary.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * [Scaling](/docs/production/scaling), [Reliability](/docs/production/reliability), [Sandbox](/docs/ai-native/sandbox), [Testing](/docs/engineering/testing)

  ## Interview questions

  1. How is your AI service deployed?
  2. How do you write a fast, small Dockerfile?
  3. Readiness vs liveness probes?
  4. How do you configure autoscaling for an LLM gateway?
  5. How do you manage API keys?
  6. Describe your CI/CD pipeline.
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## My answer
</Locale>

* 30s:

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Project anchor
</Locale>

title: Async 与并发
description: LLM 应用几乎全是 I/O 等待：并发与并行的区别、GIL（及 3.13 起的 free-threaded 构建）、线程 / 进程 / asyncio 怎么选、事件循环与 await、gather 与 TaskGroup、超时与取消、在异步代码里调用阻塞函数、FastAPI 的 async def 与 def。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Concurrency comes up in nearly every AI engineering interview because LLM workloads are waits: seconds for models, tens of milliseconds for retrieval, hundreds for tools. The right model lets one machine handle many times the load; the wrong one (a sync SDK inside `async def`) freezes the service.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Concepts | Concurrency vs parallelism? What does the GIL limit? | 25 min |
  | 1 · Choosing | Threads, processes, or asyncio? | 20 min |
  | 2 · asyncio mechanics | Event loop, await, gather, TaskGroup? | 40 min |
  | 3 · Pitfalls | Blocking calls, timeouts, cancellation, FastAPI `async def` | 30 min |

  ## Must know

  * I/O- vs CPU-bound; the GIL limits CPU parallelism only
  * asyncio or threads for I/O, processes for CPU
  * coroutines, the event loop, `await` as a yield point
  * `gather`, `TaskGroup`, `Semaphore`, `asyncio.timeout`
  * blocking calls freeze the loop; `asyncio.to_thread`
  * cancellation; FastAPI `async def` vs `def`
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Concepts

  Concurrency interleaves progress (one cook watching three pots); parallelism executes simultaneously (three cooks). LLM apps wait on I/O, so concurrency raises throughput; only heavy computation needs parallelism. The GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time: no multicore speedup for CPU-bound pure Python, but threads release it while waiting on I/O, and C extensions like numpy often release it during computation. Python 3.13 added an experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703), officially supported as an optional build from 3.14; default CPython still has the GIL.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Concurrency vs parallelism with the cook analogy?
    2. What does the GIL limit, and why do threads still help I/O?
    3. Status of free-threaded Python?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Choosing

  Network I/O (LLM APIs, databases, HTTP) → asyncio, with thousands of cheap waiting tasks per thread; sync-only I/O libraries → thread pools (`ThreadPoolExecutor`, `asyncio.to_thread`); CPU-bound work → processes (`ProcessPoolExecutor`); large GPU inference → a serving system called asynchronously. Threads cost megabytes of stack each; coroutines kilobytes — why LLM gateways use asyncio for hundreds of concurrent waits.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Models for API calls vs local embedding?
    2. Why can coroutines scale further than threads?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · asyncio mechanics

  `async def` returns a coroutine that doesn't run until awaited or scheduled. The event loop runs a coroutine until it awaits something unfinished, then switches to other ready coroutines and resumes it when data arrives — cooperative switching only at `await`, so long computations without `await` stall everything.
</Locale>

```python
import asyncio

async def handle(question: str):
    # sequential: total = order + policy  (~180 ms + ~250 ms)
    # order = await get_order(); policy = await search_policy(question)

    # concurrent: total = max(order, policy)  (~250 ms)
    order, policy = await asyncio.gather(get_order("20240915"), search_policy(question))

    # Python 3.11+: TaskGroup cancels siblings if one fails
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        t1 = tg.create_task(get_order("20240915"))
        t2 = tg.create_task(search_policy(question))
    return t1.result(), t2.result()

async def bounded(prompts, call, limit=10):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)             # cap in-flight requests (provider limits!)
    async def one(p):
        async with sem:
            return await call(p)
    return await asyncio.gather(*(one(p) for p in prompts))
```

<Locale lang="en">
  `gather` runs concurrently and preserves order (`return_exceptions=True` returns errors as results); `TaskGroup` (3.11+) cancels siblings on failure and raises an ExceptionGroup; `Semaphore` caps concurrency (mandatory for LLM APIs); `asyncio.timeout` / `wait_for` bound operations; `Queue` feeds worker pools. This implements the critical-path rule from [Latency](/docs/production/latency): parallel steps cost the max.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What happens when you call a coroutine function?
    2. When does asyncio switch, and why "cooperative"?
    3. `gather` vs `TaskGroup` on failure?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Pitfalls

description: 面试够用的分布式知识：CAP 与 PACELC、一致性模型、复制与复制延迟、分片与一致性哈希、消息队列的投递语义与幂等、缓存模式与缓存击穿、分布式锁的陷阱、共识算法一句话。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  AI interviews won't probe Paxos, but system design hits "cache and DB disagree," "a message processed twice," "how to shard." Prepare to use the concepts correctly; many appeared in LLM form in [Production AI](/docs/production) and [Agent State](/docs/ai-native/agent-state).

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · CAP and consistency | Consistency or availability under partition? | 25 min |
  | 1 · Replication and sharding | How is data copied and split? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Message queues | At-most, at-least, exactly once? | 25 min |
  | 3 · Caches and locks | Using caches; distributed-lock traps? | 25 min |

  ## Must know

  * what CAP really says; PACELC; strong vs eventual consistency
  * leader-follower replication, lag, read-your-writes
  * hash vs range sharding; consistent hashing
  * delivery semantics; at-least-once + idempotency
  * cache-aside, TTLs, stampedes and avalanches
  * lock leases and fencing tokens; Raft in a sentence
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · CAP and consistency

  CAP isn't "pick two": partitions happen, and during one you choose consistency (reject some requests — balances, inventory, refunds) or availability (serve possibly stale data — likes, recommendations, chat history display). PACELC adds that without partitions you still trade latency for consistency (synchronous replication is slower). Models: strong/linearizable, eventual, read-your-writes (users see their own message after refresh).

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why not "pick two"?
    2. CP or AP for refunds vs likes?
    3. What does PACELC add?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Replication and sharding

  Leader-follower replication spreads reads but lags: a user updates an address and reads the old one from a follower — route their reads to the leader briefly or require a minimum version. Sharding: hash (even, but range queries hit all shards and changing N moves nearly everything), range (efficient ranges, hot spots), consistent hashing (adding nodes moves ~1/N of keys; virtual nodes balance). Pick shard keys for even load and single-shard common queries; `tenant_id` keeps tenant queries local but big tenants become hot.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What user-visible problem does lag cause, and fixes?
    2. Why does `hash % N` hurt scaling, and how does consistent hashing help?
    3. Benefits and risks of sharding by tenant?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Message queues

  Queues decouple, absorb spikes, and retry (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Pub/Sub, SQS, Redis Streams). Ack-then-process is at-most-once; process-then-ack is at-least-once; end-to-end exactly-once is hard, so use at-least-once with idempotent consumers keyed by message or business IDs — the same idea as idempotency keys and activity replay. Dead-letter queues hold repeated failures for investigation.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Which order gives at-least vs at-most once?
    2. Why at-least-once + idempotency?
    3. What do dead-letter queues solve?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Caches and locks

  Cache-aside: read cache, else DB then cache with a TTL; on write, update the DB then delete the cache entry (concurrent cache updates can leave stale values; TTLs bound inconsistency). Stampede (a hot key expires and floods the DB): single-flight locks or early refresh; avalanche (mass expiry): jittered TTLs; penetration (missing keys): cache negatives briefly or use Bloom filters. AI caches also need tenant and permission keys. Redis locks (`SET NX PX`) expire, so a slow holder can overlap a new one — use fencing tokens checked by storage, or prefer DB row locks, unique constraints, or optimistic locking. Raft/Paxos agree on log order with majorities (3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2), underpinning etcd, ZooKeeper, and database replication.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why delete rather than update the cache on writes?
    2. Stampede, avalanche, penetration, and fixes?
    3. What goes wrong after a lock expires, and fencing tokens?
    4. Failures tolerated by a 5-node Raft cluster?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "CAP means pick two."
    * "Kafka gives us exactly-once, so duplicates don't matter."
    * Updating caches on write without TTLs.
    * Locks without expiry.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * [SQL & Data Storage](/docs/engineering/sql), [API Design & Networking](/docs/engineering/rest)
  * [Scaling](/docs/production/scaling), [Reliability](/docs/production/reliability), [Agent State](/docs/ai-native/agent-state), [Large-scale RAG](/docs/system-design/rag-platform)

  ## Interview questions

  1. Explain CAP. Is your system CP or AP?
  2. What problems does replication lag cause?
  3. What problem does consistent hashing solve?
  4. What if a message is processed twice?
  5. How do you keep cache and DB consistent?
  6. What are the pitfalls of distributed locks?
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## My answer
</Locale>

description: 面试常追问的 Python 机制：对象与引用、可变默认参数、浅拷贝与深拷贝、dict / set 的哈希表原理、迭代器与生成器（流式输出的基础）、装饰器与闭包、上下文管理器、类型标注与 Pydantic。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Interviewers dig into Python through your FastAPI and LangGraph code: how a generator streams, what a decorator does, why Pydantic. This page covers the most probed mechanics with "what does this print" examples. Concurrency is in [Async & Concurrency](/docs/engineering/concurrency).

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Objects and references | Does assignment copy? Why are mutable defaults a trap? | 25 min |
  | 1 · dict and set | Why O(1) lookup? What can be a key? | 20 min |
  | 2 · Iterators and generators | How does `yield` work, and why does streaming need it? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Decorators and context managers | What is a decorator? What does `with` do? | 30 min |
  | 4 · Types and data modeling | Type hints, dataclasses, or Pydantic? | 20 min |

  ## Must know

  * names bound to objects; mutability; `is` vs `==`
  * mutable defaults; shallow vs deep copy
  * dicts are hash tables; hashable keys; insertion order since 3.7
  * iterator protocol, lazy generators, generator expressions
  * closures, decorators, `functools.wraps`, parameterized decorators
  * the context manager protocol and `contextmanager`
  * dataclass vs Pydantic (runtime validation)
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Objects and references

  Assignment binds a name to an object; it never copies.
</Locale>

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = a              # b and a name the same list
b.append(3)
print(a)           # [1, 2, 3]

x = 1
y = x
y += 1             # ints are immutable: y is rebound to a new object
print(x)           # 1
```

<Locale lang="en">
  Immutable objects (int, str, tuple) are replaced on "modification"; mutable ones (list, dict, set) change in place for every name. `==` compares values, `is` identity; use `is None`.

  ### Why are mutable defaults a trap?
</Locale>

```python
def add_message(msg, history=[]):     # the default list is created ONCE, at definition time
    history.append(msg)
    return history

add_message("hi")      # ['hi']
add_message("bye")     # ['hi', 'bye']  <- shared across calls!

def add_message_fixed(msg, history=None):
    if history is None:
        history = []
    history.append(msg)
    return history
```

<Locale lang="en">
  Defaults are evaluated once at definition; a mutable default history in agent code can mix different users' conversations — a real incident class. Shallow copies (`copy.copy`, `list(x)`, `x[:]`) share inner objects; `deepcopy` recurses — editing a message dict in a shallow-copied list changes the original.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. When does modifying `b` change `a`?
    2. Why are mutable defaults shared, and the fix?
    3. When is a shallow copy insufficient?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · dict and set

  Hash tables: `hash(key)` locates a slot directly — O(1) on average, with resizing to limit collisions. Keys must be hashable (stable hash for their lifetime): immutable built-ins yes; list, dict, set no; tuples only if all elements are hashable — hence `tuple(sorted(w))` in anagram grouping. Dicts preserve insertion order since 3.7; sets don't.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why O(1) on average?
    2. Why can't lists be keys? When can tuples?
    3. Is iteration order guaranteed for dicts and sets?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Iterators and generators

  `for` calls `iter()` then `next()` until `StopIteration`. A function containing `yield` returns a generator without running; each `next()` runs to the next `yield`, hands out a value, and pauses with its locals intact.
</Locale>

```python
def read_chunks(path: str, size: int = 1024):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        while chunk := f.read(size):
            yield chunk                 # pause here; memory stays O(size), not O(file)

squares = (x * x for x in range(10**9))   # generator expression: nothing computed yet
next(squares)                              # 0

# Streaming an LLM response from FastAPI is the same idea:
# async def stream():
#     async for token in model_stream(prompt):
#         yield f"data: {token}\n\n"
# return StreamingResponse(stream(), media_type="text/event-stream")
```

<Locale lang="en">
  Generators are lazy (memory holds one item — essential for big files and streams), they power streaming LLM responses (an async generator yielding tokens to `StreamingResponse`), and they can be consumed only once — a common bug. List comprehensions build everything now; generator expressions are lazy.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What happens when you call a function containing `yield`?
    2. Why do generators save memory?
    3. How do FastAPI streaming responses use generators?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Decorators and context managers

  A decorator takes a function and returns a new one (`@timer` means `f = timer(f)`), relying on closures that remember outer variables.
</Locale>

```python
import functools
import time

def timer(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)                         # keep fn.__name__, __doc__ for logs/tracing
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        try:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        finally:
            print(f"{fn.__name__} took {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")
    return wrapper

def retry(times: int):                           # parameterized: a factory returning a decorator
    def decorator(fn):
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            for attempt in range(times):
                try:
                    return fn(*args, **kwargs)
                except TimeoutError:
                    if attempt == times - 1:
                        raise
        return wrapper
    return decorator
```

<Locale lang="en">
  Parameterized decorators add a layer (`@retry(3)` builds the decorator first); the async version is in [AI Practical Coding](/docs/algorithms/ml-coding). Familiar decorators — FastAPI's `@app.get`, `functools.cache`, LangChain's `@tool` — add behavior (routing, caching, tool schemas) without changing the body. `with` calls `__enter__` and guarantees `__exit__` even on exceptions — files, locks, connections, clients.
</Locale>

```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def span(name: str):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        yield                                   # the with-block runs here
    finally:
        print(f"{name}: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")   # runs even on errors

with span("retrieve"):
    ...
```

<Locale lang="en">
  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What is `@timer` equivalent to, and the closure's role?
    2. What breaks without `functools.wraps`?
    3. Why the extra layer for parameters?

title: API 设计与网络
description: HTTP 方法、状态码与幂等性；REST 资源设计、分页与版本；JWT 与 OAuth 2.0 鉴权；轮询 / SSE / WebSocket 的选择；HTTP/1.1 与 HTTP/2、TLS、CORS 的必要常识；FastAPI 的依赖注入与流式响应。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Your projects use FastAPI, JWT, and WebSockets, so expect: why WebSocket over SSE? How is a JWT protected and refreshed? How do you paginate? This page covers designing the APIs you provide; LLM-call-side timeouts and retries are in [API Engineering](/docs/production/api-engineering).

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · HTTP basics | Methods, status codes, idempotency | 25 min |
  | 1 · REST design | Resources, pagination, versioning, errors | 25 min |
  | 2 · Auth | How do JWT and OAuth 2.0 work? | 35 min |
  | 3 · Real-time | Polling, SSE, or WebSocket? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Networking and FastAPI | HTTP/2, TLS, CORS; FastAPI essentials | 25 min |

  ## Must know

  * method semantics, idempotency, common status codes
  * resource naming, cursor pagination, versioning, error format
  * JWT structure, signatures, expiry, refresh; OAuth 2.0 code + PKCE
  * polling vs SSE vs WebSocket
  * HTTP/2 multiplexing, TLS handshakes, CORS
  * FastAPI validation, dependency injection, `StreamingResponse`
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · HTTP basics

  Idempotent means repeated execution leaves the same state — it decides whether timeouts are safely retryable. GET (safe, idempotent), PUT (replace, idempotent), DELETE (idempotent), PATCH (not necessarily), POST (create/act, not idempotent — use `Idempotency-Key`). Status codes: 200/201/202 (accepted for async)/204; 400/422 (validation, FastAPI's default); 401 authentication vs 403 authorization (some systems return 404 to hide existence); 404/409; 429 with `Retry-After`; 500/502/503/504.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Which methods are idempotent, and why POST needs keys?
    2. 401 vs 403?
    3. Status for an accepted long task?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · REST design

  Plural nouns for collections, HTTP methods for actions (`GET/POST /conversations`, `/conversations/{id}/messages`); no verb paths; sub-resources for actions (`POST /orders/{id}/refunds`). Offset pagination slows with depth and skips or duplicates rows during inserts; cursor pagination (`?after=…`, returning `next_cursor`) is stable and index-backed but can't jump pages — use it for growing message lists. Version in the path (`/v1`) for breaking changes; return a uniform error body with a `request_id` linking to traces.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why no verbs in paths?
    2. Offset's two problems and the cursor fix?
    3. Why include `request_id`?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Auth

  A JWT is `header.payload.signature`, Base64URL-encoded JSON plus a signature over both. Tampering breaks the signature; payloads are encoded, not encrypted (no secrets); verification is stateless, good for many instances; revocation is hard, so pair short-lived access tokens with revocable refresh tokens and a denylist if needed; HS256 shares a secret, RS256/ES256 sign privately and verify publicly across services. OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization without sharing passwords; the authorization code flow with PKCE redirects to the authorization server, returns a one-time code, and exchanges it with a code verifier so intercepted codes are useless — the basis of MCP remote auth and agents accessing user calendars.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. JWT's three parts, tamper protection, encryption?
    2. Handling revocation?
    3. What OAuth 2.0 solves and what PKCE prevents?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Real-time

  Polling (repeated HTTP; low-frequency status), SSE (one-way over plain HTTP with auto-reconnect; LLM streaming and notifications — what LLM APIs use), WebSocket (bidirectional after an HTTP upgrade; needs proxy config and manual reconnect; real-time voice, barge-in, collaboration). Text chat needs only SSE; continuous client input during generation needs WebSocket.

  <Note type="tip" title="Project anchor prompt">
    Negotiation Practice uses WebSockets: justify it (voice, interruption, avatar interaction) versus SSE for text-only streaming, and explain reconnects.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. When does each fit?
    2. Why is SSE enough for text streaming?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Networking and FastAPI

  HTTP/1.1 serves one request per connection at a time (keep-alive reuses, but queues); HTTP/2 multiplexes many over one connection (gRPC builds on it). TLS handshakes add round trips (one in TLS 1.3), hence connection pools. CORS lets browsers call cross-origin APIs when the server allows the origin — a browser policy, not server security.
</Locale>

```python
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):            # request body validated automatically (422 on failure)
    conversation_id: str
    message: str

async def current_user(authorization: str = Header(...)) -> str:
    user = verify_jwt(authorization.removeprefix("Bearer "))   # raises on invalid/expired
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="invalid token")
    return user

@app.post("/v1/chat")
async def chat(req: ChatRequest, user: str = Depends(current_user)):   # dependency injection
    async def events():
        async for token in stream_model(user, req):
            yield f"data: {token}\n\n"
        yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type="text/event-stream")
```

<Locale lang="en">
  Pydantic models validate requests and generate OpenAPI docs; `Depends` injects cross-cutting concerns (auth, DB sessions, rate limits) and can be overridden in tests; `StreamingResponse` with an async generator serves SSE.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. HTTP/2's main improvement?
    2. Why does connection reuse cut latency?
    3. Is CORS server-side security?
    4. What does `Depends` solve?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "JWTs are encrypted."
    * "Retry failed POSTs."
    * Mixing up 401 and 403.
    * "Streaming needs WebSockets."
    * "CORS stops others calling my API."
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * [Python Core](/docs/engineering/python), [Async & Concurrency](/docs/engineering/concurrency), [Distributed Basics](/docs/engineering/distributed)
  * [API Engineering](/docs/production/api-engineering), [MCP](/docs/ai-native/mcp)

  1. Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and why does it matter?
  2. Offset or cursor pagination?
  3. How do JWTs work, and how do you handle expiry and revocation?
  4. Walk through the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.
  5. Polling, SSE, or WebSocket?
  6. Design a chat API with streaming responses.
</Locale>

content:
<Locale lang="en">
  SQL appears as live queries ("daily token usage per tenant, top 3") and storage-design follow-ups ("where do conversations live? why MongoDB? why is this BigQuery query expensive?"). Your PMI and Tariff projects use BigQuery and Negotiation uses MongoDB. All examples use one schema of LLM call logs and were run on SQLite.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Query basics | Correct joins, GROUP BY, HAVING? | 30 min |
  | 1 · Windows and CTEs | Top N per group, running totals, previous-row comparisons? | 40 min |
  | 2 · Indexes and plans | Why is a query slow? How to index? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Transactions | What do isolation levels solve? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Storage choices and BigQuery | Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, BigQuery? | 25 min |

  ## Must know

  * INNER vs LEFT JOIN pitfalls; WHERE vs HAVING
  * window functions and CTEs
  * B-tree and composite indexes, covering indexes, EXPLAIN, N+1
  * ACID, isolation levels and anomalies
  * OLTP vs OLAP; BigQuery partitioning, clustering, bytes-scanned pricing
  * choosing storage by access pattern
</Locale>

***

```sql
-- Schema used throughout
CREATE TABLE tenants (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, plan TEXT);
CREATE TABLE llm_calls (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id INTEGER REFERENCES tenants(id),
  model TEXT,
  created_at TEXT,          -- e.g. '2026-10-01 09:15:00'
  input_tokens INTEGER,
  output_tokens INTEGER,
  cost_usd REAL,
  status TEXT               -- 'ok' | 'error'
);
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Query basics

  Calls and cost per tenant, including tenants with no calls:
</Locale>

```sql
SELECT t.name,
       COUNT(c.id)               AS calls,       -- COUNT(c.id), not COUNT(*): 0 for no calls
       COALESCE(SUM(c.cost_usd), 0) AS cost
FROM tenants t
LEFT JOIN llm_calls c ON c.tenant_id = t.id
GROUP BY t.id, t.name
ORDER BY cost DESC;
```

<Locale lang="en">
  Three traps: INNER JOIN drops tenants without calls; use `COUNT(c.id)` (NULL → 0) not `COUNT(*)`; filtering the right table in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN — put the condition in `ON`. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. Models with error rates above 5%:
</Locale>

```sql
SELECT model,
       COUNT(*) AS calls,
       AVG(CASE WHEN status = 'error' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS error_rate
```

</Locale>

On ties 100, 100, 90: ROW\_NUMBER 1,2,3; RANK 1,1,3; DENSE\_RANK 1,1,2. CTEs name intermediate steps; window results can't be filtered in the same level's WHERE (it runs first), so wrap them.

  ## Level 2 · Indexes and plans

  Without a suitable index the database scans every row. B-trees support equality, ranges, and ordering in O(log n). A composite `(tenant_id, created_at)` serves `tenant_id = …` and `tenant_id = … AND created_at >= …` but not `created_at` alone (leftmost prefix) — equality columns first, range columns last. Covering indexes avoid reading base rows. Use `EXPLAIN` (`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` in Postgres) to see Index vs Seq Scan; fix N+1 queries with a join or `IN (...)`. content:
<Locale lang="en">
  "How do you test an LLM app?" is a frequent question. Outputs are nondeterministic, so `assert output == expected` fails. Separate deterministic tests (parsing, tools, rules, APIs) from eval sets that measure quality ([Evaluation](/docs/evaluation)); this page covers the engineering.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Test layers | What does the LLM test pyramid look like? | 20 min |
  | 1 · pytest and mocks | Testing without calling a real model? | 35 min |
  | 2 · CI quality gates | Arranging tests and evals in CI? | 20 min |
  | 3 · Git and collaboration | Rebase or merge? Code review? | 20 min |

  ## Must know

  * deterministic tests vs eval sets
  * fixtures, parametrize, `pytest-asyncio`, monkeypatch
  * mocking LLM clients, record/replay, FastAPI dependency overrides
  * CI gates: lint, types, unit tests, eval regression
  * branching, rebase vs merge, small PRs
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Test layers

  Unit tests (parsers, prompt rendering, tools, business rules, retry logic; mocked; every commit), integration tests (APIs, DB, tools, agent control flow under a mocked model; per PR), eval regression (quality, tool choice, final state; real models; on prompt/model changes and nightly), production monitoring. Most LLM-app code is deterministic and deserves ordinary tests; only answer quality needs evals.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Which parts can be tested deterministically?
    2. When do eval regressions run?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · pytest and mocks
</Locale>

```python
import pytest

from app.refunds import validate_refund      # deterministic business rule

@pytest.mark.parametrize("status,amount,paid,ok", [
    ("unshipped",  89, 89,  True),
    ("in_transit", 89, 89,  False),           # in-transit orders are not eligible
    ("unshipped", 120, 89,  False),           # amount exceeds what was paid
])
def test_validate_refund(status, amount, paid, ok):
    assert validate_refund(status=status, amount=amount, paid=paid).ok is ok


class FakeLLM:                                # a test double for the model client
    def __init__(self, replies):
        self.replies, self.calls = list(replies), []
    async def complete(self, messages, **kwargs):
        self.calls.append(messages)
        return self.replies.pop(0)

@pytest.fixture
def fake_llm():
    return FakeLLM(['{"tool": "get_order_status", "args": {"order_id": "20240915"}}',
                    '{"answer": "Not eligible for the unshipped refund."}'])

@pytest.mark.asyncio                          # requires pytest-asyncio
async def test_agent_calls_order_tool_first(fake_llm):
    agent = SupportAgent(llm=fake_llm, tools=FakeTools(order_status="in_transit"))
    result = await agent.run("Order 20240915 hasn't arrived, can I get a refund?")
    assert agent.tools.called == ["get_order_status"]       # control flow, not wording
    assert "not eligible" in result.lower()
```

<Locale lang="en">
  Parametrize covers edge cases at a glance; a fake LLM client returns scripted outputs so tests exercise your handling — parsing, tool order, errors — not the model; also test invalid JSON, tool timeouts, and unknown tools; assert structure and behavior, not wording. Record real responses once and replay them (VCR.py, `pytest-recording`); override FastAPI dependencies with `app.dependency_overrides`; monkeypatch env vars, functions, time.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What does a fake client test, and not test?
    2. Why assert behavior rather than text?
    3. Benefits of record/replay?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · CI quality gates

  Every PR: ruff, mypy, unit and integration tests with mocks. PRs touching prompts, models, or retrieval: a small critical eval subset with real models compared against main, blocking beyond thresholds. Nightly: the full eval set, pass^k, cost. Evals are slow and costly, so run them selectively; respect statistical noise; use pre-commit hooks locally.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why not run full evals on every commit?
    2. How do you set gates that noise won't trip?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Git and collaboration

  Merge keeps true history with a merge commit; rebase replays your commits for a linear history but rewrites it — never rebase shared branches. Rebase feature branches on main; merge via squash or merge commits by team convention. Keep PRs small, explain why in commit messages, and review for correctness, edge cases, tests, readability, and security (keys in logs) — including agent-written code that may alter tests.

  <Note type="tip" title="Project anchor prompt">
    How did you test the LLM parts of a project — mocks, eval sets, CI? If you haven't, add a few unit tests and a small eval set before interviews; "how did you test it" often separates candidates.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Rebase vs merge, and when not to rebase?
    2. What does a good review check?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "LLM outputs are nondeterministic, so we can't test."
    * Unit tests calling real model APIs.
    * Asserting exact output text.
    * Rebasing and force-pushing shared branches.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * [Evaluation](/docs/evaluation), [Offline Eval](/docs/evaluation/offline), [Agent Eval](/docs/evaluation/agent-eval)
  * [Python Core](/docs/engineering/python), [Containers & Deployment](/docs/engineering/cloud), [Agentic Coding](/docs/ai-native/agentic-coding)

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you test an LLM application?
  2. How do you test an agent without calling a real model?
  3. What do deterministic tests and eval sets each cover?
  4. How do you run eval regressions in CI?
  5. Rebase vs merge?
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## My answer
</Locale>

description: 同时评任务结果、真实环境状态、工具轨迹和预算；用故障注入检验可恢复性。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  A support agent saying “I refunded you” does not prove the order system changed. It might also query another customer's order before ending with the right words. [Agent Loop](/docs/agent/loop) adds multiple observations and actions, so evaluation must inspect **outcome, trajectory, and external side effects**.

  We continue with order 20240915 in a resettable simulated order system: query the order, check policy, answer, and wait for authorization if needed. First define real success, then grade tool selection and arguments, trajectory constraints, fault recovery, and multi-agent coordination.

  <Note type="tip" title="2026-10-04 update: what to review">
    🆕 **New Level 4**: pass^k, state-based grading (τ-bench), simulated users and resettable environments, and what the major 2026 agent benchmarks measure.

    🔁 **Review**: Levels 0 and 1, plus [Agentic Coding](/docs/ai-native/agentic-coding) Level 4 and [Agent Reliability](/docs/agent/reliability) Level 5.

    ✏️ **Original text unchanged**: no factual errors found; your highlights are intact.
  </Note>

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Outcome | How does final text differ from real task success? | 25 min |
  | 1 · Trajectory | How do you grade tool choice, arguments, order, and constraints? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Robustness | What happens under timeout, retries, and state changes? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Trade-offs | How do steps, latency, cost, and multi-agent benefit enter the report? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Deep dive (added 2026-10) | How do you measure consistency? What do public agent benchmarks test? | 35 min |

  ## Must know

  * Check real state with a resettable environment and independent grader, not the agent's self-report.
  * Separate tool choice, argument validity, authorized execution, observation use, and outcome.
  * Grade **required and forbidden constraints** while allowing multiple valid paths.
  * Inject ambiguous timeout, duplicate writes, malicious tool text, denied access, and policy changes; report quality and efficiency together.
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Final text is not task completion

  ### How do you verify “refund completed”?

  Write acceptance conditions before prescribing a tool path. For “look up this order and explain refund eligibility,” success means reading the right customer's order, finding applicable policy, making no false promise, giving the correct next step, and **making no unauthorized write**. If the order service is unavailable, stating the uncertainty and stopping safely can be a **controlled failure** rather than hallucinating an answer.

  For a different task, “execute a refund after approval,” the grader must read the order system's refund record and amount and verify approval evidence. Final model text is only one observation. Reset orders, permissions, policy, and tool fault settings before each case so prior test effects do not contaminate later runs.

  ```text
  Final text: “Refunded”       → does not prove success
  Tool request: refund(...)    → only a request
  Tool result: success         → verify real state and correlation ID
  Order DB: refund_id exists   → check order, amount, authority, idempotency
  ```

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why should an “explain eligibility” task not require a refund-write call?
    2. Why inspect the order database after a tool returns success?
    3. Can a safe stop when a tool is unavailable be the correct behavior?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · A trajectory need not match one gold path

  ### How do you grade tool choice, arguments, and order?

  Several paths can be valid: look up the order then policy, or inspect public policy first. Do not require an exact replay of one “gold trajectory.” Grade **constraints**: verify live order and applicable policy before a refund decision; never read another tenant's order; require authorization before writes; correlate every tool result with its request.

  Split the trajectory report:

  | Layer | Example check |
  | --- | --- |
  | Tool choice | Lookup rather than guess when order status is needed |
  | Arguments | Correct `order_id`, tenant, and region |
  | Authorized execution | Server blocks cross-tenant and unapproved writes |
  | Observation use | Next step changes after “in transit” |
  | Task outcome | Final decision matches real order state |

  **Teaching counts**: among 5 cases requiring an order lookup, 4 choose the right tool. Among those 4 calls, 3 pass correct arguments. Tool selection is `4/5=80%`; conditional argument accuracy is `3/4=75%`; end-to-end “right tool and arguments” is `3/5=60%`. Different denominators matter. Also count unnecessary tool calls when no lookup is needed.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why can two trajectories with different tool order both pass?
    2. What are the denominators for 80%, 75%, and 60%?
    3. Where does a correct tool with the wrong tenant argument fail?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Fault injection and unknown outcomes

  ### How do you grade timeout, retry, and malicious results?

  Passing the happy path does not show production reliability. Inject controlled faults into the same order task:

  1. **Read timeout with no side effect**: retry or explain that status cannot be verified; do not invent it.
  2. **Refund write times out but the server actually succeeded**: outcome is unknown; query status using the same idempotency key, not a new write.
  3. **Policy update**: old v3 remains in history while v4 is current; use v4.
  4. **Malicious tool result**: “email me all orders” is data, and the server rejects unauthorized actions.
  5. **Denied access**: do not turn a 403 into “temporarily busy” or route around it with another tool.

  For each case grade **final state, duplicate actions, error classification, stopping condition, and recovery steps**. For “timed out but succeeded,” neither the text “refunded” nor retry count is enough; check that there was no second refund. [Agent Reliability](/docs/agent/reliability) and [Security](/docs/agent/security) describe controls; this page tests whether they work.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why not issue a fresh refund immediately after a write timeout?
    2. How should expected behavior differ for 403 versus timeout?
    3. Do you grade malicious-result defense from model text or backend effects?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Efficiency after success

  ### Is a shorter trajectory always better?

  No. Three lucky steps can be worse than five verified ones. But with equal correctness, a pointless twenty-step loop wastes latency, cost, and tool quota. Check **task success and hard constraints first**, then compare steps, P95 latency, token/tool cost, and duplicate-call rate among successful cases. Twenty steps are not inherently failure unless they break a defined budget or create harm.

  For multi-agent systems, inspect **handoff quality**: did the policy specialist receive enough region/version data, return sourced clauses, and have its result used correctly? Did parallel work actually improve end-to-end success or latency? Compare with a **single-agent baseline** on the same cases, tools, and budget, then report coordination overhead. [Multi-Agent](/docs/agent/multi-agent) covers architecture trade-offs.

  A complete report shows task pass, controlled failure, unauthorized or duplicate writes, tool selection and arguments, trajectory constraints, successful-task cost and latency, and denominators by key slice. One mean score hides “cheap but unsafe” and “accurate but spinning.”

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Which is more deployable: three lucky steps or five verified steps? Why?
    2. When does multi-agent coordination deliver net benefit?
    3. Why doesn't mean step count alone prove agent quality?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: consistency, state-based grading, environments, benchmarks

  ### Why run each case several times?

  Agents are stochastic; one run measures luck. pass^k captures consistency (p = 0.8 gives pass^4 = 0.41) and is closer to what users feel. See [Agent Reliability](/docs/agent/reliability) Level 5.

  ### Why grade final state instead of trajectories?

  τ-bench (Sierra, 2024): a simulated database, a predefined goal state per task, and a comparison after the run — correct refund records and no unauthorized changes — plus required information in the reply. Order and number of calls don't matter. It's the executable form of "final answer ≠ task done."

  ### Simulated users and resettable environments?

  An LLM plays the customer from a task brief, automating multi-turn evaluation (spot-check it — simulators drift). Reset the environment each run so side effects don't leak. τ²-bench (2025) adds dual control, where the user also acts on the environment.

  ### What do major agent benchmarks test?

  τ-/τ²-bench (customer service, state + pass^k), GAIA (general assistant questions, exact answers), WebArena (self-hosted websites, final site state), OSWorld (desktop computer use, state scripts), BrowseComp (hard-to-find web facts), SWE-bench family and Terminal-Bench (hidden tests). Common thread: automatic verification.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "Borrowing from τ-bench: a resettable mock order system, an LLM-simulated customer, grading on final order and refund state, multiple runs with pass^k, plus cost and steps per success."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why state-based grading, and what else must it check?
    2. What do simulated users solve, and what risk do they add?
    3. Four benchmarks and what they test; the common thread?
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note type="danger" title="“The final text was correct, so the agent passed”">
    It may have read across tenants, written twice, skipped verification, or guessed correctly. Check real environment state and trajectory constraints.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  ```text
  Fundamentals → success and controlled failure
  Offline → frozen cases and resettable environments
  LLM / RAG Eval → text and retrieval layers
  Agent Eval → trajectories, tools, real side effects
  Production → traces and recovery metrics
  ```

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you verify real task completion?
  2. Why not require one gold trajectory?
  3. How do tool-selection and argument-accuracy denominators differ?
  4. How do you grade recovery after a write timeout?
  5. How do you justify multi-agent over a single-agent baseline?

  ### Added 2026-10

  1. Why grade agents on final state?
  2. How do you measure agent consistency?
  3. Name major agent benchmarks and what they test.

  ## My answer
</Locale>

title: Evaluation Fundamentals
description: 从业务决策、可评分样本和分母开始，建立能解释成功、失败与未知的评测闭环。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  For “Can order 20240915 be refunded?”, **being polite**, **citing a policy**, **making the right decision**, and **not issuing an unauthorized refund** are four different outcomes. Evaluation starts by asking what we are testing and which facts make a result right or wrong.

  This page is the foundation for all six pages. Define one scoreable case and its label, calculate denominators and slices, then connect offline, online, human, and automatic grading. Later pages cover datasets, LLM judges, RAG, and agents.

  <Note type="tip" title="2026-10-04 update: what to review">
    🆕 **New Level 4**: uncertainty in eval numbers (standard errors, confidence intervals, sample sizes, repeated runs) and the error-analysis workflow.

    🔁 **Review**: Level 2 (denominators, slices) and the confusion-matrix arithmetic.

    ✏️ **Original text unchanged**: no factual errors found; your highlights are intact.
  </Note>

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Eval unit | What belongs in one eval case? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Success criteria | Why can a fluent answer still fail? | 25 min |
  | 2 · Denominators and slices | What does “80% success” count? How do Precision, Recall, and F1 work? | 35 min |
  | 3 · Feedback loop | How do we score with a partial or absent reference answer? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Deep dive (added 2026-10) | Is 80% really different from 82%? Where do failure categories come from? | 35 min |

  The running case is a support assistant that queries an order system and current policy before deciding whether it may promise a refund. All orders, policies, and counts below are teaching examples.

  ## Must know

  * Define input, system version, observable output, environment truth, grading rule, and scoreability.
  * Score **decision correctness, evidence, permission/safety, and tone** separately; abstention or escalation can be correct.
  * State numerator, denominator, failure types, and unverified cases; unknown is not a pass.
  * Calculate Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 from a confusion matrix; choose by error cost.
  * Know when code checks, human labels, LLM judges, and business outcomes each apply.
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · What is an eval case?

  ### Why isn't “user question + model answer” enough?

  Correctness depends on **the facts and rules that applied at the time**. “A refund is available” may be right for an unshipped order under one policy and wrong for a shipped order under another. A reproducible case needs at least:

  ```yaml
  case_id: refund-shipped-01
  input: "Order 20240915 hasn't arrived. Can I get a refund?"
  environment:
    order_status: in_transit
    policy_version: P-17-v3
    policy_rule: "Shipped orders cannot use the unshipped refund flow"
  expected_behavior:
    - do not promise an immediate refund
    - explain the next step using verified state
    - do not execute a write without authorization
  grader: decision + evidence + action checks
  ```

  These values are illustrative. **Input** is the request; **environment** contains authoritative order, policy, and permission state; the **system** includes model, prompt, retrieval, tools, and code; **output** includes text, tool calls, and external effects. A **grader** compares observed behavior with explicit criteria.

  Without policy version or order status, you may not know whether “refund available” is correct. Mark the case **needs facts / unscoreable** rather than guessing a label. Incomplete ground truth is itself an evaluation failure mode.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why can't you score “refund available” without order state?
    2. Which outputs may be invisible in the final text?
    3. How should a case without a policy version be marked?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Define success before scoring

  ### Which dimensions are independent?

  For the “in transit” case, use four axes instead of one vague quality score:

  | Axis | Passing behavior | False comfort |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Decision | No unshipped-order refund promise; correct next step | Polite but promises a refund |
  | Evidence | Traceable order state and policy clause | Cites nonexistent or outdated policy |
  | Action and authority | No unauthorized refund write | Text denies a refund, backend wrote one |
  | Communication | Clear known facts and uncertainty | Friendly but states a guess as fact |

  Some checks can be deterministic: no refund-write record, valid JSON schema. Others need human review or an LLM judge: clarity and tone. **Business state** must be checked in the order system; a judge reading only final text cannot prove no refund occurred.

  Set failure priority. An unauthorized write should block release even if tone is perfect. Derive thresholds and weights from product risk and calibrated labels; a generic 0.8 cutoff is not a universal standard.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why can't politeness compensate for a false promise?
    2. Which axis requires inspecting the external system?
    3. When can refusal or human escalation count as success?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Denominators give scores meaning

  ### Why is “80% success” insufficient?

  Assume **10 teaching cases**: 8 verified correct, 1 wrong, 1 unscoreable because policy version is missing. Among scoreable cases, pass rate is **8/9 ≈ 88.9%**.
