title: Evaluation
description: Eval 已经不是 RAG 专属。从 golden set 到线上回归，才是 AI Engineer 思维。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Evaluation asks more than “do we have a score?” It asks **which real tasks became more reliable, which risks remain unverified, and which layer failed**. All six pages follow one cat-food support refund case in dependency order: Fundamentals → Offline → LLM → RAG → Agent → Production.

  <CardGrid>
    <Card title="Fundamentals" description="Scoreable cases, success criteria, denominators, and unknowns." href="/docs/evaluation/fundamentals" />

    <Card title="Offline Eval" description="Golden sets, label governance, paired comparisons, release gates." href="/docs/evaluation/offline" />

    <Card title="LLM Evaluation" description="Judge multi-turn dialogue quality by dimension, compare pairs, calibrate with people." href="/docs/evaluation/llm-eval" />

    <Card title="RAG Evaluation" description="Calculate retrieval metrics; separate finding, supplying, using, and answering." href="/docs/evaluation/rag-eval" />

    <Card title="Agent Evaluation" description="Real state, tool trajectories, fault recovery, and cost." href="/docs/evaluation/agent-eval" />

    <Card title="Production Eval" description="Traces, pending outcomes, controlled rollouts, incident regressions." href="/docs/evaluation/production-eval" />
  </CardGrid>

  For concrete metrics, start with [Fundamentals Level 2](/docs/evaluation/fundamentals) for confusion matrices, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, and denominators. [LLM Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/llm-eval) grades multi-turn dialogue quality by dimension, calculates pairwise win rate, and audits judge misses. [RAG Evaluation Levels 1–2](/docs/evaluation/rag-eval) covers Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR, nDCG, and groundedness. [Agent Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/agent-eval) measures task state, tool use, and side effects. [Production Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/production-eval) separates verified pass rate, coverage, and pending outcomes. For similarly named metrics, state the **unit, positive class, ground truth, denominator, and cost of mistakes**.

  ## What you should be able to do

  1. Define input, environment truth, expected behavior, and scoreability for a support decision; explain the denominator.
  2. Build an offline set with common traffic and risky edges; compare fixes and regressions case by case.
  3. Choose graders for open text, calibrate judges with people, and calculate retrieval metrics.
  4. Verify real agent state and trajectory under timeout, denied access, and duplicate writes.
  5. Use production traces, mature outcomes, and controlled rollout to turn failures into labeled regressions.

  ## October 2026 review guide

  You've finished this section. On 2026-10-04 each page gained a deep-dive level; original text is unchanged and your highlights and MyQuestion entries remain. Each page's green note lists exactly what to learn and review.

  | Priority | Page → new content |
  | --- | --- |
  | 🔴 Must learn | All six Level 4s, starting with [Fundamentals](/docs/evaluation/fundamentals) (confidence intervals, error analysis) |
</Locale>

title: LLM Evaluation
description: 给开放式回答选择合适 grader：确定性检查、语义方法、rubric、成对比较与人工校准。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Many phrasings can correctly explain one refund decision. Exact string matching rejects good answers, but asking a judge model whether a response “looks good” may let a false promise through. **Choose a grader for the property being tested.**

  Following [Fundamentals](/docs/evaluation/fundamentals) and [Offline](/docs/evaluation/offline), start with deterministic checks, understand semantic measures, use an anchored LLM judge to score multi-turn dialogue by dimension, compare pairs, then calibrate against human labels. The running case is the reply for order 20240915.

  <Note type="tip" title="2026-10-04 update: what to review">
    🆕 **New Level 4**: Cohen's kappa on Level 3's table, judge-bias mitigations, LMArena and Bradley-Terry ratings, the 2026 benchmark landscape.

    🔁 **Review**: Level 3 (calibration) and Level 2 (pairwise bias).

    ✏️ **Original text unchanged**: no factual errors found; your highlights are intact.
  </Note>

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Method matching | When do exact, overlap, semantic, and rule checks apply? | 25 min |
  | 1 · Judge | How do you score multi-turn conversation quality by dimension? | 40 min |
  | 2 · Pairwise | Which A/B answer is better, and what biases matter? | 25 min |
  | 3 · Calibration | How do you measure and correct disagreement with people? | 30 min |
  | 4 · Deep dive (added 2026-10) | What's left of 70% agreement after chance? Which public benchmarks matter now? | 35 min |

  ## Must know

  * Know what exact match, BLEU/ROUGE, and embedding similarity measure; similarity is not factual correctness.
  * Give judges one observable dimension, input, evidence, rubric, output schema, and an uncertainty option.
  * Separate relevance, completeness, context consistency, grounding, instruction following, uncertainty, and communication; report per-dimension pass rates and hard failures.
  * Blind pairwise comparison, swap answer order, allow ties; validate any claim of stability on the task.
  * Check false passes against human labels, pin judge versions, and monitor drift and grading cost.
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Pick the right ruler

  ### Why not use only exact match or embedding similarity?

  For a structured target such as `decision=not_eligible_for_unshipped_refund`, **exact match** is useful. To check “do not call the refund write tool,” inspect the actual tool trace or database state. Both are more direct than asking a judge model to infer what happened.

  **BLEU/ROUGE** measure text or n-gram overlap with a reference; they say little about business correctness. **Embedding similarity** measures semantic closeness and may rate “refundable” and “not refundable” similarly because the topic is almost identical except for negation. Human review or an LLM judge fits more open properties such as clarity and explanation completeness.

  Split one answer into checks:

  ```text
  Reply: “The order is in transit; under P-17 it cannot use the
          unshipped refund flow. Please follow the return process.”
  Decision field          → rule / exact match
  Actually in transit?    → order system and query time
  Policy citation valid?  → current versioned clause
  Explanation clear?      → human or rubric judge
  Refund executed?        → write-operation record
  ```

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. When is exact match the best choice?
    2. Why can semantic similarity mislead on a single negation?
    3. How do you prove no refund was executed without asking a judge to guess?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Write an auditable judge

  ### How does a rubric turn “good answer?” into criteria?

  Ask a judge to assess one axis, such as “is the refund decision supported?” Supply the **question, verified order and policy evidence, candidate reply, and criteria**:

  ```text
  Input: question + verified order state + current policy + candidate reply
  Output: {verdict: pass|fail|uncertain, cited_claims: [...], reason: ...}
  pass: no promise conflicting with state/policy; explain basis and next step
  fail: promise forbidden refund, invent status, or cite obsolete policy
  uncertain: decisive evidence missing or conflicting
  ```

  `pass|fail|uncertain` is illustrative notation; an implementation should use a real enum schema. Ask for specific claims and evidence so humans can audit decisions, but a judge's explanation can also be wrong. Compare it with source traces. Pin test inputs, judge model, and rubric version; otherwise score changes may reflect a changed ruler.

  Do not collapse axes with different risks into one 1–5 score. Grade decision, evidence, and tone separately, and treat critical errors as hard failures. The judge also needs sufficient evidence: without order state it cannot reliably decide eligibility.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why provide current policy instead of only the candidate reply?
    2. How is `uncertain` different from `fail`?
    3. Why can't new-rubric scores be directly compared to old ones?
  </Note>

  ### Which metrics should a judge use for multi-turn quality?

  Define the **evaluation unit** first. To grade the latest assistant turn, supply the user and assistant turns up to that point, applicable policy, and tool results already observed. To grade the whole dialogue, include state changes across turns and the final outcome. A last reply alone cannot reveal context tracking, and later customer feedback must not be leaked into a turn-level grade.

  This is an **example task-specific rubric**, not a universal metric standard. Score each dimension separately as `2=met`, `1=partly met`, or `0=failed`. Use `N/A` when the dimension does not apply and `unknown` with human review when evidence is insufficient. Adapt the anchors to the task and risk.

  | Conversation-quality dimension | Observable 2-point behavior here | Typical 0-point failure |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Relevance / helpfulness | Answers the current refund question with an actionable next step | Avoids the question with generic apologies |
  | Completeness | Explains verified state, applicable constraint, and next step; asks for missing decisive facts | Omits a region or policy condition that changes the decision |
  | Context consistency | Uses the supplied order and region; updates the decision after a correction | Reasks for known facts or keeps relying on corrected stale state |
  | Grounding / correctness | Key claims match current order and policy evidence; decision matches authoritative state | Invents “refund completed” or promises a refund under obsolete policy |
  | Instruction following / boundaries | Explains authority limits under support rules; does not expose other orders | Bypasses identity verification or promises an unauthorized action on user request |
  | Uncertainty / clarification | Asks only for decisive missing facts and says a decision is pending | Declares eligibility confidently without checking the order |
  | Clarity / tone | Explains limits and next steps concisely and respectfully to a worried customer | Blames the customer, pads with boilerplate, or hides uncertainty behind reassurance |

  Suppose the customer already supplied order ID and region and said the package is in transit; the system verified `in_transit` and policy `P-17-v3`. Candidate A sounds empathetic but says “I refunded you”: communication may score well, but **facts/authority hard-fail**. Candidate B correctly rejects the unshipped refund path but asks for the order ID again and gives no next step: factuality passes while context consistency and completeness suffer. Require a score per dimension, the triggering dialogue span, and evidence IDs. Verify order state and actual refund writes with tools or database checks, not the judge's confident wording.

  Report a **per-dimension pass rate** = `score-2 conversations / applicable conversations with sufficient evidence`, alongside `N/A`, `unknown`, and the `0/1/2` distribution. A **whole-dialogue quality pass rate** = `conversations meeting every required dimension with no hard failure / scoreable conversations`. Do not average dimension scores and call it “80% quality”: politeness cannot offset a false refund promise. A judge produces a **rubric grade**, not a verified customer-resolution rate; the latter belongs in [Production Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/production-eval). The mix of dimension-specific rubrics, independent state checks, and human calibration follows [Anthropic's conversational-agent eval example](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) and [OpenAI's eval guidance](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices).

  <Note title="Self-check: multi-turn quality">
    1. The user supplied an order ID, but the assistant asks again. Which dimension loses credit?
    2. Why can empathetic candidate A not pass through an average score after claiming a false refund?
    3. What external evidence is needed before accepting a judge's claim that the issue was resolved?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Pairwise comparison and bias

  ### How do you ask whether A is better than B fairly?

  If both A and B make the correct refund decision but differ in explanation, pairwise comparison asks a judge to choose under the **same question, evidence, and criteria**. It can be easier to discriminate than assigning two abstract 1–5 scores, but is not bias-free. Blind the names, swap display order, and allow **ties** or “insufficient evidence.”

  Example: A gets the decision right in 30 words but omits the next step; B explains it in 120 words. B may win for completeness. If B also invents “free returns,” it should fail despite length and confidence. LLM judges can exhibit **position, verbosity, style, and model-family biases**; their sizes vary by task and model. [MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)

  Do not use preference voting to establish whether an unauthorized write occurred. Pairwise grading suits expression quality or overall preference, while factual and safety constraints deserve direct checks.

  Define the denominator of **pairwise win rate**. On 20 matched dialogues under the same evidence and budget, suppose A wins 8, B wins 7, and 5 tie. A's strict win rate is `8/20=40%`; among non-ties it is `8/15≈53.3%`; with a predeclared half point per tie it is `(8+0.5×5)/20=52.5%`. These are different metrics. Report the raw win/loss/tie counts, tie convention, and how many judgments flip after swapping positions. A preference win cannot override a factual hard failure.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why judge again after swapping A and B?
    2. Why must a longer B that invents free returns not win?
    3. Which metrics should not rely on pairwise preference alone?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Calibrate against people

  ### How do you quantify “the judge mostly agrees with experts”?

  On **10 teaching cases**, experts mark 6 pass and 4 fail. The judge confusion table is:

  | | Human pass | Human fail |
  | --- | ---: | ---: |
  | Judge pass | 5 | 2 |
  | Judge fail | 1 | 2 |

  Agreement is `(5+2)/10 = 70%`. More concerning, **false-pass rate among human failures is 2/4 = 50%**. Ten cases illustrate the arithmetic, not a stable population estimate. If the two false passes are unauthorized refunds, the judge cannot be the only release gate.

  Apply the [Fundamentals confusion matrix](/docs/evaluation/fundamentals) with **“detect a failure” as the positive class**: TP=2 (human fail, judge fail), FP=1 (human pass, judge fail), FN=2 (human fail, judge pass), TN=5. The judge's failure-detection **Precision=`2/(2+1)=66.7%`, Recall=`2/(2+2)=50%`, and F1=`2×2/(2×2+1+2)≈57.1%`**. Its 50% failure Recall corresponds to the 50% false-pass rate above: both divide by the four human failures. Name the positive class in an interview; treating “pass” as positive gives different Precision and Recall from the same table.

  Calibrate by ① expert-labeling sliced cases and resolving disputes; ② reviewing case-level disagreements, especially false passes; ③ changing rubric, evidence, threshold, or using deterministic checks; ④ retesting on cases **not used to tune the judge**; and ⑤ sampling audits after version changes. Look for systematic errors across languages, order states, and answer lengths.

  <Note type="danger" title="Do not let a judge validate itself">
    Using one judge to create labels, tune its rubric, and report “agreement” with those labels is circular. High-consequence decisions need independent people or authoritative systems.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What are agreement and false-pass rates in the table?
    2. Why is 70% agreement insufficient for a refund safety gate?
    3. Why use a fresh holdout after editing the rubric?
    4. With “detect failure” as positive, what are the judge's Precision, Recall, and F1?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: kappa, judge bias, Arena, benchmarks

  ### Why correct 70% agreement for chance?

  Cohen's kappa = (observed − expected) / (1 − expected). Level 3's table: humans 6 pass / 4 fail, judge 7 pass / 3 fail; expected chance agreement = 0.6×0.7 + 0.4×0.3 = 0.54; kappa = 0.16 / 0.46 ≈ 0.35 — only "fair," consistent with the 50% false-pass rate. Kappa matters most with imbalanced labels.

  ### Mitigating judge bias?

  Position: evaluate both orders, treat disagreement as a tie or review. Verbosity: rubric says length earns nothing. Self-preference: judge from a different model family or ensemble. Confident-but-wrong: give reference facts and check evidence first. Scale drift: binary or few-level rubrics with anchors. Binary + specific rubric + reasoning before verdict beats 1–10 scores.

  ### LMArena?

  Formerly Chatbot Arena: anonymous pairwise user votes converted into Bradley-Terry ratings (Elo-like). It reflects open-chat preference but is style-sensitive (hence style-controlled rankings), and *The Leaderboard Illusion* (2025) argued private pre-release testing of variants biases it. It isn't your task accuracy.

  ### Which public benchmarks matter in 2026?

  Saturated: MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval. Knowledge/reasoning: GPQA Diamond, Humanity's Last Exam. Coding/agents: SWE-bench Verified/Pro, Terminal-Bench. Tool use: τ-/τ²-bench. Abstraction: ARC-AGI-2. Benchmarks saturate and get contaminated; use them to shortlist, then decide on private evals.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Compute kappa from Level 3's table.
    2. Four judge biases and fixes?
    3. How does LMArena score models, and its limits?
    4. Why is MMLU uninformative now?
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  ```text
  Fundamentals → target property and truth
  Offline → expert labels and holdout
  LLM Evaluation → graders for open text
  RAG / Agent → retrieval- and trajectory-specific grading
  ```

  ## Interview questions

  1. When do exact match, BLEU/ROUGE, embeddings, and judges fit?
  2. What belongs in a usable rubric?
  3. Why swap answer order in pairwise grading?
  4. How do you calculate a judge's false-pass rate?
  5. When is an LLM judge insufficient alone?
  6. Which dimensions and denominators would you report for multi-turn conversation quality?
  7. A wins 8, B wins 7, and 5 tie. What is A's win rate under your tie rule?

  ### Added 2026-10

  1. What is Cohen's kappa, and why isn't raw agreement enough?
  2. What biases do LLM judges have, and how do you mitigate them?
  3. What does an LMArena ranking tell you, and not?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

* 30s:
* 2min:

</Locale>

</Locale>

  ### How does a rubric turn “good answer?” into criteria?

  Ask a judge to assess one axis, such as “is the refund decision supported?” Supply the **question, verified order and policy evidence, candidate reply, and criteria**:

  Input: question + verified order state + current policy + candidate reply
  Output: {verdict: pass|fail|uncertain, cited_claims: [...], reason: ...}
  pass: no promise conflicting with state/policy; explain basis and next step
  fail: promise forbidden refund, invent status, or cite obsolete policy
  uncertain: decisive evidence missing or conflicting

is illustrative notation; an implementation should use a real enum schema. Ask for specific claims and evidence so humans can audit decisions, but a judge's explanation can also be wrong.   Do not collapse axes with different risks into one 1–5 score. Grade decision, evidence, and tone separately, and treat critical errors as hard failures. The judge also needs sufficient evidence: without order state it cannot reliably decide eligibility.

To grade the whole dialogue, include state changes across turns and the final outcome. A last reply alone cannot reveal context tracking, and later customer feedback must not be leaked into a turn-level grade.

  | Grounding / correctness | Key claims match current order and policy evidence; decision matches authoritative state | Invents “refund completed” or promises a refund under obsolete policy |

  Example: A gets the decision right in 30 words but omits the next step; B explains it in 120 words. B may win for completeness. If B also invents “free returns,” it should fail despite length and confidence. LLM judges can exhibit **position, verbosity, style, and model-family biases**; their sizes vary by task and model.   ## Level 3 · Calibrate against people

  ### How do you quantify “the judge mostly agrees with experts”?

  On **10 teaching cases**, experts mark 6 pass and 4 fail. The judge confusion table is:

  | | Human pass | Human fail |
  | --- | ---: | ---: |
  | Judge pass | 5 | 2 |
  | Judge fail | 1 | 2 |

  Agreement is

. More concerning, **false-pass rate among human failures is 2/4 = 50%**. Ten cases illustrate the arithmetic, not a stable population estimate. If the two false passes are unauthorized refunds, the judge cannot be the only release gate.

  Apply the [Fundamentals confusion matrix](/docs/evaluation/fundamentals) with **“detect a failure” as the positive class**: TP=2 (human fail, judge fail), FP=1 (human pass, judge fail), FN=2 (human fail, judge pass), TN=5. The judge's failure-detection **Precision=

**. Its 50% failure Recall corresponds to the 50% false-pass rate above: both divide by the four human failures. Name the positive class in an interview; treating “pass” as positive gives different Precision and Recall from the same table.

  Calibrate by ① expert-labeling sliced cases and resolving disputes; ② reviewing case-level disagreements, especially false passes; ③ changing rubric, evidence, threshold, or using deterministic checks; ④ retesting on cases **not used to tune the judge**; and ⑤ sampling audits after version changes. Look for systematic errors across languages, order states, and answer lengths.

  <Note type="danger" title="Do not let a judge validate itself">
    Using one judge to create labels, tune its rubric, and report “agreement” with those labels is circular. High-consequence decisions need independent people or authoritative systems.
  </Note>

    1. What are agreement and false-pass rates in the table?
    2. Why is 70% agreement insufficient for a refund safety gate?
    3. Why use a fresh holdout after editing the rubric?
    4. With “detect failure” as positive, what are the judge's Precision, Recall, and F1?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: kappa, judge bias, Arena, benchmarks

  ### Why correct 70% agreement for chance?

  Cohen's kappa = (observed − expected) / (1 − expected). Level 3's table: humans 6 pass / 4 fail, judge 7 pass / 3 fail; expected chance agreement = 0.6×0.7 + 0.4×0.3 = 0.54; kappa = 0.16 / 0.46 ≈ 0.35 — only "fair," consistent with the 50% false-pass rate. Kappa matters most with imbalanced labels.

  ### Mitigating judge bias?

  Position: evaluate both orders, treat disagreement as a tie or review. Verbosity: rubric says length earns nothing. Self-preference: judge from a different model family or ensemble. Confident-but-wrong: give reference facts and check evidence first. Scale drift: binary or few-level rubrics with anchors. Binary + specific rubric + reasoning before verdict beats 1–10 scores.

  ### LMArena?

  Formerly Chatbot Arena: anonymous pairwise user votes converted into Bradley-Terry ratings (Elo-like). It reflects open-chat preference but is style-sensitive (hence style-controlled rankings), and *The Leaderboard Illusion* (2025) argued private pre-release testing of variants biases it. It isn't your task accuracy.

  ### Which public benchmarks matter in 2026?

  Saturated: MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval. Knowledge/reasoning: GPQA Diamond, Humanity's Last Exam. Coding/agents: SWE-bench Verified/Pro, Terminal-Bench. Tool use: τ-/τ²-bench. Abstraction: ARC-AGI-2. Benchmarks saturate and get contaminated; use them to shortlist, then decide on private evals.

    1. Compute kappa from Level 3's table.
    2. Four judge biases and fixes?
    3. How does LMArena score models, and its limits?
    4. Why is MMLU uninformative now?
  </Note>

  ## Connections

title: Offline Evaluation
description: 构建覆盖故障模式的 golden set，用固定环境、配对比较和发布门槛验证改动。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  [Fundamentals](/docs/evaluation/fundamentals) defined one scoreable support case. Now turn cases into an **offline dataset** that compares system versions repeatedly. If you collect only easy “unshipped order, clear policy” examples, a new model can improve aggregate score while failing shipped-order exceptions, tenant boundaries, or tool timeouts.

  This page covers dataset construction, labels, paired comparisons, release gates, and leakage for the same support case. Real randomized traffic splitting belongs in [Production Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/production-eval). Offline A/B means two versions on the **same cases and environment**, not an online experiment.

  <Note type="tip" title="2026-10-04 update: what to review">
    🆕 **New Level 4**: significance for paired comparisons (McNemar, bootstrap), synthetic eval data, keeping eval sets healthy.

    🔁 **Review**: Level 2 (paired comparison) and [Fundamentals](/docs/evaluation/fundamentals) Level 4 first.

    ✏️ **Original text unchanged**: no factual errors found; your highlights are intact.
  </Note>

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Dataset | What makes a golden set representative of the task and its risks? | 25 min |
  | 1 · Labels | Who annotates, and how are disagreements, versions, and contamination handled? | 25 min |
  | 2 · Comparison | How do A and B run fairly on the same cases? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Gates | What blocks release, and how do you avoid overfitting? | 30 min |
  | 4 · Deep dive (added 2026-10) | Is B really better than A, or noise? How do you build synthetic data? | 35 min |

  ## Must know

  * Separate representative traffic, rare high-risk cases, and incident regressions; report each denominator.
  * Freeze input, environment truth, policy, and grader versions; have domain experts resolve ambiguous labels.
  * Compare versions on paired cases and inspect both fixes and regressions.
  * Set hard gates for critical constraints and softer quality gates; keep development and untouched holdout splits.
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Build data that exposes failures

  ### How should a golden dataset be sampled?

  “Golden” means trustworthy expected behavior and provenance, not necessarily one exact reference sentence. Start with task and risk slices:

  | Slice | Example | Why |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Common path | Unshipped and currently refundable | Represents normal demand |
  | Business exception | Shipped but customer says “not arrived” | Tests delivery-versus-shipment distinction |
  | Missing information | No order ID or region | Tests clarification and abstention |
  | Tool failure | Order API timeout or no policy result | Tests controlled failure |
  | Permission and safety | Someone else's order or malicious document | Tests boundaries |
  | Incident regression | A real previous failure | Prevents recurrence |

  Sources include deidentified production traces, expert-created edge cases, historical incidents, and synthetic variants. Synthetic cases add coverage but need realism checks and should not silently dominate the denominator. Track source, scenario version, language, policy version, and sampling method.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why can random common traffic miss critical failures?
    2. Why can't an all-hard-cases set represent the overall product?
    3. Must a golden set contain exact reference sentences?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Labels need quality control

  ### Who labels correctness, and how do you avoid truth drift?

  Whether an order qualifies under policy is domain logic. A subject-matter expert should confirm it; an engineer supplies tool traces but cannot infer policy correctness from fluency. Store `case_id`, source order state, policy ID/version/effective date, expected decision, permitted action, refusal condition, and annotator. **Freeze a simulated environment** for repeatable runs rather than querying one live order forever as its status changes.

  For disputed cases, use independent labels followed by adjudication and retain disagreement reasons. When policy changes, either bind old cases to v3 for regression or relabel them for v4; do not silently change truth while retaining old scores. Mark unscoreable cases `needs_review`, not pass or fail.

  Leakage can arise when eval orders are copied into examples or training, near-duplicate questions from one customer appear in development and holdout, or developers repeatedly inspect holdout errors while tuning prompts. Split and deduplicate by customer/event or policy version; restrict holdout exposure. Public benchmarks add breadth, but private business cases validate the actual task.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why is one live production order a poor permanent label?
    2. How do you handle cases when policy v3 becomes v4?
    3. What happens if near-duplicates from one customer span development and holdout?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Compare paired cases

  ### How do you calculate an offline A/B comparison without trusting the mean blindly?

  Freeze **10 teaching cases**, a simulated order database, policy snapshot, grader, and call budget. Version A passes 6; B passes 8. But case-level comparison shows B fixes 3 while regressing on 1 “must not issue an unauthorized refund” case. Net change is `(+3 - 1) / 10 = +20 percentage points`. That single regression may trip a hard safety gate.

  ```text
  Same cases      A pass, B pass    5
                  A fail, B pass    3  ← fixes
                  A pass, B fail    1  ← regression
                  A fail, B fail    1
  Total           A 6/10           B 8/10
  ```

  Ten cases illustrate paired arithmetic; they are **not enough to claim population improvement**. Real comparisons should report numerator/denominator by slice, the difference, and uncertainty. Small differences need more independent cases or confidence intervals. Repeated generations for one case reveal model variance but are not independent user examples.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why freeze the environment, not only the user question?
    2. Why might B be blocked despite two more passes?
    3. Can +20 points on ten cases be extrapolated to all users?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Regression gates and holdout

  ### What should block release?

  Tie gates to product risk, not “ship whenever the average rises.” An illustrative release contract:

  ```text
  Hard: zero cross-tenant leaks and unauthorized refund writes in the test set;
        no regression on critical policy exceptions
  Quality: decision correctness on labeled cases at least matches baseline
  Operations: P95 latency and cost per case within agreed budgets
  Review: inspect new failures, judge disagreement, unscoreable cases
  ```

  “Zero” means **zero observed in this test set**, not proven zero population risk; scale sample size with risk. Put a small fast set in CI for smoke and hard constraints, a larger frozen regression set at release, and an untouched holdout to check overfitting. For failures, inspect case-level traces to locate retrieval, context, model, tool, or policy changes.

  Public benchmarks compare broad capability; private sets test business behavior. Neither replaces the other. After offline gates, use controlled shadow/canary or a true online A/B to test user impact in [Production Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/production-eval).

  <Note type="warning" title="A CI score is not a product outcome">
    Offline data cannot cover every policy update, real user phrasing, or environment fault. Passing a gate controls known risks to a degree; it does not end observation after release.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why does zero observed leaks not prove zero leak probability?
    2. What do the CI small set, release regression set, and holdout each do?
    3. If offline improves but online worsens, which distribution shifts do you inspect?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: significance, synthetic data, maintenance

  ### Is B really better than A?

  Only discordant cases carry information. With 200 cases, b = 8 (A right, B wrong) and c = 18 (A wrong, B right): A 79%, B 84%. McNemar: `(|b − c| − 1)² / (b + c) = 81/26 ≈ 3.12 < 3.84` at α = 0.05 — not yet significant, because only 26 cases changed. A paired bootstrap (resample cases 1,000 times, take the 2.5th–97.5th percentile of the difference) works for any metric; a CI excluding 0 means significant.

  ### How do you build synthetic eval data?

  Define dimensions (order state × intent × difficulty × phrasing), cover high-risk cells, generate a few per cell, human-check realism and labels, dedupe and filter. It fills edge cases; it doesn't replace production samples.

  ### How do you keep the set healthy?

  Add incidents and new failure categories; limit holdout exposure and rebuild it periodically (Goodhart's law); version the eval set and compare models on the same version.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. McNemar for b = 5, c = 20?
    2. Why only discordant pairs?
    3. Steps of a paired bootstrap?
    4. How to generate synthetic data, and its risk?
    5. Why does peeking at the holdout ruin it?
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  ```text
  Fundamentals → scoreable cases
  Offline → frozen data, paired comparison, release gates
  Production → real traffic and failure feedback
  ```

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you build a golden set that covers traffic and risky edges?
  2. How do you prevent label drift after policy changes?
  3. Why might you block B despite 8/10 versus 6/10?
  4. How do you avoid overfitting the eval set?
  5. How does offline comparison differ from an online A/B test?

  ### Added 2026-10

  1. How do you show an improvement isn't noise?
  2. How do you build synthetic eval data, and what are the risks?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

  ## Level 0 · Build data that exposes failures

  ### How should a golden dataset be sampled?

  “Golden” means trustworthy expected behavior and provenance, not necessarily one exact reference sentence. Start with task and risk slices:

  | Slice | Example | Why |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Common path | Unshipped and currently refundable | Represents normal demand |
  | Business exception | Shipped but customer says “not arrived” | Tests delivery-versus-shipment distinction |
  | Missing information | No order ID or region | Tests clarification and abstention |
  | Tool failure | Order API timeout or no policy result | Tests controlled failure |
  | Permission and safety | Someone else's order or malicious document | Tests boundaries |
  | Incident regression | A real previous failure | Prevents recurrence |

  Sources include deidentified production traces, expert-created edge cases, historical incidents, and synthetic variants. Synthetic cases add coverage but need realism checks and should not silently dominate the denominator. Track source, scenario version, language, policy version, and sampling method.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why can random common traffic miss critical failures?
    2. Why can't an all-hard-cases set represent the overall product?
    3. Must a golden set contain exact reference sentences?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Compare paired cases

  ### How do you calculate an offline A/B comparison without trusting the mean blindly?

  Freeze

But case-level comparison shows B fixes 3 while regressing on 1 “must not issue an unauthorized refund” case. Net change is `(+3 - 1) / 10 = +20 percentage points`. That single regression may trip a hard safety gate.

  ```text
  Same cases      A pass, B pass    5
                  A fail, B pass    3  ← fixes
                  A pass, B fail    1  ← regression
                  A fail, B fail    1
  Total           A 6/10           B 8/10
  ```

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Regression gates and holdout

  ### What should block release?

  Tie gates to product risk, not “ship whenever the average rises.” An illustrative release contract:

text
  Hard: zero cross-tenant leaks and unauthorized refund writes in the test set;
        no regression on critical policy exceptions
  Quality: decision correctness on labeled cases at least matches baseline
  Operations: P95 latency and cost per case within agreed budgets
  Review: inspect new failures, judge disagreement, unscoreable cases

“Zero” means **zero observed in this test set**, not proven zero population risk; scale sample size with risk. Put a small fast set in CI for smoke and hard constraints, a larger frozen regression set at release, and an untouched holdout to check overfitting. For failures, inspect case-level traces to locate retrieval, context, model, tool, or policy changes.

  Public benchmarks compare broad capability; private sets test business behavior. Neither replaces the other. After offline gates, use controlled shadow/canary or a true online A/B to test user impact in [Production Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/production-eval).

  <Note type="warning" title="A CI score is not a product outcome">
    Offline data cannot cover every policy update, real user phrasing, or environment fault. Passing a gate controls known risks to a degree; it does not end observation after release.
  </Note>

    1. Why does zero observed leaks not prove zero leak probability?
    2. What do the CI small set, release regression set, and holdout each do?

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: significance, synthetic data, maintenance

  ### Is B really better than A?

  Only discordant cases carry information. With 200 cases, b = 8 (A right, B wrong) and c = 18 (A wrong, B right): A 79%, B 84%. McNemar:

at α = 0.05 — not yet significant, because only 26 cases changed. A paired bootstrap (resample cases 1,000 times, take the 2.5th–97.5th percentile of the difference) works for any metric; a CI excluding 0 means significant.

  ### How do you build synthetic eval data?

  Define dimensions (order state × intent × difficulty × phrasing), cover high-risk cells, generate a few per cell, human-check realism and labels, dedupe and filter. It fills edge cases; it doesn't replace production samples.

  ### How do you keep the set healthy?

  Add incidents and new failure categories; limit holdout exposure and rebuild it periodically (Goodhart's law); version the eval set and compare models on the same version.

<Locale lang="en">
  An offline golden set blocks known failures, but production brings new policies, real user wording, tool faults, and delayed outcomes. Mature evaluation means **knowing which online behavior is verified, which still awaits truth, and how to turn new failures into reproducible tests**.

  This page connects the previous five through the same cat-food support case: traces, online sampling and denominators, shadow/canary/A/B, and an incident in which the assistant falsely promises a refund.

  <Note type="tip" title="2026-10-04 update: what to review">
    🆕 **New Level 4**: A/B sample sizes, guardrail vs primary metrics, SRM checks, novelty effects, sync guardrails vs async online evals.

    🔁 **Review**: Level 2 and your two MyQuestion answers; see also rewritten [Observability](/docs/production/observability) and [Reliability](/docs/production/reliability) Level 4.

    ✏️ **Original text unchanged**: no factual errors found; your highlights are intact.
  </Note>

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Observability | What belongs in a replayable AI trace? | 25 min |
  | 1 · Online scoring | Which production cases can be scored, and which must wait? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Rollout | What do shadow, canary, and A/B each establish? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Feedback loop | How does an incident become a regression without chasing only recent failures? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Deep dive (added 2026-10) | How much traffic does an A/B test need? How do guardrails and online evals split work? | 30 min |

  ## Must know

  * Correlate request, config version, retrieval IDs, tool calls/results, business state, and final reply while protecting sensitive data.
  * Separate live proxies, sampled human/judge labels, and delayed business outcomes; report denominators, pending, and unscoreable.
  * Shadow avoids real side effects, canary limits exposure, and A/B estimates real user impact.
  * Preserve incident evidence, expert-label it, freeze a test environment, add regression, and maintain representative/holdout data.
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · A trace should answer “what changed?”

  ### What does a support trace minimally record?

  Use a correlation ID across the request:

  ```text
  request_id / tenant_scope / time
  model + prompt + tool-schema + policy/index versions
  task category and allowed actions
  retrieval query → candidate IDs/ranks → selected context IDs
  tool name, normalized arguments, call ID, result/status, duration
  final decision, cited clauses, reply
  verified order/refund state and human approval if any
  token usage, latency, errors, fallback
  ```

  Raw messages, orders, and identity data are sensitive. Apply minimization, redaction, access control, retention limits, and auditability. If raw text cannot be retained, keep linkable versions, source IDs, error types, and an authorized review path. A **trace records observable facts, not hidden chain-of-thought**; model text saying “I thought it through” is not tool-execution evidence.

  These fields let you distinguish old-policy retrieval, correct-policy omission, failed evidence use, and stale order-tool state. A final reply alone cannot do that.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why are prompt and final response insufficient to diagnose RAG failures?
    2. Why correlate a tool request and result with a call ID?
    3. Without sensitive raw text, what audit information should remain?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Online metrics must state what is verified

  ### How do you report success when outcomes have not matured?

  Customers may confirm resolution days after the support reply. Counting those requests as immediate success treats a **pending outcome** as truth. Monitor deterministic proxies now: unauthorized writes, tool errors, output schema, citation existence. Sample human or calibrated-judge reviews for explanation quality. Count business resolution after order or customer feedback matures.

  An illustrative production window samples **100 cases**: 70 verified pass, 10 verified fail, and 20 awaiting order/customer outcome. Pass rate among scored cases is `70/80 = 87.5%`; verification coverage is `80/100 = 80%`; 20% remain pending. If pending cases are mostly complex complaints, 87.5% may be selected upward and cannot be presented as full-traffic success.

  Slice by policy version, language, order state, tool fault, and customer segment. Report sampling fraction, filtering rules, and human-review backlog. Silently dropping unlabeled cases makes the system appear better over time. Alert on observable violations or suspicious traces, then review them; an uncalibrated judge score is not absolute truth.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. How do you report 70 pass, 10 fail, and 20 pending?
    2. Why could 87.5% be optimistic if pending cases are complex?
    3. How do immediate proxies differ from delayed business KPIs?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Validate progressively after release

  ### What do shadow, canary, and online A/B each establish?

  **Shadow / replay** runs a new version on historical or mirrored requests without showing its output to users; write tools must be disabled, simulated, or isolated. It compares quality and cost but cannot prove real user response. **Canary** sends a small fraction of real requests to the new version and watches errors, latency, and unauthorized-action signals with stop and rollback rules. **A/B** randomly assigns a stable unit such as user or session to versions and estimates real impact under specified outcomes and guardrails; avoid a customer switching versions across turns.

  For refund support, a primary outcome may be evidence-backed real issue resolution. Guardrails include false promises, unauthorized writes, escalation rate, latency, and cost. If resolution takes days to mature, do not declare victory from next-day judge scores. Predefine sample size and observation window, then inspect slices and uncertainty. Exercise risky write actions in controlled environments before limited exposure.

  <MyQuestion q="Is A/B testing the user test that comes after offline eval?">
    **It commonly follows offline evaluation and basic system validation, but having users test a product does not by itself make it A/B.** Offline eval repeatedly runs candidates on fixed cases to check known quality and safety gates. Dogfooding, UAT, or a pilot lets people try real tasks and expose unseen wording, reversals, and workflow confusion without necessarily comparing versions. A/B randomly assigns two release-qualified versions to comparable traffic by a stable user or session unit, then estimates the difference in predefined outcomes over an observation window with guardrails.

    For a negotiation agent, first test V6 and V7 on the same offline cases for offer state, number ownership, unauthorized actions, and stopping conditions. Internal users may then reveal a new pattern such as accepting a price only if payment terms change. If both versions pass the gates and traffic is sufficient, an online A/B can compare verified task completion while monitoring false promises, latency, and cost. **A/B does not replace offline safety gates.** With little traffic, use paired offline comparisons, internal UAT, and a limited pilot, while stating that the online causal evidence remains limited.
  </MyQuestion>

  <MyQuestion q="What testing rounds does an agent usually pass before launch, and where do A/B and canary fit?">
    Progress according to the risk each step must resolve. This is a common path, **not a required nine-stage or week-by-week schedule**:

    1. **Developer and component tests:** check tool permissions, arguments/schema, state updates, retries, and stop conditions; a refund-write tool should reject unauthorized requests.
    2. **Offline eval:** compare versions on normal, boundary, historical-failure, adversarial, and tool-failure cases against quality and safety release gates.
    3. **Integration / end-to-end tests:** exercise frontend, API, agent, tools, database, and external services for session, auth, and connection failures.
    4. **Internal dogfooding / UAT:** have staff and domain experts do real tasks; capture UX surprises and add verified failures to the offline set.
    5. **Staging load and reliability tests:** measure p95 latency, timeouts, errors, model quota, and cost under concurrency.
    6. **Limited pilot:** let a small target-user group test whether offline quality carries into real tasks.
    7. **Controlled rollout:** where traffic and safety allow, A/B randomly compares user outcomes for two qualified versions; canary increases exposure gradually while watching failure guardrails and retaining rollback. Their purposes differ, and a project may combine or omit them according to risk.
    8. **Full release and continuous evaluation:** monitor traces and mature outcomes, adjudicate new failures, add regressions, and evaluate the next version.

    Each step needs evidence and a gate for moving forward. A five-second local run does not establish five-second latency at a hundred concurrent users; positive pilot feedback also does not establish the causal comparison of a randomized A/B.
  </MyQuestion>

  <Note type="warning" title="Shadow side effects must be isolated">
    Mirroring live requests to a new agent with a real refund-write tool is not harmless shadowing. Simulate, make read-only, or isolate writes from production state.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why doesn't shadow success prove business KPI improvement?
    2. Why randomize by stable user/session unit in A/B?
    3. How should refund writes behave in shadow?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Turn one incident into an eval

  ### How does a false refund promise become a reliable regression?

  Suppose a production reply says “it has not arrived, so you can get an immediate refund.” The trace shows `in_transit`, while current policy disallows the unshipped-order refund flow. Do not merely paste an exception into the prompt:

  1. Preserve a deidentified trace: customer wording, order state and query time, policy version, retrieved and selected evidence, model/tool versions, final reply, and any write.
  2. Have a domain expert confirm truth and expected behavior; locate whether “not arrived” became “not shipped,” the wrong policy was selected, or supplied evidence was ignored.
  3. Reproduce in a resettable environment with explicit graders: no unshipped-refund promise, correct shipped-order process, no unauthorized write.
  4. Add a fixed incident regression, run baseline and proposed fix, and check other slices for collateral regressions.
  5. Monitor the same failure class and mature business outcomes in production to confirm improvement beyond the single case.

  Incident suites can overrepresent last week's problems. Keep representative random traffic, high-risk boundary sets, and untouched holdout alongside regressions, and update policy versions deliberately. A trace **without verifiable environment state or expert adjudication remains pending**, not an absolute-correctness case. [Offline Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/offline) data governance still applies.

  <Note type="tip" title="Answer interviews with evidence">
    Use “trace → root-cause layer → frozen case → regression gate → limited rollout.” Naming retrieval, context, model, tool, or business-rule failure is more useful than “we continuously optimize.”
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why not patch the prompt with the incident reply alone?
    2. Without order state at the time, can you definitively mark the case wrong?
    3. How do you avoid an incident-only eval set?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: A/B statistics and continuous online eval

  ### How much traffic does an A/B test need?

  Per arm, `n ≈ 16 × p(1−p) / δ²` (α = 0.05, 80% power). At p = 85% and δ = 2 points, ≈ 5,100 conversations per arm — about 10 days at 1,000 a day split evenly; 1 point needs 4×. Low-traffic products must lean on offline evals.

  ### Which metrics?

  One pre-declared primary metric (verified resolution), guardrail metrics that block launch if worse (wrong refund promises, escalations, P95 latency, cost), and diagnostics (turns, tool calls).

  ### Common traps?

  Sample ratio mismatch (a 50/50 split landing 52/48 at scale signals a bug — check first), novelty effects, peeking and stopping early, and delayed outcomes.

  ### Guardrails vs online evals?

  Synchronous guardrails run before the user sees output and block (fast, cheap, deterministic); asynchronous online evals score samples afterward to track trends and find new failures (judges, batchable). New failures found online become guardrails and offline cases.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Baseline 90%, detect 3 points — per-arm n?
    2. Primary, guardrail, diagnostic metrics with examples?
    3. What is SRM and why check it first?
    4. Guardrails vs online evals?
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note type="danger" title="“The online judge scored 90, so ship”">
    The judge may lack live order state, policy version, or side effects, and the sample may be biased. Combine offline gates, observable production guardrails, mature business outcomes, and human review.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  ```text
  Offline gate → Shadow / replay → Canary → A/B / production
                      ↑                    ↓
               Fixed regressions ← Trace + verified truth
  ```

  ## Interview questions

  1. What must a production AI trace record?
  2. How do you report 70 pass, 10 fail, and 20 pending?
  3. What can shadow, canary, and A/B establish?
  4. How does a hallucination become a reproducible regression?
  5. How do you prevent an incident-only eval set?

  ### Added 2026-10

  1. How many samples does an A/B test need?
  2. What are common A/B testing pitfalls?
  3. How do synchronous guardrails differ from async online evals?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

  ## Level 3 · Turn one incident into an eval

  ### How does a false refund promise become a reliable regression?

  Suppose a production reply says “it has not arrived, so you can get an immediate refund.” The trace shows

, while current policy disallows the unshipped-order refund flow. Do not merely paste an exception into the prompt:

  1. Preserve a deidentified trace: customer wording, order state and query time, policy version, retrieved and selected evidence, model/tool versions, final reply, and any write.
  2. Have a domain expert confirm truth and expected behavior; locate whether “not arrived” became “not shipped,” the wrong policy was selected, or supplied evidence was ignored.
  3. Reproduce in a resettable environment with explicit graders: no unshipped-refund promise, correct shipped-order process, no unauthorized write.
  4. Add a fixed incident regression, run baseline and proposed fix, and check other slices for collateral regressions.
  5. Monitor the same failure class and mature business outcomes in production to confirm improvement beyond the single case.

  Incident suites can overrepresent last week's problems. Keep representative random traffic, high-risk boundary sets, and untouched holdout alongside regressions, and update policy versions deliberately. A trace **without verifiable environment state or expert adjudication remains pending**, not an absolute-correctness case. [Offline Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/offline) data governance still applies.

    Use “trace → root-cause layer → frozen case → regression gate → limited rollout.” Naming retrieval, context, model, tool, or business-rule failure is more useful than “we continuously optimize.”
  </Note>

    1. Why not patch the prompt with the incident reply alone?
    2. Without order state at the time, can you definitively mark the case wrong?
    3. How do you avoid an incident-only eval set?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: A/B statistics and continuous online eval

  ### How much traffic does an A/B test need?

  Per arm,

(α = 0.05, 80% power). At p = 85% and δ = 2 points, ≈ 5,100 conversations per arm — about 10 days at 1,000 a day split evenly; 1 point needs 4×. Low-traffic products must lean on offline evals.

  ### Which metrics?

  One pre-declared primary metric (verified resolution), guardrail metrics that block launch if worse (wrong refund promises, escalations, P95 latency, cost), and diagnostics (turns, tool calls).

  ### Common traps?

  Sample ratio mismatch (a 50/50 split landing 52/48 at scale signals a bug — check first), novelty effects, peeking and stopping early, and delayed outcomes.

  ### Guardrails vs online evals?

  Synchronous guardrails run before the user sees output and block (fast, cheap, deterministic); asynchronous online evals score samples afterward to track trends and find new failures (judges, batchable). New failures found online become guardrails and offline cases.

    2. Primary, guardrail, diagnostic metrics with examples?
    3. What is SRM and why check it first?
    4. Guardrails vs online evals?
  </Note>

    The judge may lack live order state, policy version, or side effects, and the sample may be biased. Combine offline gates, observable production guardrails, mature business outcomes, and human review.
  </Note>

content:
<Locale lang="en">
  A wrong refund answer can come from missing current policy in retrieval, failing to select a retrieved clause into context, ignoring an exception during generation, or using stale evidence. “Was the answer good?” cannot localize the fault. [RAG](/docs/rag) explains the pipeline; this page explains **how to grade each layer**.

  We continue with order 20240915. An order tool supplies live state; retrieval supplies policy. For hand calculations, assume exactly two current policy passages are relevant to this question. Rankings and numbers are teaching examples, not production measurements.

  <Note type="tip" title="2026-10-04 update: what to review">
    🆕 **New Level 4**: how the four RAGAS metrics are computed, reference-based vs reference-free evaluation, synthetic RAG test sets, retrieval eval without labels.

    🔁 **Review**: Levels 1 and 2; read Level 3 alongside [Construction](/docs/context/construction) Level 4.

    ✏️ **Original text unchanged**: no factual errors found; your highlights are intact.
  </Note>

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Layers | Retrieved, assembled, and used correctly: which step is which? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Retrieval metrics | Calculate Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR, and nDCG. | 35 min |
  | 2 · Generation metrics | Distinguish faithfulness, relevance, correctness, and completeness. | 30 min |
  | 3 · Debugging | With high recall but low answer accuracy, where do you inspect first? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Deep dive (added 2026-10) | How are RAGAS metrics computed? How do you evaluate retrieval without labels? | 30 min |

  ## Must know

  * Separate retrieval candidates, passages actually assembled, generated claims, and the final business decision.
  * Calculate Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR, and binary nDCG against one gold relevance set.
  * Explain why grounded answers can still be wrong or incomplete; citations must support specific claims.
  * Debug by layer rather than immediately changing model or temperature.
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Three gates in RAG

  ### Why can a correct retrieved document still lead to a wrong answer?

  Trace the flow:

  ```text
  Question + order state
    → retrieval Top-K candidates
    → filter/rerank/assemble current context
    → model-generated claims
    → business decision and citations
  ```

  Suppose current exception `P-17` appears in Top-5. If assembly includes only an old FAQ due to budget, **retrieval passed but assembly failed**. If `P-17` is supplied but the answer says an in-transit order may use the unshipped refund flow, **evidence use/generation failed**. If the reply cites `P-17` but live order state has changed, **dynamic state or version control failed**. Log candidate IDs, selected IDs, claims, and final order state separately.

  <Note title="Four layers are not one metric">
    Retrieval recall asks whether correct material reached candidates. Context coverage asks whether the model received it. Faithfulness asks whether claims are supported by supplied evidence. Task correctness asks whether the decision matches real order and policy state. One layer can pass while another fails.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. If `P-17` was in Top-5 but not in context, which layer failed?
    2. If `P-17` was supplied but the reply contradicts it, which layer is suspect?
    3. Why check live order state even if the answer cites a policy?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Calculate four retrieval metrics

  ### What does one Top-5 ranking tell us?

  The gold relevant passages are `A` (shipped-order exception) and `B` (regional condition). Retrieval returns:

  | Rank | Passage | Relevant? |
  | ---: | --- | --- |
  | 1 | Obsolete policy X | No |
  | 2 | Current clause A | Yes |
  | 3 | Product promotion Y | No |
  | 4 | Current clause B | Yes |
  | 5 | Returns FAQ Z | No |

  **Recall@5** = retrieved relevant / total gold relevant = `2/2 = 1.0`. **Precision@5** = relevant in Top-5 / 5 = `2/5 = 0.4`. **Reciprocal rank** uses the first relevant hit: `1/2 = 0.5`. **MRR** averages reciprocal ranks over multiple queries; one query has RR, not an average.

  With binary relevance, `DCG@5 = 1/log2(2+1) + 1/log2(4+1) ≈ 0.631 + 0.431 = 1.062`. Ideal ranking places A and B first: `IDCG@5 = 1 + 0.631 = 1.631`, so `nDCG@5 ≈ 1.062/1.631 = 0.651`. nDCG reflects ranking quality even though both gold passages were retrieved.

  These metrics require **gold relevance labels**. Real questions may have several sufficient evidence sets, and document-level labels can hide passage-level differences. Annotators must define relevance and K. Apply consistent permission and policy-version rules before scoring; obsolete X must not count as current evidence.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why doesn't Recall@5=1 prove a good ranking?
    2. Why is one query RR rather than MRR?
    3. What happens to nDCG if A and B move to ranks 1 and 2?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · What generation metrics ask

  ### Can a faithful answer still be wrong?

  **Faithfulness / groundedness** commonly asks whether each claim is supported by the **evidence supplied to the model**. **Answer relevance** asks whether it addresses the question. **Answer correctness** compares with authoritative truth. **Completeness** asks whether required conditions were covered. **Context relevance** asks whether supplied passages actually matter. Libraries define and compute these differently; state your rubric in an interview.

  Suppose an answer claims ① the order is in transit; ② shipped orders cannot use the unshipped refund flow; ③ return shipping is always free. Evidence supports the first two but not the third. A teaching claim-support rate is `2/3`. Actual [DeepEval Faithfulness](https://deepeval.com/docs/metrics-faithfulness) uses a judge to extract and compare claims against retrieval context, with results depending on judge and configuration. More importantly, an answer perfectly faithful to **obsolete policy** may still be **wrong for the business today**.

  Check citations claim by claim. A reply might cite `[P-17]`, but P-17 says nothing about free returns: a formatted citation is not evidence. If region is missing, a good system may say it cannot yet decide instead of presenting a complete-sounding conclusion.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why can an answer faithful to old policy still be wrong?
    2. Are “about refunds” and “correct refund decision” the same metric?
    3. Why verify which claim `[P-17]` actually supports?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Turn metrics into debugging actions

  ### With high Recall@K and low answer accuracy, where do you look?

  For each failed trace, inspect **gold in retrieval candidates → gold in final context → claims and citations → live order/policy truth**. If retrieval passed but assembly failed, tune [Context Construction](/docs/context/construction). If evidence arrived but claims lack support, inspect generation constraints, the model, or grader. If evidence is stale, repair indexing/version control and authoritative lookup. A total score does not tell you to change temperature.

  A small diagnostic grid:

  | Gold in final context? | Answer right? | Possible meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Yes | Yes | Case works; still check citations and cost |
  | Yes | No | Evidence use, conflict resolution, or model |
  | No | No | Retrieval or assembly missed evidence |
  | No | Yes | May be a lucky guess or incomplete gold labels; investigate |

  Without gold documents, have experts annotate passages for a small representative set first, then expand. Human-check retrieved results or use weak supervision to propose labels for review. Do not let one automated judge create “truth” and then claim validation against itself. Online you also need resolution, feedback, and freshness in [Production Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/production-eval).

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. If recall is high but the correct clause never enters context, which layer changes first?
    2. Without gold documents, how do you create a trustworthy small set?
    3. Why isn't a correct answer with no gold evidence automatically RAG success?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: computing RAGAS metrics, and evaluating without labels

  ### How are the four RAGAS metrics computed?

  Faithfulness: split the answer into atomic claims, check each against retrieved context, supported / total (no reference needed). Answer relevancy: generate questions from the answer and average their embedding similarity to the original (no reference). Context precision: judge each retrieved chunk's relevance, rank-weighted (usually needs a reference). Context recall: split the reference answer into claims and check each is attributable to the context (needs a reference). Example: three claims, the free return shipping isn't in context → faithfulness 2/3 — it catches invented promises, not stale-but-retrieved policy.

  ### Reference-based or reference-free?

  Reference-based judges correctness but needs labels — use offline. Reference-free judges grounding and relevance cheaply — use for online sampling, escalating issues to human labeling.

  ### Synthetic RAG test sets?

  Sample passages, generate question + reference + source passage, evolve into reasoning, multi-passage, and conditional questions, filter, and spot-check. Mix with real queries, which are messier.

  ### Retrieval without labels?

  LLM relevance judgments on top-k (calibrated on a small labeled set), synthetic questions whose source passage is the known answer (recall@k, MRR), and implicit online signals.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. How are faithfulness and context recall computed, and which needs a reference?
    2. Why does answer relevancy reverse-generate questions?
    3. When reference-based vs reference-free?
    4. How do you build a synthetic set, and why multi-passage questions?
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note type="danger" title="“RAG accuracy is 90%”">
    Without naming retrieval recall, claim support, final decision accuracy, or user resolution, the number cannot direct engineering work.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  ```text
  Offline → versioned gold cases
  Retrieval → Recall / Precision / MRR / nDCG
  Construction → whether gold evidence entered context
  Generation → faithfulness / relevance / correctness
  Production → new data and real user outcomes
  ```

  ## Interview questions

  1. Calculate Recall, Precision, RR, and nDCG for the Top-5 example.
  2. How do you debug high recall but wrong answers?
  3. How do faithfulness and correctness differ?
  4. How do you start without gold documents?
  5. Why check citations claim by claim?

  ### Added 2026-10

  1. How are faithfulness and context recall actually computed?
  2. How do you evaluate retrieval without human labels?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

  ### Can a faithful answer still be wrong?

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Turn metrics into debugging actions

  ### With high Recall@K and low answer accuracy, where do you look?

  For each failed trace, inspect **gold in retrieval candidates → gold in final context → claims and citations → live order/policy truth**. If retrieval passed but assembly failed, tune [Context Construction](/docs/context/construction). If evidence arrived but claims lack support, inspect generation constraints, the model, or grader. If evidence is stale, repair indexing/version control and authoritative lookup. A total score does not tell you to change temperature.

  A small diagnostic grid:

  | Gold in final context? | Answer right? | Possible meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Yes | Yes | Case works; still check citations and cost |
  | Yes | No | Evidence use, conflict resolution, or model |
  | No | No | Retrieval or assembly missed evidence |
  | No | Yes | May be a lucky guess or incomplete gold labels; investigate |

  Without gold documents, have experts annotate passages for a small representative set first, then expand. Human-check retrieved results or use weak supervision to propose labels for review. Do not let one automated judge create “truth” and then claim validation against itself. Online you also need resolution, feedback, and freshness in [Production Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/production-eval).

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. If recall is high but the correct clause never enters context, which layer changes first?
    2. Without gold documents, how do you create a trustworthy small set?
    3. Why isn't a correct answer with no gold evidence automatically RAG success?
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Deep dive: computing RAGAS metrics, and evaluating without labels

  ### How are the four RAGAS metrics computed?

  Faithfulness: split the answer into atomic claims, check each against retrieved context, supported / total (no reference needed). Answer relevancy: generate questions from the answer and average their embedding similarity to the original (no reference). Context precision: judge each retrieved chunk's relevance, rank-weighted (usually needs a reference). Context recall: split the reference answer into claims and check each is attributable to the context (needs a reference). Example: three claims, the free return shipping isn't in context → faithfulness 2/3 — it catches invented promises, not stale-but-retrieved policy.

  ### Reference-based or reference-free?

  Reference-based judges correctness but needs labels — use offline. Reference-free judges grounding and relevance cheaply — use for online sampling, escalating issues to human labeling.

  ### Synthetic RAG test sets?

  Sample passages, generate question + reference + source passage, evolve into reasoning, multi-passage, and conditional questions, filter, and spot-check. Mix with real queries, which are messier.

  ### Retrieval without labels?

  LLM relevance judgments on top-k (calibrated on a small labeled set), synthetic questions whose source passage is the known answer (recall@k, MRR), and implicit online signals.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. How are faithfulness and context recall computed, and which needs a reference?
    2. Why does answer relevancy reverse-generate questions?
    3. When reference-based vs reference-free?
    4. How do you build a synthetic set, and why multi-passage questions?
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note type="danger" title="“RAG accuracy is 90%”">
    Without naming retrieval recall, claim support, final decision accuracy, or user resolution, the number cannot direct engineering work.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  Generation → faithfulness / relevance / correctness
  Production → new data and real user outcomes
