  ## Level 2 · LoRA: training just two small matrices

  ### What's the core idea behind LoRA?

  Most of a model's parameters live in the weight matrices W of its linear layers (see the linear layer in [Attention & Transformer](/docs/llm/transformer) Level 0). **LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)** does three things to each W it targets:

  1. **Freeze W** — it never changes during training
  2. Add two small matrices **A** and **B** alongside it, whose product **B · A** serves as W's change ΔW
  3. **Train only A and B**

W:  shape [d_out, d_in]      frozen
  A:  shape [r, d_in]          trained    squeezes the input down to r dims
  B:  shape [d_out, r]         trained    expands from r dims back to the output size

  forward pass:  y = W · x  +  (α / r) · B · (A · x)

**r is called the rank**, usually 8, 16, 32, or 64 — far smaller than d (thousands). α is a scaling factor, covered shortly.

  One way to think about rank: **a rank-1 matrix is just one column of numbers times one row**, so every row is a multiple of the same row. A rank-r matrix has at most r independent "directions." LoRA uses B · A, which has rank at most r, to approximate the "low-rank weight change" from Level 1.

  ### Work out a 4 × 4, rank-1 LoRA by hand

  Take d = 4 and r = 1:

A = [1, 2, 0, 1]          shape [1, 4], a row
  B = [1, 0, 2, 1]ᵀ         shape [4, 1], a column
**B · A is a column times a row, giving a 4 × 4 matrix:**

This ΔW has 16 numbers, but A and B describe it with just **8**. Every row is a multiple of the first, so its rank is 1.

  **Computation never needs the actual 4 × 4 matrix.** With input x = \[1, 0, 1, 0], compute in the order

A · x = 1×1 + 2×0 + 0×1 + 1×0 = 1          squeeze down to 1 number
  B · 1 = [1, 0, 2, 1]                       expand back to 4 dims

Multiplying x by the full ΔW above also gives \[1, 0, 2, 1] — identical. Computing A · x first is cheaper: when d is large, squeezing to r dims and expanding back costs far less than a d × d multiply.

  ### How many parameters does it save? Work it out for LLaMA 3 8B

  Adding LoRA to one linear layer adds this many parameters:

  $$
  \text{LoRA parameters} = r \times d_{in} + d_{out} \times r = r \times (d_{in} + d_{out})
  $$

  **One 4096 × 4096 matrix, r = 8:**

original matrix:  4096 × 4096        = 16,777,216 parameters
  LoRA:             8 × (4096 + 4096)  = 65,536 parameters       just 0.39%

**All of LLaMA 3 8B.** Each Transformer block has 7 linear layers (attention's 4 projections + the FFN's 3 matrices; see [Attention & Transformer](/docs/llm/transformer) Levels 7 and 8):

  | Linear layer | input → output dims | Notes |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | q\_proj | 4096 → 4096 | 32 query heads × 128 dims |
  | k\_proj | 4096 → 1024 | GQA: 8 KV heads × 128 dims |
  | v\_proj | 4096 → 1024 | same |
  | o\_proj | 4096 → 4096 | attention output projection |
  | gate\_proj | 4096 → 14336 | SwiGLU gate |
  | up\_proj | 4096 → 14336 | SwiGLU expansion |
  | down\_proj | 14336 → 4096 | SwiGLU projection back down |

  There are 32 layers. LoRA parameter counts under different settings:

  | Setting | Trained parameters | Share of all parameters | Adapter file (bf16) |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | r = 8, on q and v only (the original LoRA paper's setup) | 3,407,872 | 0.042% | about 6.5 MiB |
  | r = 16, on all 7 linear layers | 41,943,040 | 0.52% | about 80 MiB |
  | r = 64, on all 7 linear layers | 167,772,160 | 2.09% | about 320 MiB |

  Take the common r = 16 on all linear layers: only about 42 million parameters are trained, and at 16 bytes per parameter their gradients and optimizer state need only about **0.62 GiB** — negligible next to the 128 GB of full fine-tuning.

  <Note title="LoRA saves training state, not the base weights" type="warning">
    The frozen W isn't updated and has no gradients or optimizer state, but both the forward and backward passes use it, so **8B of fp16 weights (about 16 GB) still has to sit in GPU memory**, plus activations. LoRA turns 8B fine-tuning from "must use multiple GPUs" into "fits on one 40 GB or 80 GB GPU," but squeezing it onto a 24 GB consumer card also requires QLoRA from Level 3 to shrink the base weights.
  </Note>

  ### Why initialize B to 0? What is alpha?

  **Initialization**: A gets small random values and **B is set entirely to 0**. So at the start of training B · A = 0, and the model's output is **exactly** the original model's — training starts from the original model's abilities and adjusts gradually.

  If both A and B were random, ΔW would be a random perturbation from the first step, effectively scrambling the model before slowly fixing it — wasted training that can also damage existing abilities.

  **Alpha (α)**: LoRA's output is multiplied by the scaling factor α / r:

r = 16, α = 32  →  scale = 2
  r = 16, α = 16  →  scale = 1

Common settings are α = r or α = 2r. Keeping α / r fixed has a benefit: when you change the rank, the overall size of the update doesn't swing wildly, so you don't need to retune the learning rate each time.

  ### Which layers should LoRA target, and how big should the rank be?

  **Where to add it:**

  * The original LoRA paper added it only to attention's q and v projections, for the fewest parameters
  * Today it's more common to **target all linear layers** (attention + FFN). The QLoRA paper found that matching full fine-tuning quality required LoRA on all linear layers

  **How big a rank (rules of thumb):**

  | Task type | Typical rank |
  | --- | --- |
  | behavioral adjustments like format, style, and tone (e.g. review extraction) | 8 to 16 |
  | domain adaptation that has more to learn | 32 to 64 or higher |

  Bigger isn't automatically better: a higher rank means more parameters and a greater risk of overfitting small data. Starting at 16 and increasing only if quality falls short is a practical approach.

  ### After training, how is a LoRA used?

  Two ways:

  **1. Merge it back into the weights:**

  $$
  W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r} \cdot B A
  $$

  W' has exactly the same shape as W, so swapping it in changes nothing about the model's structure and **adds no inference latency**. That's LoRA's biggest advantage over adapters.

  **2. Keep the adapter separate:** load the base model once and store adapters (tens of MB) separately, loading or switching them as needed. That's how one base model serves many tasks — details in Level 6.

  <Note title="When you explain LoRA in an interview, say the numbers" type="tip">
    "LoRA freezes the original weights and trains only low-rank matrices B and A. For an 8B model with r = 16 on all linear layers, that's about 42 million trained parameters, 0.5% of the total, in an 80 MB adapter file. B starts at zero so training begins from the original model, and afterward it can be merged back in with zero added inference latency." That lands far better than "LoRA is low-rank adaptation."
  </Note>

  ## Level 3 · QLoRA: compressing the base weights to 4 bits

  ### LoRA already saves so much — why is QLoRA needed?

  Level 2 ended on this: LoRA removes gradients and optimizer state, but the frozen base weights still have to sit in GPU memory in fp16. LLaMA 3 8B's weights alone are about 16 GB, and with activations on top, a 24 GB consumer GPU struggles to fit it.

  **QLoRA's idea is straightforward: the base weights aren't being trained, so store them in 4 bits; LoRA's A and B stay in 16-bit and train as usual.** The QLoRA paper used this to fine-tune a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU.

  To understand it, you first need to know what quantization is.

  ### What is quantization? Work out an int4 example

  **Quantization** stores numbers with fewer bits. fp16 uses 16 bits per number; int4 uses 4 bits and can represent only 16 distinct integers. The trick is to find a **scale** that maps the floating-point numbers onto that small integer grid.

  The simplest scheme, symmetric absmax quantization, on four weights with int4 ranging from −7 to 7:

original weights w = [0.12, −0.50, 0.33, 0.90]

  ① scale        = largest absolute value / 7 = 0.90 / 7 = 0.1286
  ② quantize     q = round(w / scale) = round([0.93, −3.89, 2.57, 7.00]) = [1, −4, 3, 7]
  ③ store        four 4-bit integers + one scale
  ④ dequantize   w' = q × scale = [0.129, −0.514, 0.386, 0.900]

  error = w − w' = [−0.009, 0.014, −0.056, 0.000]

Storage drops from 4 × 16 bits to 4 × 4 bits (plus one scale), at the cost of a small rounding error in each number.

  At compute time the GPU **temporarily dequantizes** the 4-bit weights back to 16 bits for the matrix multiply, so memory is saved but every computation pays an extra dequantization step.

  ### Why are outliers the hard part, and how does group-wise quantization help?

  Suppose one weight in the group is unusually large:

One outlier inflates the scale so much that everything else rounds to 0 and the information is lost entirely.

  **Group-wise (block-wise) quantization**: instead of one scale for the whole matrix, compute a separate scale for every small group (say, every 64 numbers). Put the three small numbers in their own group:

The cost is storing many more scales: one 32-bit scale per 64 weights adds 32 / 64 = **0.5 bits** per weight on average.

  ### What are NF4 and double quantization?

  QLoRA adds two improvements on top of group-wise quantization:

  **1. NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat)**: pretrained weights are roughly normally distributed around 0 — most values are close to 0 and large ones are rare. A uniform integer grid like the one above wastes many of its levels on large values that hardly ever occur. NF4 places its 16 values according to the normal distribution: **levels are dense near 0 and sparse far from it**, so the same 4 bits represent common values more accurately.

  **2. Double quantization**: group-wise quantization's extra 0.5 bits come from those 32-bit scales. Double quantization **quantizes the scales themselves** (grouping them again and compressing to 8 bits), cutting that overhead from about 0.5 bits per weight to about 0.127.

  QLoRA also uses **paged optimizers**: when GPU memory suddenly runs tight, optimizer state is moved temporarily to CPU memory, avoiding the occasional out-of-memory crash when training on long sequences.

  ### How much memory does QLoRA fine-tuning of LLaMA 3 8B take?

  Putting it all together:

all 7 linear-layer types in NF4 + double quantization   6.98B × 4.127 bits ≈ 3.60 GB
  embedding and LM head kept in bf16                      1.05B × 2 bytes    ≈ 2.10 GB    (usually not quantized)
  LoRA r = 16 parameters and training state               41.9M × 16 bytes   ≈ 0.67 GB
  total                                                                      ≈ 6.4 GB     plus activations

The three approaches side by side:

  | Approach | Weights + training state | Typical hardware |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Full fine-tuning | about 128 GB | several 80 GB GPUs + ZeRO |
  | LoRA (fp16 base) | about 16.7 GB | one 40 GB or 80 GB GPU |
  | **QLoRA (4-bit base)** | **about 6.4 GB** | **one 24 GB consumer GPU** |

  Activations scale with sequence length and batch size. With activation checkpointing (see [Training](/docs/llm/training) Level 5), QLoRA training of an 8B model at sequence lengths around 2K usually fits on a 24 GB GPU.

  Configured with Hugging Face

python
  import torch
  from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
  from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

  bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
      load_in_4bit=True,
      bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
      bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
      bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,   # compute in bf16 after dequantizing
  )
  model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
      "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct", quantization_config=bnb_config
  )
  lora_config = LoraConfig(
      r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
      target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
                      "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
  )
  model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config)
  model.print_trainable_parameters()   # trainable params should be 41,943,040, matching Level 2's hand count

### What does QLoRA give up?

  | Cost | Why |
  | --- | --- |
  | **Slower training** | every forward and backward pass dequantizes the 4-bit weights back to 16 bits |
  | **Possibly a small quality gap** | the base weights carry quantization error. The QLoRA paper reported results close to 16-bit fine-tuning on its benchmarks, but it's still worth measuring on your own task |
  | **Harder merging** | the adapter was trained against the quantized base. Merging directly into 4-bit weights is awkward; the common approach is to merge into the fp16 base and re-quantize for deployment (see Level 6 and [Inference](/docs/llm/inference) Level 4) |

  <Note title="In a project deep-dive, frame “why QLoRA” as a trade-off under hardware limits" type="tip">
    "We only had 24 GB GPUs. The 8B model's fp16 weights alone are 16 GB, so even LoRA didn't fit. QLoRA brought the base down to about 6 GB at the cost of slower training, and when we compared against 16-bit LoRA on the validation set, the gap was acceptable." That gives your decision a rationale beyond "I used QLoRA," and it holds up under follow-up questions.

  ## Level 4 · Data and training setup

  LoRA and QLoRA solve "does it fit, and can it train." What the model actually learns is decided by the data and the training setup.

  ### What does the training data look like?

  It uses the same SFT format as [Post-training](/docs/llm/post-training) Level 1 — each example is a conversation:

Training needs two things (reasoning in Post-training Level 1):

  * use LLaMA 3 Instruct's **original chat template** to turn the conversation into a token sequence
  * **compute loss only on the assistant's response**, not the system or user parts

  Notice one detail: once trained, the system prompt no longer needs the long block of rules and few-shot examples — one sentence is enough. That's Level 0's "train the rules into the weights and shorten the prompt."

  ### How much data do you need, and how do you prepare it?

  For format, style, and judgment-consistency tasks, **a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality examples** is usually enough. This example uses 2,000 labeled reviews.

  Good data needs to be:

  | Requirement | What it means in this example |
  | --- | --- |
  | **Correctly labeled** | every JSON has been checked by a person |
  | **Consistent** | write a labeling guide first — e.g., is "pricey but worth it" mixed or positive? — and settle it before labeling |
  | **Representative** | all five aspects; purely positive, purely negative, mixed, and no-aspect reviews; short and long, colloquial, slang |
  | **Deduplicated** | keep only one of any duplicate or near-identical reviews |
  | **No test leakage** | test reviews don't overlap with training reviews |

  Data usually comes from one of three places: human labeling from scratch (most expensive); pre-labeling with a stronger model followed by human review and correction (common and cost-effective); or collecting human-corrected results from production logs.

  <Note title="The labeling guide is half the work" type="tip">
    If labelers disagree, the model learns the disagreement. If "pricey but worth it" is labeled mixed by some and positive by others, the model will waver on reviews like it. So before labeling at scale, align the guide on a few dozen hard examples. Saying in an interview "we wrote a labeling guide first and here are the edge cases we settled" sounds far more professional than "we prepared 2,000 examples."
  </Note>

  ### How do you split training, validation, and test sets?

training set    2,000 examples   used to update parameters
  validation set    200 examples   used during training to check progress, pick checkpoints, tune hyperparameters
  test set          200 examples   used once at the end to report final results; never used for any tuning decision

* **Label the test set separately and carefully** — it decides whether the numbers you report are trustworthy
  * **Split by time or by product rather than purely at random**: reviews of the same product tend to look alike, so a random split can leave "close relatives" of training examples in the test set and inflate the metrics

  ### How do you set the hyperparameters?

  A common QLoRA starting configuration:

  | Hyperparameter | Typical value | Notes |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | rank r | 16 | 8 to 16 is usually enough for behavioral tasks (Level 2) |
  | alpha α | 32 | α = 2r, a scale of 2 |
  | LoRA dropout | 0.05 | a little dropout on the LoRA branch to prevent overfitting |
  | target layers | all linear layers | Level 2 |
  | learning rate | 1e-4 to 2e-4 | LoRA typically uses a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning |
  | epochs | 1 to 3 | small datasets overfit easily; don't train too many passes |
  | effective batch size | 16 | use gradient accumulation if memory is short (see [Training](/docs/llm/training) Level 2) |
  | max sequence length | long enough for the longest example | too short truncates responses |
  | learning-rate schedule | brief warmup + cosine decay | see Training Level 2 |

  Count the steps:

2,000 examples ÷ batch 16 = 125 steps per epoch
  3 epochs = 375 steps

With so few steps, warmup is usually just ten to twenty steps.

  ### How do you spot overfitting?

  Watch **training loss** and **validation loss** together (illustrative numbers):

epoch    training loss    validation loss
  1        0.62             0.58
  2        0.35             0.41       ← lowest validation loss
  3        0.18             0.47       ← training still falling, validation rising: overfitting

When training loss keeps falling but validation loss starts rising, the model is memorizing the training set. Pick **the checkpoint with the best validation performance** (epoch 2 here), not the last one.

  Beyond loss, check task metrics on the validation set directly (valid-JSON rate, aspect extraction accuracy), because a lower loss doesn't necessarily mean more accurate extraction.

  Common fixes for overfitting: fewer epochs, a lower learning rate or rank, more diverse data, more dropout.

  ### What are the common pitfalls?

  <Note title="A wrong chat template or missing end token means the model won't stop" type="warning">
    If responses in the training data don't end with the correct end marker, the model never learns to stop when it's done, and after deployment it keeps writing after the JSON. Training and inference must use the same template (see [Post-training](/docs/llm/post-training) Level 1).
  </Note>

  <Note title="Counting the prompt in the loss" type="warning">
    The model spends effort learning to repeat the instructions and reviews, and those easy-to-predict tokens drag the training loss down — it looks great while real performance gets worse.
  </Note>

  <Note title="A max length that's too short truncates responses" type="warning">
    Anything past the max length is simply cut off. If the part cut off is the assistant's response, the model learns to write half a JSON. Check the token-length distribution of your data before training.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: by now you should be able to answer">
    1. What format does fine-tuning data use, and what two things must training get right?
    2. What does good fine-tuning data require, and why does the labeling guide matter so much?
    3. What are the training, validation, and test sets each for, and why avoid a purely random split?
    4. Name a common set of QLoRA hyperparameters. How many steps is 2,000 examples at batch 16 for 3 epochs?
    5. How do you spot overfitting from the loss curves, and which checkpoint should you pick?
    6. Name two common fine-tuning pitfalls.
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 5 · Evaluation and catastrophic forgetting

  ### How do you prove fine-tuning actually worked?

  First, turn "worked" into something you can compute. For review extraction on 200 test reviews:

  | Metric | How it's computed |
  | --- | --- |
  | Valid-JSON rate | share of outputs that parse and have every field |
  | Sentiment accuracy | share with the correct sentiment |
  | Aspect precision / recall / F1 | compared aspect by aspect (worked out below) |
  | Exact-match rate | share where the whole JSON matches the reference exactly |

  **Compute aspect F1 by hand.** Add up every aspect across the 200 reviews:

the model extracted 400 aspects in total
  the references contain 420 aspects in total
  360 of them match

  precision P = 360 / 400 = 0.900     how many of the extracted aspects are right
  recall    R = 360 / 420 = 0.857     how many of the aspects that should be found were found
  F1 = 2 × P × R / (P + R) = 0.878

**Compare against several baselines** to show what fine-tuning actually contributed (illustrative numbers):

  | Approach | Valid-JSON rate | Exact-match rate |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Prompting only (3 examples) | 85.0% | 75.0% |
  | Prompting + constrained decoding | 100% | 78.0% |
  | QLoRA fine-tuning | 98.5% | 90.5% |
  | QLoRA fine-tuning + constrained decoding | 100% | 91.0% |

  This table makes one important point clear: **constrained decoding fixes the format, but the accuracy gain comes mainly from fine-tuning** — exactly the analysis from Level 0.

  <Note title="Categorize the remaining errors; they decide what data to collect next" type="tip">
    Go through the 19 reviews still wrong after fine-tuning and group them by cause: borderline sentiment like "pricey but worth it," unseen slang, reviews mentioning three or more aspects… Whichever group is largest is where the next round of data goes. "Look at errors → categorize → collect targeted data" is the most effective fine-tuning iteration loop, and describing it scores well in interviews.
  </Note>

  ### Why check general abilities too?

  Level 1 covered catastrophic forgetting: training on one narrow task can degrade existing abilities. Task metrics alone won't reveal it.

  So after fine-tuning, run a set of general checks against **the original instruct model** as a control:

  * **General ability**: small subsets of common benchmarks, such as knowledge QA, math reasoning, and code
  * **Off-task behavior**: ask it an ordinary question and see whether it also answers in JSON
  * **Safety behavior**: does it still decline harmful requests?

  An illustrative regression check:

original instruct model    after fine-tuning
  general knowledge QA (subset)            68.0%                     66.5%     small drop, acceptable
  math reasoning (subset)                  79.0%                     77.0%
  answers ordinary questions in JSON          0%                       12%     ← needs fixing
  refusal rate on harmful requests           95%                       88%     ← needs fixing

<Note title="Even entirely harmless training data can weaken safety alignment" type="warning">
    Research has found that fine-tuning a safety-aligned model on ordinary, harmless data can still make it more willing to carry out harmful requests. So any fine-tuned model served to users needs safety evaluation in its regression tests — don't assume "the data was fine, so safety is fine."
  </Note>

  ### How do you mitigate catastrophic forgetting?

  | Approach | Why it works |
  | --- | --- |
  | **Use LoRA instead of full fine-tuning** | only a few parameters change and the original weights stay put. Research has found LoRA "learns less, but also forgets less" |
  | **Mix in a small amount of general instruction data** | training isn't about just one task, so the model isn't pushed entirely toward JSON |
  | **Fewer epochs, a lower learning rate or rank** | the smaller the change, the less forgetting |
  | **A separate adapter per task** | the base model stays unchanged; unload the adapter when the task isn't needed and you have the original model back (Level 6) |

  Back to the "answers ordinary questions in JSON" problem above: the most direct fix is to apply the adapter only on the review-extraction endpoint, and route every other request to the original model without the adapter.

  ### When is LLM-as-judge appropriate?

  For tasks like review extraction, which have reference answers you can compare programmatically, **prefer computed metrics** — they're accurate and cheap.

  Use LLM-as-judge only when outputs are open-ended text that can't be compared word for word (say, fine-tuning a support-reply model): have a strong model compare responses before and after fine-tuning and compute a win rate. For its pitfalls, like position and length bias, see [Post-training](/docs/llm/post-training) Level 6 and [LLM Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/llm-eval).

  <Note title="Self-check: by now you should be able to answer">
    1. What metrics can evaluate review extraction? By hand: with 50 aspects extracted, 60 in the references, and 45 matching, what are P, R, and F1?
    2. Why compare against baselines like "prompting + constrained decoding"?
    3. After fine-tuning, why check general abilities and safety behavior, and what exactly do you check?
    4. What are the ways to mitigate catastrophic forgetting?
    5. Which tasks suit computed metrics, and which actually need LLM-as-judge?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 6 · Deployment and engineering choices

  ### How do you deploy a trained adapter? Merge it or not?

  Two options, each with its place:

  | | Merge into the base | Keep a separate adapter |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | How | W' = W + (α / r) · B · A, giving a complete new model | load the base once and attach the adapter (about 80 MiB) at runtime |
  | Inference latency | identical to the original model | the LoRA branch adds a little computation |
  | Deployment shape | one complete model per task (about 16 GB in fp16) | one base + many adapters |
  | Good for | a single task where the lowest latency matters | many tasks or many customers sharing one base |

  **When merging a QLoRA adapter**, as Level 3 noted, don't merge into the 4-bit weights. Merge into the **original fp16 base** to get a complete fp16 model, then re-quantize for deployment with a method like AWQ or GPTQ (see [Inference](/docs/llm/inference) Level 4). Always rerun the test-set metrics after merging to confirm nothing dropped.

  ### How does one base model serve many LoRAs at once?

  Suppose three adapters were trained on the same LLaMA 3 8B: review extraction, support replies, and summarization.

option A: fully fine-tune (or merge) each task and deploy three complete models
            3 × 16 GB ≈ 48 GB

  option B: one base + three LoRA adapters (r = 16)
            16 GB + 3 × 80 MiB ≈ 15.2 GiB

  and with one adapter per customer for 100 customers
            16 GB + 100 × 80 MiB ≈ 15 GiB + 7.8 GiB

Option B saves an enormous amount of memory. More importantly, **serving systems like vLLM and S-LoRA can mix requests for different adapters in the same batch**: review-extraction and support-reply requests are computed together, sharing the base model's computation and diverging only in their LoRA branches. When there are too many adapters to fit, they can be swapped between GPU memory and CPU memory.

  Attaching an adapter in vLLM:

python
  from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams
  from vllm.lora.request import LoRARequest

  llm = LLM(model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct",
            enable_lora=True, max_lora_rank=16)
  outputs = llm.generate(
      prompts,
      SamplingParams(temperature=0),
      lora_request=LoRARequest("review-extract", 1, "/adapters/review-extract"),
  )

<Note title="Multi-LoRA serving makes a custom model per customer affordable" type="tip">
    If every customer needs a custom model, full fine-tuning costs grow linearly with the number of customers; with multi-LoRA serving, adding a customer adds just a tens-of-MB adapter sharing the same GPU as everyone else. It's a strong answer to "how would you personalize a model for many tenants." How batches mix different requests is covered in [Inference](/docs/llm/inference) Level 2.
  </Note>

  ### How do you choose between full fine-tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA?

  | | Full fine-tuning | LoRA | QLoRA |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Training memory (8B) | about 128 GB + activations | about 17 GB + activations | about 6.4 GB + activations |
  | Training speed | fast (but needs many GPUs) | fast | slower (dequantization overhead) |
  | Quality ceiling | highest | close to full on most tasks | usually close to LoRA |
  | Storage per task | a complete 16 GB model | tens to hundreds of MB of adapter | same as LoRA |
  | Catastrophic forgetting risk | higher | lower | lower |

  How to choose:

  * **Full fine-tuning**: a very large dataset (hundreds of thousands of examples or more), a domain or language far from the original model, a push for the quality ceiling — and enough GPUs
  * **LoRA**: the default for the vast majority of tasks when you have a 40 GB or 80 GB GPU
  * **QLoRA**: constrained hardware, like only 24 GB GPUs, and willingness to trade slower training for memory

  ### So how do you choose between RAG, prompting, and fine-tuning — and combine them?

  The core distinction fits in one sentence: **RAG handles the knowledge an answer relies on; fine-tuning handles how the answer is given**, and prompting is the zero-cost starting point to try before either (the full ladder is in [Post-training](/docs/llm/post-training) Level 6).

  | Need | Approach | Why |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Knowledge changes often and needs cited sources | RAG | updating documents takes effect immediately and stays traceable |
  | Output format, judgment, and domain language must be consistent | fine-tuning (LoRA) | a behavior problem; you can't add enough prompt examples |
  | **Must use internal knowledge *and* answer in a fixed format with correct citations** | **RAG + fine-tuning** | SFT on "question with retrieved passages → well-formed answer" teaches the model how to use retrieval results and cite them |
  | Prompts too long; cost and latency pressure | fine-tuning | train the rules into the weights and shorten the input |
  | Replace a large model with a small one on a narrow task | fine-tuning (often with training data generated by the large model) | small models are far cheaper to serve |
  | Requirements still changing fast; only a few dozen examples | prompting | fastest iteration, no training cost |

  <Note title="Fine-tuning data is a snapshot of knowledge at one moment" type="warning">
    Facts baked into fine-tuning data (prices, policies, product specs) start going stale the moment the model ships. Whenever an answer depends on information that changes, fetch that information at request time through RAG or tool calls, and let fine-tuning handle only format and behavior.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Don't treat it as a multiple-choice question in interviews" type="tip">
    Real systems often use all three at once: the prompt defines the task, RAG supplies the grounding, and LoRA keeps format and judgment consistent. When asked "RAG or fine-tuning," first split the requirement into its knowledge and behavior parts, then propose a solution for each — far more seasoned than picking one.
  </Note>

  ### Recap: what decisions did the running example make along the way?

  | Step | Decision | Reason |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Try prompting first | 75% exact match | establish a baseline and see the types of problems |
  | Fix the format | add constrained decoding | format problems don't need fine-tuning |
  | Decide to fine-tune | QLoRA, r = 16, all linear layers | what remained was judgment and slang; only 24 GB GPUs available |
  | Prepare data | write a labeling guide; 2,000 train, 200 validation, 200 test, split by product | consistent labels, no leakage |
  | Train | learning rate 2e-4, 3 epochs, pick epoch 2 with the best validation score | avoid overfitting |
  | Evaluate | 90.5% exact match, aspect F1 0.878; regression tests found ordinary questions answered in JSON | proves it works, and surfaces the side effect |
  | Deploy | attach the adapter only on the review-extraction endpoint, with vLLM multi-LoRA serving | other requests are unaffected; one base serves many tasks |

  Once deployed, how this model holds up under concurrency and keeps latency and cost in check is the subject of the next page, [Inference](/docs/llm/inference).

  <Note title="Self-check: by now you should be able to answer">
    1. When does merging an adapter make sense, and when should you keep it separate? How should a QLoRA adapter be merged?
    2. How much memory does one base serving 3 tasks save compared with 3 complete models, and what else does multi-LoRA serving buy you?
    3. When is each of full fine-tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA appropriate?
    4. What are RAG and fine-tuning each responsible for, and when should they be combined?
    5. Why shouldn't facts that change be written into fine-tuning data?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Traps

  <Note title="Don't say a LoRA-tuned model is always slower at inference" type="danger">
    A LoRA can be merged back into the original weights, after which the model's structure is identical and there's no added latency at all. Only when adapters are kept separate for multi-LoRA serving is there a little extra computation in the LoRA branch.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Don't say QLoRA means quantizing a model to 4-bit for inference" type="danger">
    QLoRA is a **fine-tuning method**: during training the frozen base is compressed to 4-bit to save memory, while the adapters stay 16-bit and get trained. How you quantize for deployment is a separate question (see [Inference](/docs/llm/inference) Level 4).
  </Note>

  <Note title="Don't say fine-tuning will make the model remember the latest product knowledge" type="danger">
    Knowledge that changes and needs citations belongs in RAG. Fine-tuning is good at behavior: format, judgment, style.
  </Note>

  <Note title="LoRA saving memory doesn't mean an 8B model fits easily on a 24 GB GPU" type="warning">
    LoRA saves gradients and optimizer state, but the frozen fp16 base weights (about 16 GB) and activations remain. Fitting in 24 GB takes QLoRA plus activation checkpointing.
  </Note>

  <Note title="A higher rank isn't automatically better" type="warning">
    A higher rank means more parameters and more overfitting on small data. Start at 8 to 16 for behavioral tasks and go higher only if quality falls short.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Judging fine-tuning by training loss alone" type="warning">
    Falling training loss may just mean memorizing the training set. Look at task metrics on the validation set, report on a separate test set, and run regression tests on general ability and safety behavior.
  </Note>

  <Note title="A purely random test split can inflate the metrics" type="warning">
    Reviews of the same product or from the same user are highly similar, so a random split leaves "close relatives" of training data in the test set. Splitting by time, product, or user is more reliable.
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Connections
</Locale>

Prompt → not enough → RAG (knowledge) / Fine-tuning (behavior)
                              ↓
     full fine-tuning: 16 bytes/param → too expensive for most teams
                              ↓
     LoRA: freeze W, train B·A (rank r) → ~0.5% of params, mergeable
                              ↓
     QLoRA: NF4 base + double quantization + 16-bit adapters → one 24 GB GPU
                              ↓
     labeling guide → train / val / test → hyperparameters → best checkpoint
                              ↓
     evaluation: task metrics + regression (general, safety) → forgetting?
                              ↓
     deploy: merge + re-quantize, or multi-LoRA serving → Inference

content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Don't start round one with the Transformer paper. Build interview-grade notes in this order: Token → Attention & Transformer → Training → SFT/DPO → Fine-tuning → Inference.

  Every topic has to reach the same bar: **explain it + draw it + answer why + connect it to production**. Don't chase paper count.

  <CardGrid>
    <Card title="Tokenization" description="BPE / WordPiece; how tokens drive context window, latency, and cost." href="/docs/llm/tokenization" />

    <Card title="Attention & Transformer" description="Starting from encoders and decoders: self-attention, the Transformer block, decoder-only, KV cache, GQA." href="/docs/llm/transformer" />

    <Card title="Post-training" description="SFT → preference optimization → RLHF / DPO → instruction following." href="/docs/llm/post-training" />

    <Card title="Fine-tuning" description="Full / LoRA / QLoRA / PEFT. Must answer: RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompting." href="/docs/llm/fine-tuning" />

    <Card title="Inference" description="Prefill / decode, KV cache, batching, quantization." href="/docs/llm/inference" />
  </CardGrid>

  ## Plan for this column

  1. Tokenization: why token count matters more than word count; why Chinese and code cost more
  2. Attention & Transformer: go from encoders and decoders to decoder-only, draw a block, explain the KV cache and MHA / MQA / GQA

  4. Fine-tuning anchored on the LLaMA + QLoRA project; answer RAG vs fine-tuning first

title: Inference
description: 把模型部署成服务：TTFT / TPOT 与吞吐、continuous batching、PagedAttention、量化、投机解码、FlashAttention，以及多卡部署和每百万 token 的成本。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Training a model is a one-time cost; inference costs money on every request and every token. For most LLM applications, **latency and cost happen almost entirely at inference time**. In interviews, questions about the KV cache, batching, quantization, and tokens/sec are what separate "can call an API" from "understands LLM systems."

  This page assumes you've studied [Attention & Transformer](/docs/llm/transformer), especially Level 8: prefill and decode, why the KV cache can be cached, why decode is limited by memory bandwidth, GQA, and the basic idea of FlashAttention. That page covers the **principles**; this one covers **how to turn a model into a service that's fast, cheap, and holds up under concurrency**.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · What a request goes through | From arriving at the service to returning, what happens on the GPU? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Measuring an inference service | What are TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, and throughput? Why do latency and throughput pull against each other? | 35 min |
  | 2 · Batching | Why does batching raise throughput so much? What does static batching waste? How do continuous batching and chunked prefill work? | 45 min |
  | 3 · Managing KV cache memory | Why does reserving memory waste most of it? How does PagedAttention manage the KV cache like an operating system? What is prefix caching? | 45 min |
  | 4 · Quantization | How do int8, int4, and FP8 work out? Why are outliers the hard part? What do GPTQ and AWQ do? Is quantization always faster? | 45 min |
  | 5 · Speculative decoding | Why does "guess, then verify" speed things up without changing the output? When does it help and when doesn't it? | 35 min |
  | 6 · Kernel and runtime optimizations | Why is FlashAttention fast? What overhead do kernel fusion and CUDA Graphs remove? | 25 min |
  | 7 · Deployment, scaling, and cost | What if the model doesn't fit on one GPU? How do you pick a serving framework? How do you compute cost per million tokens? Self-host or use an API? | 40 min |

  Each Level ends with a few self-check questions — **if you can't answer them, don't move on yet**. The page takes about 5 hours over several sessions; `/drill` remembers where you stopped.

  One example runs through the whole page: **deploying the LLaMA 3 8B review-extraction model fine-tuned on the previous page, [Fine-tuning](/docs/llm/fine-tuning)**. We follow a typical request — about 1,000 tokens of instructions plus a review in, about 200 tokens of JSON out — starting from its latency and working all the way to how many such requests one 80 GB GPU can serve at once and what a million tokens costs.

  ## Must know

  * the full path of a request: queueing, tokenization, prefill, decode, detokenization, streaming
  * TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, throughput, P50 / P99, SLOs and goodput, the latency–throughput trade-off
  * why batching raises decode throughput; what static batching wastes; continuous batching and chunked prefill
  * KV cache memory budgets, fragmentation, PagedAttention's blocks and block tables, prefix caching
  * quantization math (absmax, groups, outliers), weight-only vs. weight + activation quantization, GPTQ / AWQ / FP8, KV cache quantization, and quantization's real effect on speed
  * the speculative decoding loop, acceptance rate and expected speedup, draft options, where it helps and where it doesn't
  * FlashAttention's IO-aware idea, kernel fusion, CUDA Graphs
  * tensor-parallel serving, scaling with replicas, mainstream serving frameworks, cost per million tokens, self-hosting vs. APIs
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Recap: what a request goes through on the GPU

  ### Recap first: prefill, decode, and the KV cache

  [Attention & Transformer](/docs/llm/transformer) Level 8 covered these; here's a quick pass using the page's running request:

  * **Prefill**: run the whole prompt through the model at once, computing every position in parallel, producing the first output token and storing every token's K and V in the KV cache
  * **Decode**: each step generates just 1 new token, reading all the model weights and the existing KV cache, then appending the new token's K and V
  * **KV cache size**: LLaMA 3 8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dims per head, fp16) takes **128 KiB per token**
  * **Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound**: each step needs little compute; the time goes into reading well over ten GB of weights and KV cache out of GPU memory

  That page covered the why; this one covers how to turn it into a service that works well.

  ### What's the full path of a request, from arriving at the service to returning?

  The running request: review extraction with the LLaMA 3 8B model fine-tuned on the previous page, [Fine-tuning](/docs/llm/fine-tuning), with **about 1,000 input tokens** (instructions plus the review) and **about 200 output tokens** (the JSON).

  ```
  ① the client sends an HTTP request
  ② it enters the scheduler queue and waits for GPU capacity       ← queueing time
  ③ the tokenizer turns the text into 1,000 token ids               (on the CPU)
  ④ Prefill: one forward pass over all 1,000 tokens
     → produces output token 1
     → writes the KV cache for 1,000 tokens (about 125 MiB)
  ⑤ Decode: generate 1 token per step and append to the KV cache, 199 steps in total
     → the KV cache ends at 1,200 tokens (about 150 MiB)
  ⑥ detokenize as tokens are generated and stream chunks back to the client
  ⑦ an end token or the length limit is reached → free this request's KV cache
  ```

  ### Why do prefill and decode have different bottlenecks?

  The two phases of the same request behave completely differently:

  | | Prefill | Decode |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Tokens processed at once | 1,000 in this example | 1 per step |
  | Main bottleneck | **compute**: big matrix multiplies, plus attention's n² | **memory bandwidth**: every step reads all the weights and the KV cache |
  | GPU compute cores | fully busy | mostly waiting for data |
  | User experience it drives | how soon the first word appears (TTFT) | how fast words keep coming (TPOT) |

  That difference decides **which phase** every later optimization targets:

  | Optimization | Mainly improves | On this page |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Batching | decode throughput | Level 2 |
  | Chunked prefill | long prompts blocking other requests' decode | Level 2 |
  | PagedAttention | KV cache memory utilization → concurrency | Level 3 |
  | Prefix caching | skipping repeated prefill | Level 3 |
  | Quantization | memory and decode speed | Level 4 |
  | Speculative decoding | decode speed | Level 5 |
  | FlashAttention | memory and speed for prefill and long context | Level 6 |

  <Note title="In interviews, split the request into its two phases before talking optimizations" type="tip">
    When asked "how would you optimize LLM inference," start with "inference has prefill and decode: prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and sets TPOT," then walk through techniques for each phase. That framework instantly brings order to a sprawling question.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: by now you should be able to answer">
    1. What do prefill and decode each do, and what's each one's bottleneck?
    2. Draw the full path of a request from arriving at the service to returning.
    3. For this request with 1,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens, roughly how big is the KV cache at the end?
    4. Do batching, quantization, and speculative decoding mainly optimize prefill or decode?
  </Note>
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Measuring an inference service

  "The service is slow" isn't something you can optimize. First pin down **which metric** is slow, and only then will you know whether to work on prefill, decode, or queueing.

  ### What are TTFT, TPOT, and end-to-end latency?

  | Metric | Meaning | Mainly determined by |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | **TTFT** (time to first token) | from sending the request to receiving the first output token | queueing + tokenization + prefill |
  | **TPOT** (time per output token) | the average gap between consecutive tokens during decode, also called ITL (inter-token latency) | how long each decode step takes |
  | **End-to-end latency** | from sending the request to receiving the complete response | TTFT + TPOT × number of output tokens |

  Work it out with the running request. Suppose TTFT = 150 ms, TPOT = 20 ms, and 200 output tokens:

  ```
  end-to-end latency = TTFT + TPOT × (200 − 1)
                     = 0.15 + 0.02 × 199
                     = 4.13 seconds

  the "typing speed" users perceive = 1 / TPOT = 1 / 0.02 = 50 tokens / second
  ```

  Note it's 199, not 200: the first token is already counted in TTFT.

  **Different scenarios care about different metrics:**

  | Scenario | Cares most about | Why |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Chat interface (streaming) | TTFT and TPOT | the user is watching the screen; a fast first word and a steady stream feel good |
  | Offline batch extraction (like this page's review task) | throughput and cost per unit | nobody's watching a screen, so processing a large batch at once is cheapest |
  | Multi-step agent calls | end-to-end latency per call × number of steps | one task may chain a dozen calls, and latency adds up |

  ### What is throughput, and how does it relate to latency?

  **Throughput** is how much the whole service processes per unit of time, usually measured as output tokens per second or completed requests per second.

  Latency is **one user's** view; throughput is **the whole system's** view, and they often pull against each other: the more requests one GPU serves at once, the more tokens it outputs per second in total, so throughput rises — but each request gets less of the compute, so everyone perceives slower speed. Why that happens, and by how much, Level 2 works out with numbers.

  ### What are P50 and P99, and why isn't the average enough?

  **P50**: sort every request's latency from smallest to largest and take the value at the 50% mark (the median). **P99**: the value at the 99% mark, representing the slowest 1% of requests.

  Suppose we measured end-to-end latency for 100 requests:

  ```
  90 requests  about 4 seconds
   9 requests  about 8 seconds     (e.g. especially long outputs, or caught in a queueing spike)
   1 request   30 seconds          (e.g. preempted and requeued)

  average = (90 × 4 + 9 × 8 + 1 × 30) / 100 = 4.62 seconds
  P50     = 4 seconds
  P99     = 8 seconds
  max     = 30 seconds
  ```

  An average of 4.62 seconds looks fine, but it's neither what most people experience (4 seconds) nor a reflection of the worst cases. **Production commitments are usually set on P99**, because at high request volumes 1% is a lot of users.

  Common sources of tail latency: especially long inputs or outputs, queueing during traffic spikes, and requests preempted and recomputed when memory runs short.

  An **SLO (service level objective)** writes those expectations down as explicit numbers, for example:

  ```
  P99 TTFT < 500 ms
  P99 TPOT < 50 ms
  ```

  ### What is goodput?

  **Goodput** is the number of requests completed per second **that also meet the SLO**.

  ```
  system A: completes 10 requests/s, but 30% exceed the SLO   → goodput = 7
  system B: completes 8 requests/s, all within the SLO        → goodput = 8
  ```

  By throughput, A is better; by goodput, B is. A system that runs huge batches for high throughput while blowing its latency targets isn't actually useful to anyone.

  ### How do you measure an inference service?

  * **Load-test with a realistic request distribution**: input and output lengths should follow production, not a single uniform short prompt
  * **Ramp up concurrency step by step**, recording throughput, P50, and P99 latency at each level, and plot the throughput–latency curve
  * **Find the highest concurrency that still meets the SLO** — that decides how much traffic one GPU can take, and therefore the cost (Level 7)

  Frameworks like vLLM ship with benchmarking scripts, and general-purpose load-testing tools work too.

  <Note title="Load tests need realistic input and output lengths" type="warning">
    Benchmark with 100-token prompts and 50-token outputs and throughput will look far higher than production: prefill is fast, the KV cache is small, and batches can grow huge. Plan hardware from numbers like that and you'll come up short after launch.
  </Note>

  <Note title="When asked “the service got slow, how do you investigate,” ask which metric first" type="tip">
    TTFT went up → check queueing, whether prompts got longer, whether prefill is being crowded out by other requests. TPOT went up → check whether the batch is too large, whether the KV cache is nearly full, whether long-prompt prefills are interrupting decode. End-to-end latency rose while TTFT and TPOT look normal → outputs got longer. Pin down the metric, then the phase — that's the basic approach to inference performance problems (more on [Latency](/docs/production/latency)).
  </Note>

  ## Level 2 · Batching: one GPU serving many requests

  ### Why does batching raise decode throughput so much?

  Back to Level 0's conclusion: **each decode step spends most of its time reading the weights out of GPU memory**, while the GPU's compute cores mostly sit idle.

  * **batch = 1**: read all the weights once (about 16 GB) and produce 1 token
  * **batch = 32**: read the weights once, do each of the 32 requests' small computations **in parallel**, and produce 32 tokens in one step

  The cost of reading the weights is shared across 32 requests; what's added is only each request's own computation and reading each request's KV cache, so each step gets only slightly slower.

  With assumed numbers:

  ```
  batch = 1:   20 ms per step → throughput = 1 / 0.020  = 50 tokens / second      TPOT per user 20 ms
  batch = 32:  25 ms per step → throughput = 32 / 0.025 = 1,280 tokens / second   TPOT per user 25 ms
  ```

  **Total throughput rises about 25x, while each user's perceived speed drops only 25%.** That's the latency–throughput tug-of-war from Level 1, and most of the time it's a very good deal.

  Keep growing the batch and computation eventually catches up with the read overhead: decode shifts from memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound, step time starts climbing noticeably with batch size, and throughput gains flatten. The other ceiling is memory: every request needs its own KV cache, so how big a batch can get also depends on whether the KV caches fit (Level 3).

  ### What does static batching waste?

  The simplest form of batching is **static batching**: gather a batch of requests, run them together, **wait until the whole batch has finished generating**, then move on to the next batch.

  The trouble is that output lengths within a batch vary widely. Suppose a batch of 3 requests needs 10, 50, and 200 tokens:

  ```
  step:        1 ────── 10 ────── 50 ───────────────── 200
  request A:   ██████████ done, then idles for 190 steps
  request B:   ██████████████████████ done, then idles for 150 steps
  request C:   ██████████████████████████████████████████ done
  request D:   waits outside until the batch finishes at step 200
  ```

  Compute the utilization of the GPU's "seats":

  ```
  3 seats × 200 steps = 600 seat-steps
  actually used = 10 + 50 + 200 = 260
  utilization = 260 / 600 = 43.3%
  ```

  More than half the time, seats sit empty. And new requests wait until the whole batch ends, so their TTFT gets very long.

  ### How does continuous batching fix it?

  **Continuous batching** moves scheduling from "per batch" to "per step": **after every decode step, the scheduler checks** — requests that have finished leave immediately, and waiting requests join immediately.

  ```
  step:        1 ────── 10 ────── 50 ───────────────── 200
  request A:   ██████████
  request D:             ███████████████████...    takes A's seat at step 11
  request B:   ██████████████████████
  request E:                         ██████████...  takes B's seat at step 51
  request C:   ██████████████████████████████████████████
  ```

  Seats stay almost always full, and new requests don't wait for a whole batch to end. The approach was first introduced by the Orca system and is now standard in serving frameworks like vLLM, TGI, and SGLang; TensorRT-LLM calls it in-flight batching.

  <Note title="Continuous batching is the biggest lever on inference cost" type="tip">
    On the same GPU, switching from static to continuous scheduling can take utilization from around half to nearly full — cutting the cost per token almost in half. When asked "how would you cut inference cost," continuous batching should be one of the first answers (how to compute the cost is in Level 7).
  </Note>

  ### Does a new request's prefill stall requests already decoding? What is chunked prefill?

  Yes. A new request has to go through prefill when it joins. If its prompt is long — say 8,000 tokens — that step is very compute-heavy (Level 0: prefill is compute-bound), and every other request decoding in the same step has to wait for it. The result: **one long prompt comes in and every user currently generating stalls for a moment, producing a TPOT spike**.

  **Chunked prefill**: split a long prompt's prefill into small chunks, process one chunk per step alongside the ongoing decode, and keep each step's total token count within a budget.

  ```
  unchunked:  8,000 prefill tokens packed into one step → that step is very slow and every decode request stalls
  chunked:    512 tokens per chunk → 8,000 / 512 ≈ 16 chunks over 16 steps
              each step = 1 prefill chunk + the ongoing decode tokens → decode keeps flowing smoothly
  ```

  The cost is a slightly longer TTFT for the long-prompt request itself, in exchange for steady TPOT for everyone else. vLLM supports chunked prefill.

  ### What does batching cost, and how do you set it per scenario?

  | | Small batch | Large batch |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | TPOT per user | low | higher |
  | Total throughput | low | high |
  | Cost per token | high | low |
  | KV cache memory | small | large, possibly the limit (Level 3) |
  | Good for | interactive chat, speed-sensitive | offline batch jobs, cost-sensitive |

  In the running example:

  * if review extraction is **an offline job over a full day of data**, push the batch as large as possible for throughput and cost
  * if the same model also serves **live chat**, cap the maximum batch according to the TPOT SLO from Level 1 — better to serve fewer users than to make everyone wait

  <Note title="With very large batches, other optimizations behave differently" type="warning">
    Once the batch is large enough that decode becomes compute-bound, the read overhead quantization saves (Level 4) is no longer the main bottleneck, so its speedup shrinks; speculative decoding (Level 5) relies on idle GPU compute, which large batches use up, so its gains fall too. When evaluating any inference optimization, state the batch size it was measured at.
  </Note>

  ## Level 3 · Managing KV cache memory: PagedAttention and prefix caching

  Level 2 noted that how big a batch can get is ultimately limited by whether the KV caches fit. This Level works out the memory math, then shows how vLLM pushes memory utilization from well under half to nearly full.

  ### On an 80 GB GPU, how much memory does the KV cache get?

  ```
  total GPU memory                                   80 GB
  serving frameworks typically use about 90%         about 72 GB     (vLLM's default gpu_memory_utilization = 0.9)
  LLaMA 3 8B fp16 weights                            about 16 GB
  activations, temporary buffers, etc.               a few GB
  left for the KV cache                              assume about 50 GiB
  ```

  The KV cache's unit cost (worked out in [Attention & Transformer](/docs/llm/transformer) Level 8):

  ```
  per token:  2 × 32 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB
  the running request (1,200 tokens):  1,200 × 128 KiB ≈ 150 MiB
  ```

  ### Why does reserving memory up front waste most of it?

  When a request arrives, **nobody knows how many tokens it will end up generating**. The simplest approach reserves one contiguous chunk per request sized for the maximum context — say 8,192 tokens:

  ```
  reserved per request:   8,192 × 128 KiB ≈ 1 GiB
  concurrent requests:    50 GiB / 1 GiB = 50
  actually used:          1,200 tokens ≈ 150 MiB
  wasted:                 1 − 150 / 1,024 ≈ 85%
  ```

  Of the reserved 1 GiB, this request uses only 15%. The waste comes from three places:

  | Kind of waste | What it is |
  | --- | --- |
  | **Internal fragmentation** | space that was reserved but never used (the 85% above) |
  | **External fragmentation** | enough free memory in total, but split into many non-contiguous pieces that can't hold a new contiguous reservation |
  | **No sharing** | many requests start with the same system prompt, yet each stores its own identical KV cache |

  The vLLM paper measured that earlier serving systems wasted 60% to 80% of KV cache memory this way.

  ### How does PagedAttention work?

  The idea comes from **virtual memory paging** in operating systems:

  * split the KV cache into **fixed-size blocks** — vLLM defaults to 16 tokens per block
  * a request's blocks **don't need to be contiguous** in GPU memory; they can live anywhere
  * each request has a **block table** mapping "logical block N" to "physical block M in GPU memory"
  * **allocate on demand**: request the next block only when the current one fills up

  ```
  request A's block table            physical blocks in GPU memory
  logical block 0  →  physical 7     [ 0 ][ 1 ][ 2:A ][ 3 ][ 4 ][ 5 ][ 6 ][ 7:A ] ...
  logical block 1  →  physical 2
  logical block 2  →  physical 12    (A's three blocks are scattered, and that works fine)
  ```

  During attention, a dedicated kernel follows the block table to fetch K and V from each physical block — hence the name "PagedAttention."

  **Work out the waste by hand:**

  ```
  a request with 1,200 tokens  →  1,200 / 16 = 75 blocks, exactly full, no waste
  a request with 1,210 tokens  →  needs 76 blocks; the last holds only 10 tokens, leaving 6 slots empty
  ```

  **Each request wastes less than one block** (at most 15 tokens' worth), instead of 85% under up-front reservation.

  Back to the 80 GB GPU:

  ```
  up-front reservation:  50 GiB / 1 GiB    = 50 requests
  PagedAttention:        50 GiB / 150 MiB  ≈ 341 requests of this size
  ```

  The number of concurrent requests the KV cache can hold rises about 7x (actual concurrency is still bounded by the TPOT SLO from Levels 1 and 2). The vLLM paper reported 2–4x higher throughput than the serving systems of the time.

  ### What if memory still runs out?

  A request's KV cache keeps growing as it generates. If every block is used up at some step, the scheduler has to **preempt** some requests to free blocks for others:

  * **Swap**: move the preempted request's KV blocks to CPU memory temporarily and bring them back later
  * **Recompute**: free its KV blocks outright and redo its prefill when its turn comes again

  Either way the preempted request slows down noticeably — one of the sources of tail latency from Level 1. That's why memory planning needs headroom rather than cutting it close to the average.

  ### What is prefix caching, and why is it so useful?

  Many requests begin identically: the same system prompt, the same format instructions, the same few-shot examples. Redoing prefill for that part on every request and storing a separate KV cache for each wastes both compute and memory.

  **Prefix caching**: cache the KV blocks for a shared prefix, and when a later request starts with exactly the same content, reuse those blocks and **skip that part of prefill**. PagedAttention's block structure makes sharing the same physical blocks across requests easy.

  Suppose that in the running request, 600 of the 1,000 input tokens are system instructions and format rules identical on every request:

  ```
  TTFT:     each request only needs prefill for the remaining 400 tokens

  memory:   100 requests online at once
            without sharing:  100 × 600 × 128 KiB ≈ 7.3 GiB
            with sharing:     600 × 128 KiB = 75 MiB, stored once
  ```

  vLLM supports automatic prefix caching, and SGLang manages prefix sharing with a radix tree (RadixAttention).

  <Note title="API providers' prompt caching works the same way" type="tip">
    Model APIs discount input tokens that hit the cache, and prefix caching is what's behind it: the KV cache for the shared prefix is already computed and stored, so no prefill is needed. When designing prompts, **put stable content (system prompt, tool definitions, long documents) first** and variable content after it to maximize hits (see [Caching](/docs/context/caching)).
  </Note>

  <Note title="The prefix must match token for token from the very first token" type="warning">
    A single differing token at the start means nothing after it can be reused. Putting the current time, a user name, or a request ID at the beginning of the prompt defeats prefix caching entirely.
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Quantization: storing the model in fewer bits

  [Fine-tuning](/docs/llm/fine-tuning) Level 3 covered the basic math of quantization (absmax, groups, outliers) to save memory **during training**. This Level covers quantization **for deployment**: how it affects memory, speed, and quality all at once.

  ### Why quantize for inference?

  Two benefits:

  1. **Less memory**: the same GPU can hold a bigger model, or leave more room for the KV cache and more concurrent requests
  2. **Faster decode**: decode is memory-bandwidth-bound (Level 0), so smaller weights mean less data to read each step

  LLaMA 3 8B's weight size at different precisions:

  ```
  fp16 / bf16    about 16.1 GB
  int8           about 8.0 GB
  int4           about 4.1 GB     (with one 16-bit scale per 128 weights)
  ```

  ### Work out int8 quantization by hand — how big is the error?

  Take the same weights from Fine-tuning Level 3, this time quantized to int8 (values from −127 to 127):

  ```
  w      = [0.12, −0.50, 0.33, 0.90]
  scale  = 0.90 / 127 = 0.00709
  q      = round(w / scale) = [17, −71, 47, 127]
  w'     = q × scale = [0.1205, −0.5031, 0.3331, 0.9000]
  error  = [−0.0005, 0.0031, −0.0031, 0.0000]
  ```

  Compare with the int4 result on that page, where the largest error was 0.056. **int8's largest error is just 0.0031 — more than an order of magnitude smaller.** Halving the bits sharply reduces how many values can be represented, and the error grows with it. That's why int8 is usually nearly lossless while int4 needs more careful methods.

  ### Quantize only the weights, or the activations too?

  | Approach | Common notation | At compute time | Mainly speeds up | Requires |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | **Weight-only** | W4A16, W8A16 | weights are dequantized to 16-bit on the fly | small-batch decode (less data to read) | optimized kernels |
  | **Weights and activations** | W8A8, FP8 | matrix multiplies run directly in 8-bit | prefill and large batches (the computation itself shrinks) | hardware support; FP8, for example, needs newer GPUs |

  "W4A16" means 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations.

  **Why are activations harder to quantize?** Research has found that a few channels in large models' activations take on values far larger than the rest (outliers), and the effect grows with model size. Recall the Fine-tuning Level 3 example: one outlier of 8.0 squashed every other number in its group to 0. Weights can be processed carefully offline, but activations are computed live for every request and are much harder to control.

  Methods like SmoothQuant **move the difficulty from activations to weights**: divide the outlier activation channels by a factor and multiply the corresponding weights by the same factor. The math comes out identical, but the activations are now smooth and easy to quantize.

  ### What do GPTQ and AWQ each do?

  The simplest approach rounds every weight to the nearest int4 (round-to-nearest), which often costs noticeable quality. Better methods run a small batch of **calibration data** through the model to see what matters most:

  * **GPTQ**: quantizes weights column by column. The error introduced by each quantized column is compensated by adjusting the weights not yet quantized, keeping the layer's overall output as unchanged as possible
  * **AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization)**: observes that only a small fraction of weight channels really matter — the ones multiplied by large activations — and scales those channels up before quantization to protect them from error

  Both are usually used for **weight-only int4**, the most common format for deploying open models at 4 bits.

  <Note title="Calibration data should look like real traffic" type="tip">
    The data you calibrate with determines which inputs the model holds up best on. The running review-extraction model should be calibrated with real review requests, not generic text. Mentioning this in an interview shows you've actually deployed quantized models.
  </Note>

  ### Can the KV cache be quantized too?

  Yes. Switching the KV cache from fp16 to FP8 halves it per token:

  ```
  fp16:  128 KiB per token    →  50 GiB holds about 341 requests of 1,200 tokens (Level 3)
  FP8:   64 KiB per token     →  50 GiB holds about 682
  ```

  With long context and high concurrency, this often raises concurrency more than quantizing the weights does. vLLM supports an FP8 KV cache. The quality impact is usually small, but always measure it on long-context tasks.

  ### Is quantization always faster? How much quality does it cost?

  **Not necessarily faster.**

  * at small batch, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, and weight-only int4 reads 4x less data, so it's usually noticeably faster
  * at large batch, decode has already become compute-bound (Level 2), and the dequantization overhead can cancel out the gain
  * without optimized kernels, int4 can even be slower than fp16

  **Quality has to be measured.**

  * int8 and FP8 are usually close to lossless
  * int4 typically loses a little, and the drop is often more noticeable for **small models, math and code, and long context**

  For the running example, the full process is:

  ```
  ① merge the LoRA adapter into the fp16 base (Fine-tuning Level 6)
  ② calibrate with real review data and quantize to int4 with AWQ
  ③ rerun the metrics on the same 200-example test set and compare exact match against the fp16 version
  ④ load-test at the target batch size to confirm speed and P99 latency actually improved
  ```

  <Note title="Don't say int4 quantization makes it 4x faster" type="danger">
    Weights 4x smaller doesn't mean 4x faster. The real speedup depends on batch size, whether decode is bandwidth- or compute-bound, and whether optimized kernels exist — at large batch there may be no speedup at all. When reporting quantization gains, state the batch size and test setup alongside them.
  </Note>

  ## Level 5 · Speculative decoding: guess first, then verify in one pass

  ### What does speculative decoding take advantage of?

  Put two facts from earlier together and you have the whole idea:

  1. **Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound** (Level 0): each step's time goes mostly to reading weights, leaving plenty of GPU compute idle
  2. **One forward pass produces predictions at every position** (teacher forcing from [Attention & Transformer](/docs/llm/transformer) Level 5): feed in k tokens and a single pass tells you what the model would predict at each of those k positions

  So if you can **cheaply guess the next k tokens**, the large model needs only **one forward pass** to check all k of them. The cost of reading the weights stays the same, but you may confirm several tokens at once.

  ### How does speculative decoding work? Walk through one round

  Two roles:

  * **Target model**: the large model you actually want to use — here, our LLaMA 3 8B
  * **Draft model**: a small model from the same family that shares the tokenizer, whose job is to guess quickly

  The running example outputs JSON. The model has generated `{"sentiment": "` so far, and then (the token splits are illustrative):

  ```
  ① the draft model guesses 4 tokens in a row:   mixed   ",   "positive   ":

  ② the target model takes all 4 tokens at once in one forward pass
     and gets its own prediction at each position:

     position   draft guessed   target predicts   result
     1          mixed           mixed             ✓ accept
     2          ",              ",                ✓ accept
     3          "positive       "positive         ✓ accept
     4          ":              ": [              ✗ mismatch, stop here

  ③ accept the first 3 draft tokens, plus the target's own prediction at position 4
     → one target pass produced 4 tokens
  ```

  If all 4 are accepted, the target's prediction at the last position gives a bonus token too — 5 in one pass.

  This shows the comparison under greedy decoding (always the most likely token). When sampling, verification uses a rejection-sampling rule to decide what to accept, which **guarantees the final output distribution is exactly the same as generating one token at a time with the target model alone**.

  ### How much faster is it? Compute the expectation

  Let α be the probability each draft token is accepted (the acceptance rate), with k guesses per round. The average number of tokens produced per target forward pass is:

  ```
  E = (1 − α^(k+1)) / (1 − α)
  ```

  With k = 4:

  | Acceptance rate α | Average tokens per target pass | Speedup after draft cost |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0.5 | 1.94 tokens | 1.38x |
  | 0.8 | 3.36 tokens | 2.40x |
  | 0.9 | 4.10 tokens | 2.93x |

  The last column assumes one draft token costs 0.1x a target step, so a round costs `1 + 4 × 0.1 = 1.4` in total and the speedup is E / 1.4.

  **Conclusion: the acceptance rate is everything.** Raising it from 0.5 to 0.9 takes the speedup from 1.4x to nearly 3x; if it's too low, the cost of wrong guesses can even make things slower overall.

  <Note title="Structured output like JSON is ideal for speculative decoding" type="tip">
    Much of JSON is completely predictable: brackets, quotes, commas, fixed field names. A draft model guesses these easily, so acceptance rates are high. Review extraction, code completion, and templated replies are all scenarios where speculative decoding pays off well.
  </Note>

  ### Besides a small model, what other ways are there to guess?

  | Approach | How it guesses | Characteristics |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | **Small draft model** | a small model from the same family generates first | general-purpose; takes extra memory and its own KV cache |
  | **Prompt lookup / n-gram** | copy a matching continuation straight from the input | needs no extra model; works well when output quotes the input heavily (rewriting, extraction, answering from retrieved documents) |
  | **Medusa** | add several extra output heads to the target model that predict multiple future positions at once | no separate draft model, but the heads need training |
  | **EAGLE** | a very light module guesses using the target model's internal features | usually higher acceptance than a separate small model; also needs training |

  ### When does it help, and when doesn't it?

  | Helps | Doesn't help or even slows things down |
  | --- | --- |
  | small batches and interactive use, with idle GPU compute | very large batches where decode is already compute-bound and there's no idle compute (Level 2) |
  | predictable output: JSON, code, templated text | hard-to-guess output: creative writing at high temperature |
  | draft and target are similar, so acceptance is high | draft and target differ a lot, so acceptance is low |
  | memory to spare | memory so tight the draft model and its KV cache don't fit |

  <Note title="Don't say speculative decoding lowers output quality" type="danger">
    Correctly implemented speculative decoding produces **exactly the same** output distribution as generating one token at a time with the target model; the draft model affects only speed, not results. It's a lossless speedup.
  </Note>
