<Locale lang="en">
  Cost questions come in two forms: "estimate the monthly bill for this traffic" tests arithmetic; "the bill tripled — what do you do?" tests whether you know where money goes. "Cache and use a smaller model" invites follow-ups like "at what hit rate does caching pay off?" and "if the small model fails and escalates to a human, did you save anything?"

  This page covers billing line items, a hand-calculated RAG bill, **why agent loops grow tokens roughly quadratically**, quantified caching/batching/routing savings, and budget guardrails with attribution.

  Same running example. **Illustrative prices**: large model $3 / M input, $15 / M output; small model $1 / $5. These match the order of magnitude of mid- and small-tier models in 2025–2026; check official pricing before interviews — the method matters more than the numbers.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Line items | What does a request pay for? Why is output pricier? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Monthly bill | What does a 100k-DAU support bot cost per month? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Agent cost curve | Why is a 20-turn agent far more than 20× a single call? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Quantified levers | What do caching, batch, routing, and trimming save — and when not? | 40 min |
  | 4 · Unit economics | Why cost per resolved task, not cost per request? | 20 min |
  | 5 · Guardrails and attribution | How do you stop runaway loops and attribute spend? | 20 min |

  **Levels 1–3 are the core** — work them on paper. About 2.5 hours.

  ## Must know

  * line items: input, cache write, cache read, output including thinking, embeddings, rerank, tools/search, infra, humans
  * the monthly formula, computed to order of magnitude in two minutes
  * cumulative agent input ≈ `T × S + Δ × T(T-1)/2`, and how caching flattens it
  * caching break-even, when Batch APIs apply, expected cost of a cascade
  * cost per resolved task = total cost / resolved tasks, including retries and human fallback
  * guardrails: per-task token/turn caps, tenant quotas, anomaly detection, kill switch
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Line items

  ### What does one request pay for?

  Input tokens (system prompt, tool definitions, history, retrieved docs — usually the largest *count*), cache writes (~1.25× input at some providers, more for longer TTLs), cache reads (often ~10% of input price; Anthropic explicit caching ≈ 0.1×, OpenAI automatic caching varies by model), output tokens including tool-call arguments and **thinking tokens** (often the largest *spend*), embeddings, reranking, tool/search fees, infra (vector DB, trace storage, GPUs), and human escalation — frequently the real dominant cost.

  ### Why is output 4–8× the price of input?

  Input is processed in parallel during prefill at high GPU utilization; output decodes one token at a time, rereading all weights for each. Two corollaries: thinking tokens bill at output rates, and cutting 500 output tokens saves about as much as cutting 2,500 input tokens at a 5× ratio.

  <Note type="warning" title="Tokens people forget">
    Tool definitions on every call (40 MCP tools can add 10–20k tokens), images, retries, and structured-output repair calls.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. List six line items. Which dominates token count? Which dominates spend?
    2. Why does trimming output often save more than trimming input?
    3. Why do many MCP tools raise cost?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Monthly bill

  ### 100k DAU, 5k input, 1k output — what's the monthly cost?

  State assumptions first: 3 requests per user per day → 300k requests/day; large model at $3/$15; 30 days.

  ```
  per request = 5,000 × 3/1M + 1,000 × 15/1M = $0.015 + $0.015 = $0.030
  per day = $9,000;  per month ≈ $270,000
  ```

  Input and output contribute equally: 5× the tokens at 1/5 the price.

  ### With caching?

  4,000 of the 5,000 input tokens are a stable prefix. At 95% hit rate and cache reads at 0.1×, average input cost falls to about $0.0049, the request to $0.0199, and the month to ≈ $179k (−34%). Output is now three-quarters of spend; halving answer length saves another ~$67k.

  ### With routing?

  Send 70% of simple intents to the small model ($1/$5): about $0.0066 per request, blended ≈ $0.0106, ≈ $95k/month. That's model spend only — routing errors have a quality cost (Level 4).

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    Give the order of magnitude in 30 seconds, then say where it goes and what you'd cut next, with the eval you'd run before routing.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Compute the base monthly bill from memory.
    2. After caching, why does output dominate and what do you cut next?
    3. Why isn't routing savings automatically real savings?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Agent cost curve

  ### Why do multi-step tool calls blow up budgets?

  LLM APIs are stateless; every turn resends the full history. With fixed prefix `S`, per-turn growth `Δ`, and `T` turns:

  ```
  total input ≈ T × S + Δ × T(T-1)/2
  ```

  With S=8k, Δ=2k: 1 turn ≈ 8k tokens ($0.024); 10 turns ≈ 170k ($0.51); 20 turns ≈ 540k ($1.62); 50 turns ≈ 2.85M ($8.55). Twenty turns cost 67×, not 20×.

  ### Why does caching matter so much for agents?

  Agent history is append-only, so nearly the whole input of each turn hits the prefix cache; only the new `Δ` pays full or write price. Twenty turns drop from $1.62 to about $0.32 — roughly 5× cheaper. That's why harnesses never edit earlier history, reorder tools, or put timestamps in the system prompt, and why the 2026-07-28 MCP spec asks servers to return `tools/list` in deterministic order.

  ### What else cuts agent cost?

  Clear stale tool results (costs one cache break — see [Context Compaction](/docs/ai-native/compaction)), isolate exploration in sub-agents that return short summaries, truncate tool output, and cap turns and tokens.

  <Note type="danger" title="Wrong claim">
    "Each turn only sends the new message, so cost is linear in turns." The API is stateless; without caching, cumulative input grows roughly quadratically.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Write the formula and evaluate S=8k, Δ=2k, T=10.
    2. Why is agent history ideal for prefix caching, and what breaks it?
    3. Name two non-caching ways to cut agent cost.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Quantified levers

  ### When does caching not pay off?

  Write once at 1.25×, read n times at 0.1×: break-even is `1.25 + 0.1n < n + 1`, i.e. n > 0.28 — one reuse within the TTL pays. It loses when prefixes aren't stable, traffic is too sparse for the TTL, or prefixes are below the provider minimum (often 1,024 tokens).

  ### When can you use a Batch API?

  About half price for results within 24 hours: offline evals, bulk extraction, nightly summaries, labeling. Nightly LLM-as-judge sampling of support conversations belongs here.

  ### What does a cascade cost?

  `expected = c_small + p_escalate × c_large`. With $0.0066 and $0.0199: 20% escalation saves 47%, 50% saves 17%, 70% costs 3% *more* — plus the serial latency of escalated requests. See [Model Routing](/docs/application/model-routing).

  ### How do you cut cost without hurting quality?

  Pair every lever with a quality guard: prefix caching is semantically neutral; semantic caching risks near-duplicate questions with different answers and stale live data; routing needs per-intent accuracy and escalation monitoring; output caps need `finish_reason` checks; context trimming needs recall evals; lower thinking effort needs a hard-case set.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Derive the caching break-even. When does caching lose?
    2. Which support workloads can use Batch?
    3. At what escalation rate does the cascade cost more than the large model?
    4. Why is semantic caching dangerous for order questions?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Unit economics

  ### Why cost per resolved task?

  Small model: $0.02 per conversation, 60% resolution; large model: $0.06, 85%. With $3 human escalation, total cost is $1.22 vs $0.51 — the "expensive" model is less than half the cost. General form: `(model + tools + infra + retries + human fallback) / resolved tasks`. For coding agents, cost per merged PR.

  ### When does self-hosting make sense?

  It hinges on GPU utilization: GPUs bill whether busy or idle. Large, steady, predictable traffic favors self-hosting; spiky traffic favors APIs. Add engineering headcount, upgrades, and multi-region availability. Compliance, fine-tuning, and latency control often matter more than raw savings.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    Before listing levers, say the goal is cost per resolved task, not price per token.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Explain with the numbers why the pricier model is cheaper overall.
    2. What's the right denominator for a coding agent?
    3. What mainly decides whether self-hosting pays off?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 5 · Guardrails and attribution

  ### How do you stop runaway spend?

  Layer the guardrails: per call (`max_tokens`, thinking budget), per task (max turns, cumulative token/dollar cap, then hand off to a human), per tenant (quotas, rate limits), and global (spend anomaly alerts, a kill switch per feature). Add progress detection: N identical tool calls or identical errors in a row means the agent is stuck.

  ### How do you make cost data actionable?

  Record `tenant_id, feature, model, prompt_version, input/cached/cache-write/output/reasoning tokens, cost_usd, task_id, turn_index` per call. Then decompose a spike as requests × tokens per request × price × model mix, slice by tenant, feature, and prompt version, and look for loops, retry storms, or a cache-hit drop after a release.

  <Note type="tip" title="The 3× bill question">
    Decompose the factors, slice to locate, then check loops, retry storms, and cache breakage.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Design four layers of agent cost guardrails.
    2. How would trace fields locate a 3× spike in ten minutes?
    3. How do you tell a stuck agent from a working one?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "Agent cost is linear in turns." (Roughly quadratic without caching.)
    * "A smaller model saves 70%." (Ignores escalation, failure, humans.)
    * "Thinking tokens are free / billed as input." (Billed as output.)
    * "Streaming saves money." (Same tokens.)
  </Note>

  <Note type="warning" title="Likely follow-ups">
    * State assumptions before estimating.
    * Use real hit rates, never 100%.
    * Semantic caching misfires on personalized and live data.
    * Prices change; emphasize the method.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Mechanics: [Tokenization](/docs/llm/tokenization), [Inference](/docs/llm/inference), [Prompt Caching](/docs/context/caching)
  * Same section: [Latency](/docs/production/latency), [Scaling](/docs/production/scaling), [Observability](/docs/production/observability)
  * Applied: [Model Routing](/docs/application/model-routing), [Model Selection](/docs/application/model-selection), [Context Compaction](/docs/ai-native/compaction)

  ## Interview questions

  **Levels 0–1**

  1. What does an AI request pay for, and why is output pricier?
  2. Estimate monthly cost for 100k DAU at 5k in / 1k out.
  3. How does prefix caching change the bill's structure?

  **Levels 2–3**

  4. Why do agent token costs grow roughly quadratically?
  5. Why is prefix caching critical for agents, and what breaks it?
  6. Where's the caching break-even?
  7. When does a cascade cost more?

  **Levels 4–5**

  8. Why cost per resolved task?
  9. When does self-hosting beat APIs?
  10. How do you design cost guardrails for agents?
  11. The bill tripled overnight — how do you investigate?

  ## Sources

  * [Anthropic: Pricing](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/about-claude/pricing), [Prompt caching](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching), [Batch processing](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/batch-processing)
  * [OpenAI: Pricing](https://openai.com/api/pricing/), [Prompt caching](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-caching), [Batch API](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch)
  * [Anthropic Engineering: Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
  * [MCP 2026-07-28 changelog](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog)
</Locale>

Input and output contribute equally: 5× the tokens at 1/5 the price.

  ### With caching?

  4,000 of the 5,000 input tokens are a stable prefix. At 95% hit rate and cache reads at 0.1×, average input cost falls to about $0.0049, the request to $0.0199, and the month to ≈ $179k (−34%). Output is now three-quarters of spend; halving answer length saves another ~$67k.

  ### With routing?

  Send 70% of simple intents to the small model ($1/$5): about $0.0066 per request, blended ≈ $0.0106, ≈ $95k/month. That's model spend only — routing errors have a quality cost (Level 4).

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    Give the order of magnitude in 30 seconds, then say where it goes and what you'd cut next, with the eval you'd run before routing.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Compute the base monthly bill from memory.
    2. After caching, why does output dominate and what do you cut next?
    3. Why isn't routing savings automatically real savings?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Agent cost curve

  ### Why do multi-step tool calls blow up budgets?

  LLM APIs are stateless; every turn resends the full history. With fixed prefix
total input ≈ T × S + Δ × T(T-1)/2

With S=8k, Δ=2k: 1 turn ≈ 8k tokens ($0.024); 10 turns ≈ 170k ($0.51); 20 turns ≈ 540k ($1.62); 50 turns ≈ 2.85M ($8.55). Twenty turns cost 67×, not 20×.

  ### Why does caching matter so much for agents?

  Agent history is append-only, so nearly the whole input of each turn hits the prefix cache; only the new

pays full or write price. Twenty turns drop from $1.62 to about $0.32 — roughly 5× cheaper. That's why harnesses never edit earlier history, reorder tools, or put timestamps in the system prompt, and why the 2026-07-28 MCP spec asks servers to return

in deterministic order.

  ### What else cuts agent cost?

  Clear stale tool results (costs one cache break — see [Context Compaction](/docs/ai-native/compaction)), isolate exploration in sub-agents that return short summaries, truncate tool output, and cap turns and tokens.

  <Note type="danger" title="Wrong claim">
    "Each turn only sends the new message, so cost is linear in turns." The API is stateless; without caching, cumulative input grows roughly quadratically.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Write the formula and evaluate S=8k, Δ=2k, T=10.
    2. Why is agent history ideal for prefix caching, and what breaks it?
    3. Name two non-caching ways to cut agent cost.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Quantified levers

  ### When does caching not pay off?

  Write once at 1.25×, read n times at 0.1×: break-even is

, i.e. n > 0.28 — one reuse within the TTL pays. It loses when prefixes aren't stable, traffic is too sparse for the TTL, or prefixes are below the provider minimum (often 1,024 tokens).

  ### When can you use a Batch API?

  About half price for results within 24 hours: offline evals, bulk extraction, nightly summaries, labeling. Nightly LLM-as-judge sampling of support conversations belongs here.

  ### What does a cascade cost?

. With $0.0066 and $0.0199: 20% escalation saves 47%, 50% saves 17%, 70% costs 3% *more* — plus the serial latency of escalated requests. See [Model Routing](/docs/application/model-routing).

  ### How do you cut cost without hurting quality?

  Pair every lever with a quality guard: prefix caching is semantically neutral; semantic caching risks near-duplicate questions with different answers and stale live data; routing needs per-intent accuracy and escalation monitoring; output caps need

checks; context trimming needs recall evals; lower thinking effort needs a hard-case set.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Derive the caching break-even. When does caching lose?
    2. Which support workloads can use Batch?
    3. At what escalation rate does the cascade cost more than the large model?
    4. Why is semantic caching dangerous for order questions?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Unit economics

  ### Why cost per resolved task?

  Small model: $0.02 per conversation, 60% resolution; large model: $0.06, 85%. With $3 human escalation, total cost is $1.22 vs $0.51 — the "expensive" model is less than half the cost. General form:

. For coding agents, cost per merged PR.

  ### When does self-hosting make sense?

  It hinges on GPU utilization: GPUs bill whether busy or idle. Large, steady, predictable traffic favors self-hosting; spiky traffic favors APIs. Add engineering headcount, upgrades, and multi-region availability. Compliance, fine-tuning, and latency control often matter more than raw savings.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    Before listing levers, say the goal is cost per resolved task, not price per token.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Explain with the numbers why the pricier model is cheaper overall.
    2. What's the right denominator for a coding agent?
    3. What mainly decides whether self-hosting pays off?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 5 · Guardrails and attribution

  ### How do you stop runaway spend?

  Layer the guardrails: per call (

, thinking budget), per task (max turns, cumulative token/dollar cap, then hand off to a human), per tenant (quotas, rate limits), and global (spend anomaly alerts, a kill switch per feature). Add progress detection: N identical tool calls or identical errors in a row means the agent is stuck.

  ### How do you make cost data actionable?

  Record

title: Latency
description: 从 prefill / decode 机制出发拆 TTFT、TPOT 与 P95：手算关键路径、排队、思考 token 与尾延迟，再谈优化杠杆和延迟预算。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  "How would you reduce latency?" comes up in almost every AI engineering interview. An answer of "stream, use a smaller model, add caching" collapses under one follow-up: "Why does TTFT depend on prompt length while TPOT mostly doesn't?" This page starts from how one token is produced on a GPU and builds up to critical-path math, queueing, reasoning models, tail latency, and latency budgets.

  It assumes you know that transformers generate token by token. The low-level prefill/decode/KV-cache mechanics live in Levels 0–3 of [Inference](/docs/llm/inference); here we take the conclusions an API consumer needs and turn them into tools for estimating and debugging.

  Running example: the pet-food support bot. A user asks whether order `20240915`, which hasn't arrived, can be refunded. The system calls the order API, retrieves refund policy `P-17 v3`, reranks, and asks the model to answer. Millisecond values are designed for hand calculation and sized from public hardware specs; they are not vendor measurements.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Metrics | What are TTFT, TPOT, E2E, and P95? What does the user actually perceive? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Where a token comes from | Why does TTFT track prompt length and TPOT track memory bandwidth? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Critical-path math | How do serial stages, parallel stages, and agent loops add up? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Queueing and tails | Why does P95 explode at 90% utilization? Why does fan-out amplify tails? | 30 min |
  | 4 · Reasoning models | How do thinking tokens change what "first token" means? | 20 min |
  | 5 · Optimization levers | Which segment does each lever improve, and at what cost? | 30 min |
  | 6 · Budgets, SLOs, regressions | How do you set, measure, and protect a latency budget? | 20 min |

  **Levels 1 and 3 are the core**: the first lets you explain *why*, the second lets you explain *why only at peak*. About 3 hours; split into two sessions.

  ## Must know

  * precise definitions of TTFT / TPOT / E2E / P95, plus time-to-first-meaningful-content
  * prefill is compute-bound, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound; estimate a TPOT floor from bandwidth
  * critical path: max for parallel, sum for serial, multiply by loop iterations for agents
  * queueing intuition: waiting time grows nonlinearly as utilization approaches 1
  * fan-out tail amplification: `1 - 0.99^N`
  * for reasoning models, time to first *visible* token = TTFT + thinking tokens × TPOT
  * lever taxonomy: do less work, parallelize, queue less, show something earlier
  * percentiles don't add; state the denominator; compute experience from end-to-end traces
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Metrics

  ### What exactly are TTFT, TPOT, E2E, and P95?

  ```
  t0 request sent ──► t1 first output token ──► … one token every TPOT … ──► t2 last token
  ```

  * **TTFT**: `t1 - t0`. Network, queueing, prefill over the whole input, and the first decode step.
  * **TPOT** (a.k.a. inter-token latency): average gap between output tokens; its inverse is tokens/s.
  * **E2E**: `t2 - t0 ≈ TTFT + output_tokens × TPOT`.
  * **P95**: sort all latencies; 95% are at or below this value. Not the mean of the slowest 5%.

  If the 95th of 100 sorted E2E values is 4.8 s, P95 is 4.8 s even if the mean is 2.1 s — means get diluted by fast requests, which is why SLOs use percentiles.

  <Note type="warning" title="Two ways to compute TPOT">
    Averaging total decode time hides a 2-second stall; the per-gap distribution exposes it at P99. Complaints about streaming "hiccups" need the per-gap view.
  </Note>

  ### What does the user actually perceive?

  TTFT is a model-side metric. Users perceive time to the first *meaningful* content. A JSON wrapper, a filler sentence, or hidden thinking tokens all produce a fast TTFT with nothing useful on screen. For voice, what matters is the first playable audio: end of ASR + first LLM sentence + first TTS chunk. Measure at least TTFT, time to first useful content, and completion.

  <Note title="Voice budgets are tight">
    Human turn-taking gaps are a few hundred milliseconds; voice agents typically aim for roughly one second voice-to-voice. Before quoting the 1.2 s figure from the Voice project, pin down its start and end points.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Write E2E in terms of TTFT, TPOT, and output length.
    2. What does P95 = 4.8 s mean, and why not use the mean?
    3. Give two cases where TTFT is fast but the user still waits.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Where a token comes from

  ### Why does TTFT track prompt length?

  Serving has two phases. **Prefill** pushes the whole input through the model in parallel, writes the KV cache, and emits the first token. **Decode** produces one token per step, reusing the KV cache.

  Prefill processes thousands of tokens at once and saturates the matrix units — it's **compute-bound**, roughly `2 × params × input_tokens` FLOPs plus attention that grows quadratically. A 70B model on a 20k-token prompt is about 2.8e15 FLOPs; against an H100's ~1e15 dense BF16 FLOPs/s at realistic utilization, that's seconds. Tensor parallelism shortens it, but long prompts always cost TTFT.

  ### Why does TPOT track memory bandwidth instead?

  Each decode step computes one token but must **read every weight from HBM**. Little math, lots of bytes — **memory-bandwidth-bound**.

  ```
  70B × 2 bytes ≈ 140 GB;  H100 HBM ≈ 3.35 TB/s
  batch-1 TPOT floor ≈ 140 / 3350 ≈ 42 ms/token (~24 tok/s)
  ```

  Real systems beat this with tensor parallelism (each GPU reads 1/8), quantization (fewer bytes), continuous batching (one weight read serves 64 requests — throughput up, per-request TPOT roughly flat), and speculative decoding (several tokens per weight read). As an API consumer you mostly influence TPOT by picking the model and provider.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview one-liner">
    "Prefill is compute-bound so TTFT scales with input length — that's why prefix caching cuts TTFT. Decode is memory-bound, so TPOT is about bytes read per step, which is what quantization, batching, and speculative decoding attack."
  </Note>

  ### How do the KV cache and prompt caching relate?

  The KV cache is per-request: step 100 doesn't recompute the first 99 tokens. Prompt caching is cross-request: if two requests share an identical token prefix, the provider reuses that prefix's KV and **skips its prefill**. It lowers cost and TTFT, not TPOT, and needs an exact prefix — a timestamp at the top of the system prompt breaks every hit. Details in [Prompt Caching](/docs/context/caching).

  <Note type="danger" title="Wrong claim">
    "Output tokens cost more because they're harder to compute." Closer to the truth: each decode step reads all weights at low GPU utilization, so an output token occupies far more hardware time than an input token in prefill.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What bottlenecks prefill and decode, and why?
    2. Estimate the batch-1 TPOT floor from 140 GB and 3.35 TB/s.
    3. Why does continuous batching raise throughput but not change per-request TPOT much?
    4. Does prompt caching help TTFT or TPOT? What breaks it?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Critical-path arithmetic

  ### How do serial and parallel stages add up?

  Serial stages add, parallel stages take the max; the user waits on the longest path through the dependency graph.

  ```
  TTFT ≈ 40 + max(180, 250) + 120 + 700 = 1,110 ms
  E2E  ≈ 1,110 + 100 × 25          = 3,610 ms
  ```

  Speeding up the order API changes nothing — it's off the critical path. Decode is usually the largest single term. If retrieval needs order status, the two become serial and TTFT becomes 1,290 ms. Draw the real dependency graph first.

  ### How do agent loops change the math?

  Every loop iteration pays a model TTFT plus output tokens (tool-call arguments are output too). Three iterations — two tool calls and a final answer — come to about 8.4 s, versus 3.6 s for a fixed pipeline. Agent flexibility is paid for in serial model calls, and TTFT rises each turn as context grows unless the prefix is cached.

  Levers: parallel tool calls in a single turn, moving deterministic steps out of the loop into code, a small model for routing, and keeping intermediate turns terse.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    For "our agent is slow," start with: "I'd lay out each model call and tool call; the critical path is usually N serial TTFTs plus outputs." Then give parallel tool calls, workflow-ifying fixed steps, and small-model routing.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why max for parallel stages? What does optimizing an off-path stage buy you?
    2. How does TTFT change when retrieval depends on order state?
    3. Why is the agent loop slower than a pipeline, and how do you shorten it?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Queueing and tail latency

  ### Why does the same request get slower at peak?

  Queueing. With utilization `ρ`, the M/M/1 intuition is `wait ≈ service_time × ρ / (1 - ρ)`: 1× at 50%, 4× at 80%, 9× at 90%, 19× at 95%. The growth is nonlinear, which is why inference fleets keep headroom and why provider TTFT jitters at peak. Queues live in your worker pool, your outbound connection pool, the provider gateway, and the GPU batch scheduler.

  Diagnose by bucketing TTFT by input length × time of day. Long-prompt buckets slow at all hours → prefill work. Every bucket slow at peak → queueing or throttling. Cache-hit bucket fast → caching works. A handful of extreme outliers → tail causes like retries, cold starts, long outputs.

  ### Why does fan-out amplify tails?

  If each downstream call is slow 1% of the time and you fan out to N, `P(slow) = 1 - 0.99^N`: 9.6% at N=10, 39.5% at N=50 — the core point of *The Tail at Scale*. Mitigations: **hedged requests** (fire a second copy after the P95 elapses; ~5% extra load; **idempotent reads only**), partial results, and per-call deadlines carved from the overall budget.

  <Note type="warning" title="Retries create tails too">
    A retry after a 10 s timeout means the user waited at least 10 s. Design timeouts, retry counts, and the overall deadline together — see [API Engineering](/docs/production/api-engineering).
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Roughly how much does mean waiting grow from 80% to 95% utilization?
    2. How do traces distinguish "prompt too long" from "peak queueing"?
    3. With 20 downstreams each slow 1% of the time, how often is the request slow?
    4. Why must you never hedge a refund call?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Reasoning models

  ### How do thinking tokens change "first token"?

  Reasoning models (Claude extended/adaptive thinking, OpenAI reasoning models, Gemini thinking) generate thinking tokens before the visible answer. They decode at the same TPOT and are billed as output.

  ```
  time to first visible token ≈ TTFT + thinking_tokens × TPOT ≈ 0.7 s + 2,000 × 15 ms ≈ 30.7 s
  ```

  Your dashboard can show 0.7 s TTFT while the user waits 30 s. Measure time to first *visible answer* token separately. Thinking length also varies widely per query, which widens P95/P99.

  ### How do you control it?

  Set effort or thinking budgets per task tier; route easy intents to a non-thinking model; cap thinking and handle truncation; stream progress or thinking summaries; move deep-reasoning jobs to async tasks with notifications.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview signal">
    Saying "for reasoning models TTFT stops being meaningful; we track time-to-first-visible-token and the thinking-token distribution" shows you've actually shipped thinking models.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. TTFT 0.6 s, 3,000 thinking tokens, TPOT 20 ms — when does the first visible token arrive?
    2. Why do thinking models widen P99?
    3. Name three controls and their costs.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 5 · Optimization levers

  ### Which levers improve which segment?

  Group them so your answer isn't a laundry list:

  * **Do less work**: trim context (TTFT), prompt caching with stable prefixes first (TTFT + cost), cap output length (E2E), app-level answer caching (everything, but stale for live data like order status).
  * **Use something faster**: smaller model / routing / no thinking (TTFT + TPOT, quality risk), closer region or less loaded endpoint.
  * **Parallelize**: independent retrieval and tools, parallel tool calls, speculative decoding or quantization when self-hosting.
  * **Queue less**: headroom, priority queues, provisioned throughput, connection reuse and warm-up (tails).
  * **Show something earlier**: streaming, progress updates, conclusion-first answers, sentence-chunked TTS. Perceived latency only — compute and bill unchanged.

  ### How do you prove an optimization worked?

  Use the same quality set and traffic shape; report TTFT and E2E at P50/P95 along with accuracy, tokens, and cost. Dropping the reranker saves 120 ms but may miss a refund exception — that's a quality regression, not a win.

  <Note type="danger" title="Wrong claim">
    "Streaming reduced our latency." Streaming improves perceived latency; E2E, compute, and cost are unchanged.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Which metric does shorter output mainly help? Context trimming?
    2. Why is order status a bad fit for answer caching while policy explanations might be fine?
    3. Which metrics decide whether removing the reranker is worth it?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 6 · Budgets, SLOs, regressions

  ### How do you set an end-to-end budget?

  Define an SLO per scenario (e.g. 95% of text support requests show useful content within 1.5 s and complete within 6 s). Split it along the critical path — each stage's budget becomes its timeout — and propagate the remaining deadline downstream so a stage that can't finish in time degrades early (e.g. skip reranking) rather than finishing after the caller has given up.

  ### Why can't stage P95s be added?

  Adding is usually pessimistic because stages aren't slow together; but correlated slowness, retries, and fan-out can make the true tail worse. Use stage percentiles for allocation and diagnosis; compute end-to-end P95 from full traces.

  ### How do you measure and guard against regressions?

  Report success, error, timeout, and cancellation populations separately — success-only latency silently drops the slowest failures. Load-test cold starts, peak concurrency, long prompts, slow tools, 429s, and cold caches. Gate releases on P95 regressions within the same traffic bucket. Measure on the client too.

  <Note type="tip" title="Two-minute skeleton">
    Metrics and percentile SLO → critical path and deadline budgets → bucketed diagnosis (prefill vs queueing, agent turns) → four lever families plus streaming → validate every change against the same eval set.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Allocate a 6 s deadline across your RAG stages and justify it.
    2. Why can summed stage P95s be too high or too low?
    3. What does success-only latency hide?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "P95 is the mean of the slowest 5%."
    * "Streaming reduced latency." (Perceived only.)
    * "Prompt caching makes generation faster." (Prefill/TTFT only.)
    * "Sum the stage P95s to get end-to-end P95."
  </Note>

  <Note type="warning" title="Likely follow-ups">
    * For reasoning models, ask whether "TTFT" means first thinking token or first visible token.
    * Hedging and retries only for idempotent operations.
    * Off-critical-path optimizations don't change user wait.
    * State measurement boundaries and denominators before quoting project numbers.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Mechanics: [Inference](/docs/llm/inference), [Prompt Caching](/docs/context/caching), [Context Window](/docs/context/window)
  * Same section: [API Engineering](/docs/production/api-engineering), [Cost](/docs/production/cost), [Scaling](/docs/production/scaling), [Observability](/docs/production/observability)
  * Applied: [Model Routing](/docs/application/model-routing), [AI System Design](/docs/system-design)

  ## Interview questions

  **Levels 0–1**

  1. What do TTFT, TPOT, E2E latency, and P95 mean?
  2. Why does TTFT grow with prompt length while TPOT barely changes?
  3. Estimate the TPOT floor for a 70B model on one GPU.
  4. Why are output tokens priced higher than input tokens?

  **Levels 2–3**

  5. Given a RAG trace, how do you compute TTFT and completion time?
  6. Why is an agent slower than a pipeline, and how do you fix it?
  7. Why does P95 degrade nonlinearly at peak?
  8. What is tail at scale? When can and can't you hedge requests?

  **Levels 4–6**

  9. How do reasoning models change latency monitoring?
  10. List levers for TTFT versus E2E and their tradeoffs.
  11. How do you set a latency budget and propagate deadlines?
  12. Why can't stage P95s be added? What does success-only latency hide?

  ## Sources

  * [Inference page](/docs/llm/inference)
  * [The Tail at Scale (Dean & Barroso, CACM 2013)](https://research.google/pubs/the-tail-at-scale/)
  * [Anthropic: Prompt caching](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)
  * [OpenAI: Latency optimization](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/latency-optimization)
  * [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/)
</Locale>

  * **TPOT** (a.k.a. inter-token latency): average gap between output tokens; its inverse is tokens/s.
  * **E2E**:

.
  * **P95**: sort all latencies; 95% are at or below this value. Not the mean of the slowest 5%.

  If the 95th of 100 sorted E2E values is 4.8 s, P95 is 4.8 s even if the mean is 2.1 s — means get diluted by fast requests, which is why SLOs use percentiles.

  <Note type="warning" title="Two ways to compute TPOT">
    Averaging total decode time hides a 2-second stall; the per-gap distribution exposes it at P99. Complaints about streaming "hiccups" need the per-gap view.
  </Note>

  ### What does the user actually perceive?

  TTFT is a model-side metric. Users perceive time to the first *meaningful* content. A JSON wrapper, a filler sentence, or hidden thinking tokens all produce a fast TTFT with nothing useful on screen. For voice, what matters is the first playable audio: end of ASR + first LLM sentence + first TTS chunk. Measure at least TTFT, time to first useful content, and completion.

  <Note title="Voice budgets are tight">
    Human turn-taking gaps are a few hundred milliseconds; voice agents typically aim for roughly one second voice-to-voice. Before quoting the 1.2 s figure from the Voice project, pin down its start and end points.
  </Note>

    1. Write E2E in terms of TTFT, TPOT, and output length.
    2. What does P95 = 4.8 s mean, and why not use the mean?
    3. Give two cases where TTFT is fast but the user still waits.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Where a token comes from

  ### Why does TTFT track prompt length?

  Serving has two phases. **Prefill** pushes the whole input through the model in parallel, writes the KV cache, and emits the first token. **Decode** produces one token per step, reusing the KV cache.

  Prefill processes thousands of tokens at once and saturates the matrix units — it's **compute-bound**, roughly

FLOPs plus attention that grows quadratically. A 70B model on a 20k-token prompt is about 2.8e15 FLOPs; against an H100's ~1e15 dense BF16 FLOPs/s at realistic utilization, that's seconds. Tensor parallelism shortens it, but long prompts always cost TTFT.

  ### Why does TPOT track memory bandwidth instead?

  Each decode step computes one token but must **read every weight from HBM**. Little math, lots of bytes — **memory-bandwidth-bound**.

70B × 2 bytes ≈ 140 GB;  H100 HBM ≈ 3.35 TB/s
  batch-1 TPOT floor ≈ 140 / 3350 ≈ 42 ms/token (~24 tok/s)

Real systems beat this with tensor parallelism (each GPU reads 1/8), quantization (fewer bytes), continuous batching (one weight read serves 64 requests — throughput up, per-request TPOT roughly flat), and speculative decoding (several tokens per weight read). As an API consumer you mostly influence TPOT by picking the model and provider.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview one-liner">
    "Prefill is compute-bound so TTFT scales with input length — that's why prefix caching cuts TTFT. Decode is memory-bound, so TPOT is about bytes read per step, which is what quantization, batching, and speculative decoding attack."
  </Note>

  ### How do the KV cache and prompt caching relate?

  The KV cache is per-request: step 100 doesn't recompute the first 99 tokens. Prompt caching is cross-request: if two requests share an identical token prefix, the provider reuses that prefix's KV and **skips its prefill**. It lowers cost and TTFT, not TPOT, and needs an exact prefix — a timestamp at the top of the system prompt breaks every hit. Details in [Prompt Caching](/docs/context/caching).

  <Note type="danger" title="Wrong claim">
    "Output tokens cost more because they're harder to compute." Closer to the truth: each decode step reads all weights at low GPU utilization, so an output token occupies far more hardware time than an input token in prefill.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What bottlenecks prefill and decode, and why?
    2. Estimate the batch-1 TPOT floor from 140 GB and 3.35 TB/s.
    3. Why does continuous batching raise throughput but not change per-request TPOT much?
    4. Does prompt caching help TTFT or TPOT? What breaks it?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Critical-path arithmetic

  ### How do serial and parallel stages add up?

  Serial stages add, parallel stages take the max; the user waits on the longest path through the dependency graph.

Speeding up the order API changes nothing — it's off the critical path. Decode is usually the largest single term. If retrieval needs order status, the two become serial and TTFT becomes 1,290 ms. Draw the real dependency graph first.

  ### How do agent loops change the math?

  Every loop iteration pays a model TTFT plus output tokens (tool-call arguments are output too). Three iterations — two tool calls and a final answer — come to about 8.4 s, versus 3.6 s for a fixed pipeline. Agent flexibility is paid for in serial model calls, and TTFT rises each turn as context grows unless the prefix is cached.

  Levers: parallel tool calls in a single turn, moving deterministic steps out of the loop into code, a small model for routing, and keeping intermediate turns terse.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    For "our agent is slow," start with: "I'd lay out each model call and tool call; the critical path is usually N serial TTFTs plus outputs." Then give parallel tool calls, workflow-ifying fixed steps, and small-model routing.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why max for parallel stages? What does optimizing an off-path stage buy you?
    2. How does TTFT change when retrieval depends on order state?
    3. Why is the agent loop slower than a pipeline, and how do you shorten it?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Queueing and tail latency

  ### Why does the same request get slower at peak?

  Queueing. With utilization

: 1× at 50%, 4× at 80%, 9× at 90%, 19× at 95%. The growth is nonlinear, which is why inference fleets keep headroom and why provider TTFT jitters at peak. Queues live in your worker pool, your outbound connection pool, the provider gateway, and the GPU batch scheduler.

  Diagnose by bucketing TTFT by input length × time of day. Long-prompt buckets slow at all hours → prefill work. Every bucket slow at peak → queueing or throttling. Cache-hit bucket fast → caching works. A handful of extreme outliers → tail causes like retries, cold starts, long outputs.

  ### Why does fan-out amplify tails?

  If each downstream call is slow 1% of the time and you fan out to N,

: 9.6% at N=10, 39.5% at N=50 — the core point of *The Tail at Scale*. Mitigations: **hedged requests** (fire a second copy after the P95 elapses; ~5% extra load; **idempotent reads only**), partial results, and per-call deadlines carved from the overall budget.

  <Note type="warning" title="Retries create tails too">
    A retry after a 10 s timeout means the user waited at least 10 s. Design timeouts, retry counts, and the overall deadline together — see [API Engineering](/docs/production/api-engineering).
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Roughly how much does mean waiting grow from 80% to 95% utilization?
    2. How do traces distinguish "prompt too long" from "peak queueing"?
    3. With 20 downstreams each slow 1% of the time, how often is the request slow?
    4. Why must you never hedge a refund call?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Reasoning models

  ### How do thinking tokens change "first token"?

  Reasoning models (Claude extended/adaptive thinking, OpenAI reasoning models, Gemini thinking) generate thinking tokens before the visible answer. They decode at the same TPOT and are billed as output.
time to first visible token ≈ TTFT + thinking_tokens × TPOT ≈ 0.7 s + 2,000 × 15 ms ≈ 30.7 s

title: Observability
description: 一次 agent 请求的 trace 长什么样、按 OpenTelemetry GenAI 约定记哪些字段、慢 / 贵 / 错分开告警、日志脱敏，以及把线上问题变成评估用例的闭环。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Classic observability answers "where is it slow, where does it fail?" LLM systems add two questions classic tools can't answer: **what did this step cost** and **was this answer right**. Agent execution paths differ every time, so without traces debugging is nearly impossible.

  The emphasis is drawing an agent trace tree and naming the fields; tool choices get a quick pass.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Three signals | What do logs, metrics, and traces each answer? What's new for LLMs? | 15 min |
  | 1 · An agent trace | How is the span tree organized? Which OTel GenAI fields? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Alerts | How do you separate slow, expensive, and wrong? Where do quality signals come from? | 25 min |
  | 3 · Privacy | How do you debug without leaking user data into logs? | 15 min |
  | 4 · Incident to improvement | How does a production issue become a verified fix? | 15 min |

  **Level 1 is the core.** About 1.5 hours.

  ## Must know

  * logs / metrics / traces; LLM-specific cost and quality signals
  * the agent span tree: `invoke_agent` → `chat` → `execute_tool`
  * OTel GenAI fields: provider, model, token usage incl. cache, finish reason, conversation ID, tool name, plus prompt version
  * metrics and thresholds for slow / expensive / wrong; sampled online judging
  * content capture off by default, redaction, retention, access control
  * the trace → label → eval set → fix → regression loop
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Three signals

  ### What does each signal answer?

  Metrics: is there a problem and how bad (cheap aggregates for alerting). Traces: which step (causal timing across a request). Logs: what exactly happened. Debug flow: alert → traces in the window → span → logs and attributes.

  ### What's new for LLM systems?

  Cost per call aggregated to request, task, tenant, and feature; quality signals because 200 ≠ correct; the content itself, which is both the best debugging data and the most sensitive; and versions — prompt, model snapshot, index — to tie problems to releases.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. In what order do you use metrics, traces, and logs?
    2. Name four LLM-specific things to observe.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · An agent trace

  ### How is the span tree organized?

  `POST /chat` → `invoke_agent support-agent` → `chat` (turn 1, finish\_reason `tool_use`) → `execute_tool get_order_status` and `execute_tool search_policy` (with a `rerank` child) → `chat` (turn 2, `end_turn`). One glance shows two model calls dominate, cache hit rates are high, tools are fast. For a "wrong answer" report you inspect which clauses retrieval returned and whether they reached turn 2's input.

  ### Which OpenTelemetry GenAI fields?

  The GenAI semantic conventions (moved to their own repository in 2026, still evolving, widely adopted) standardize spans: name `{operation} {model}`; `gen_ai.operation.name` (`chat`, `embeddings`, `execute_tool`, `invoke_agent`); `gen_ai.provider.name`; `gen_ai.request.model` and `gen_ai.response.model`; `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` / `output_tokens` plus cache usage; `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons`; `gen_ai.conversation.id`; `gen_ai.tool.name` / `gen_ai.tool.call.id`; message content is opt-in. Add business fields: tenant, feature, prompt version, index version, task ID, cost, degradation level. Metrics include `gen_ai.client.token.usage`, `gen_ai.client.operation.duration`, `gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token`.

  <Note type="tip" title="Trace context across MCP">
    The 2026-07-28 MCP spec documents propagating `traceparent` in request `_meta`, so remote MCP server spans join the same trace.
  </Note>

  <Note type="warning" title="Always record finish_reason">
    A rising `max_tokens` rate means truncated answers — often a prompt change made the model wordier.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Draw a two-turn agent span tree.
    2. Name six GenAI fields and three business fields.
    3. Why record both request and response model?
    4. What does a rising `max_tokens` finish rate mean?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Alerts

  ### How do you separate slow, expensive, and wrong?

  Slow: TTFT/E2E P95, time to useful content. Hard errors: error rate, 429 rate, breaker state. Expensive: hourly spend versus the same hour last week, tokens per request, cache hit rate, turns per task. Soft errors: thumbs-down, escalation, judge scores, schema failures, `max_tokens` rate. Alert on symptoms users feel, not causes.

  ### Where do quality signals come from?

  Explicit feedback (direct but sparse and skewed), implicit feedback (escalation, rephrasing, abandonment — full coverage, noisy), deterministic checks (cheap, narrow), sampled LLM-as-judge (semantic, costs money — use Batch, calibrate it), and human review (accurate, slow; calibrates the judge). Watch for drift in the question mix and retrieval even when nothing shipped. See [Production Eval](/docs/evaluation/production-eval).

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Design one alert each for slow, expensive, hard error, soft error.
    2. Why alert on symptoms?
    3. What's wrong with thumbs alone?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Privacy

  ### How do you debug without leaking user data?

  Logs are often readable by far more people than production databases. Layer it: metadata only by default (OTel GenAI makes content opt-in); redact PII before writing content; sample full content for a fraction or for failures; store content separately with access control, audit, and short retention; support deletion by user ID.

  <Note type="warning" title="Tool results are sensitive too">
    Teams redact prompts and forget tool outputs — full addresses from the order API, CRM profiles.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Describe the five protection layers.
    2. What can you still debug without content?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Incident to improvement

  ### How does a production issue become a verified fix?

  "Order shows in transit but the bot says it hasn't shipped": find the trace by conversation ID → the order tool returned `in_transit` correctly, but retrieval returned the not-shipped clause and missed the in-transit clause → root cause: the retrieval query ignored order state → add the redacted conversation to the regression set → fix → verify without regressions → canary while watching that intent's escalation and judge scores. Every incident becomes an eval case.

  ### Which tools?

  Langfuse (open source, self-hostable, OTel-compatible), LangSmith (LangChain ecosystem), Arize Phoenix (open source, OTel/OpenInference), Braintrust (eval-centric), or existing APM like Datadog/Grafana ingesting GenAI spans. Choose on OTel support, self-hosting for compliance, and trace-to-eval integration.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Walk the seven steps for the in-transit incident.
    2. Why turn every incident into an eval case?
    3. Three criteria for choosing a tool?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "Error rate is low, so quality is fine."
    * "Log every prompt and response for debugging."
    * "Traces only need model calls." (Tools, retrieval, rerank too.)
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Same section: [Latency](/docs/production/latency), [Cost](/docs/production/cost), [Reliability](/docs/production/reliability)
  * Evaluation: [Production Eval](/docs/evaluation/production-eval), [Evaluation](/docs/evaluation)
  * Protocol: [MCP](/docs/ai-native/mcp)

  ## Interview questions

  1. What do logs, metrics, and traces each answer?
  2. Draw an agent trace and list the fields you record.
  3. How do you alert separately on slow, expensive, and wrong?
  4. Where do online quality signals come from?
  5. How do you debug without leaking customer data?
  6. How does a production issue become a verified improvement?

  ## Sources

  * [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai)
  * [MCP 2026-07-28 changelog](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog)
  * [Langfuse docs](https://langfuse.com/docs), [Arize Phoenix docs](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix)
  * [Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/)
</Locale>

title: Reliability
description: AI 系统的可靠性有两半：服务活着（熔断、隔舱、降级、fallback）和答案可信（输出校验、版本锁定、灰度回滚）。用 SLO 与故障注入证明它真的有效。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Classic reliability asks "is it up?" AI adds a second half: **it's up, but wrong** — HTTP 200 carrying an invented refund policy. Answering "how do you make an AI system reliable?" with only breakers and retries covers half.

  [API Engineering](/docs/production/api-engineering) covers per-request timeouts, retries, and idempotency. This page covers the whole system under dependency failure, load spikes, and model behavior changes — and how to prove the strategies work.

  Dependencies in the running example: primary model provider, backup provider, policy retrieval (`P-17 v3`), order API, refund API.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Two reliabilities | Why are "available" and "correct" different? How do SLOs and error budgets work? | 25 min |
  | 1 · Failure decision table | What do you do for timeout, 429, 5xx, no evidence, unauthorized, unknown side effect? | 25 min |
  | 2 · Breakers, bulkheads, shedding | How does a breaker move between states? How does one slow dependency sink everything? | 40 min |
  | 3 · Degradation and fallback | What can support still do safely without a model? What must a backup model satisfy? | 30 min |
  | 4 · Correctness reliability | How do you catch wrong answers inside 200s? What if the provider silently changes the model? | 30 min |
  | 5 · Proving it | How do fault injection and game days validate it? | 20 min |

  **Levels 2 and 3 are the core.** About 3 hours.

  ## Must know

  * hard vs soft failures; SLIs/SLOs for both; error budgets
  * choosing between retry, fallback, degrade, refuse, escalate, and pausing side effects
  * breaker states, transitions, and parameters
  * bulkheads, load shedding, backpressure
  * degradation ladder; eval parity and prompt compatibility for backup models
  * output validation, version pinning, canary rollout and auto-rollback
  * fault-injection matrix, game days, postmortems
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Two reliabilities

  ### Why are "available" and "correct" different?

  Hard failures (5xx, timeouts, 429) show up in classic monitoring. Soft failures — wrong answers, invented policy, invalid JSON, missed escalation — return 200. Silent drift (provider model updates, stale index, prompt edits) and unknown side effects are also invisible. Define SLIs for both halves: availability, latency, schema validity, grounded-answer rate (sampled, judged), correct-escalation rate.

  ### How do SLOs and error budgets work?

  An SLO targets an SLI; the error budget is 1 − SLO (99.9% over 30 days ≈ 43 minutes). Plenty of budget → ship fast; nearly spent → freeze risky releases. Quality SLOs get budgets too: a prompt change that drops grounded answers from 95% to 93% triggers rollback.

  <Note type="warning" title="Serial availability multiplies">
    0.999³ ≈ 99.7%. You can't promise more than the product of serial dependencies without fallbacks — the math behind backup models and degradation paths.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Give three "200 but failed" examples.
    2. Design four SLIs for the support bot.
    3. What's a 99.9% monthly budget, and what happens when it's nearly spent?
    4. Availability of three serial 99.9% dependencies?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Failure decision table

  ### Can you just retry everything?

  No. Occasional model 429/5xx → jittered retry. Persistent model failure → break the circuit, fail over or degrade. Retrieval timeout → degrade to cached policy summaries or say policy is unavailable; never let the model answer from memory. No relevant evidence → refuse and escalate (retrying returns the same nothing). Order API timeout → retry the read; otherwise say so. Unauthorized access → refuse and log a security event. Unknown refund outcome → stop side effects and reconcile. Invalid schema → one repair attempt with the error, then degrade.

  <Note type="tip" title="One-line principle">
    Retry transient, break persistent, refuse without evidence, deny unauthorized, stop and verify unknown side effects.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why do retrieval timeout and "no evidence" differ?
    2. Why isn't unauthorized access a retry or degrade case?
    3. How many repair attempts for invalid JSON?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Breakers, bulkheads, shedding

  ### When does a breaker open, and how does it prevent cascades?

  Without a breaker, every request waits out a 30 s timeout against a dying provider, exhausting your pools and starving healthy features — the dependency's outage becomes yours. A **circuit breaker** fails fast: **closed** (normal) → **open** when the failure rate in a sliding window exceeds a threshold given a minimum request count → after a cool-down, **half-open** lets a few probes through → success closes it, failure reopens it. For LLMs, count **slow calls** as failures too. Count 429s from the provider, not from your own limiter; never count 400s. While open, route to a fallback rather than erroring.

  ### How does one slow dependency sink everything? What's a bulkhead?

  If the refund API stalls at 25 s and all work shares one pool, order lookups starve too. **Bulkheads** give each dependency (or tenant) its own bounded pool — e.g. refunds max 10 concurrent — so one flooded compartment doesn't sink the ship.

  ### What are load shedding and backpressure?

  Under overload, reject some requests so the rest meet the SLO: shed low-priority traffic, requests that have already waited too long, and over-quota tenants. Backpressure tells upstream to slow down; queues must be bounded.

  <Note type="danger" title="Wrong claim">
    "A queue absorbs the load." Only short bursts. If arrivals exceed capacity, an unbounded queue just makes every request time out.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Draw the breaker states and transitions. Why a minimum request count?
    2. Why treat slow LLM calls as failures?
    3. Why do order lookups suffer when refunds slow down? How do bulkheads fix it?
    4. Why is rejecting 20% better than accepting all?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Degradation and fallback

  ### What can support still do without the primary model?

  A degradation ladder where every rung is less capable but still safe: full agent → skip reranking → backup model → **read-only mode** (answer and look up, pause all side effects; refunds become "submitted for review") → no model: templated reply with order status from the API, the original `P-17 v3` text, and a human handoff button → static page. Degrade by saying less, never by saying things that may be wrong — "let a small model answer refund policy from memory" is worse than no answer.

  ### What must a backup model satisfy?

  Eval parity on the same eval set; per-model prompt adaptation (tool formats and structured output differ); capability parity (context window, parallel tools, thinking); compliance (data residency); quota to absorb 100% of traffic; and continuous exercise — route ~1% of traffic through it so it isn't broken when you need it.

  ### When must you escalate to a human?

  No evidence, high-risk actions beyond the agent's authority, explicit user request or repeated frustration, a stuck agent, and any side-effecting request during read-only mode. Hand off with context: summary, order status, retrieved policy, and where the agent stopped.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Design a four-rung degradation ladder.
    2. Why is the no-model mode still trustworthy?
    3. List the backup-model conditions. Why route 1% through it continuously?
    4. Name four mandatory escalation cases.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Correctness reliability

  ### How do you catch wrong answers inside a 200?

  Validate before output reaches the user or triggers side effects, cheapest first: schema, business rules (refund ≤ order total; delivered orders can't use the not-shipped policy), citation checks (cited clause IDs actually retrieved), consistency with the order API, then a judge model for high-risk answers. Deterministic rule checks are the most valuable — injection can't talk its way past code. The model proposes, code validates, the system executes.

  ### What if the provider silently changes the model?

  Pin dated snapshot IDs rather than floating aliases, run the fixed eval set daily against production config, and sample live traffic for judged scoring (see [Production Eval](/docs/evaluation/production-eval)).

  ### How do you ship prompt or model changes safely?

  Prompts, model versions, indexes, and tool definitions are all release artifacts with versions and rollback. Offline eval → shadow traffic → canary 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, gated on errors, latency, grounded-answer rate, escalation rate, and feedback, with automatic rollback.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview signal">
    "We manage prompts like code: versioned, eval-gated, canaried, one-click rollback, and every trace records the prompt version."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. List four validations by cost; which is most valuable and why?
    2. Why pin dated snapshot IDs?
    3. What counts as a release artifact? Walk through a prompt rollout.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 5 · Proving it works

  ### How do you validate reliability strategies?

  Breakers and fallbacks on paper often fail in real incidents — wrong thresholds, expired backup quota, templates referencing removed fields. Inject faults: primary 503s (breaker opens, failover time), +20 s latency (slow calls trip the breaker), sustained 429 (shedding protects high priority), empty retrieval (refuse, zero fabrication), refund timeout (zero duplicates), injected tool text (zero unauthorized actions), backup also down (template mode). Then run game days against runbooks.

  ### After an incident?

  Blameless postmortems with timeline, impact, root cause, detection gaps, and actions — and turn every incident into a new fault-injection case and eval case. Track MTTD and MTTR.

  <Note type="tip" title="Two-minute skeleton">
    Two halves. Available: classify errors, retry transient, break persistent, bulkhead dependencies, shed load, degradation ladder down to a no-model template. Correct: deterministic rule checks, version pinning, canaried prompts with auto-rollback. Proven by fault injection and game days.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why inject faults instead of trusting the design?
    2. Design five fault cases with expected behavior and metrics.
    3. What's the most important output of a postmortem?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "99.9% availability means it's reliable." (Ignores soft failures.)
    * "Fail over to a cheap model answering from memory."
    * "A queue will absorb it."
    * "The fallback is written, so we're covered." (Unexercised fallbacks rot.)
  </Note>

  <Note type="warning" title="Likely follow-ups">
    * What counts as a breaker failure — 429, slow calls, 400?
    * Was the backup's prompt adapted and evaluated?
    * How do side-effect requests behave in read-only mode?
    * Aliases vs snapshot IDs.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Same section: [API Engineering](/docs/production/api-engineering), [Scaling](/docs/production/scaling), [Observability](/docs/production/observability)
  * Related: [Model Routing](/docs/application/model-routing), [Production Eval](/docs/evaluation/production-eval), [Agent Security](/docs/agent/security)

  ## Interview questions

  **Levels 0–1**

  1. Why are "available" and "correct" different for AI services?
  2. What is an error budget, and how does it drive decisions?
  3. How do you handle timeout, 429, no evidence, unauthorized, and unknown side effects?

  **Levels 2–3**

  4. Describe circuit breaker states and transitions.
  5. What is a bulkhead and what does it prevent?
  6. Why shed load under overload?
  7. What can a support bot still safely do without its model?
  8. What must you verify before failing over to a backup model?

  **Levels 4–5**

  9. How do you catch wrong answers in successful responses?
  10. How do you safely roll out a prompt change?
  11. How do you prove reliability strategies work in a real outage?

  ## Sources

  * [Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/), [Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)
  * [Martin Fowler: CircuitBreaker](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html)
  * [AWS Builders' Library: Using load shedding to avoid overload](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/using-load-shedding-to-avoid-overload/)
  * [Anthropic: Models overview](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/about-claude/models/overview)
  * [Principles of Chaos Engineering](https://principlesofchaos.org/)
</Locale>

description: 用 Little's Law 把日活换算成峰值并发与供应商配额；分清同步与队列；多层限流；按在途请求扩容；自部署时理解 GPU 吞吐与延迟的取舍。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  LLM scaling differs from typical web scaling in one essential way: **the bottleneck is usually not your servers but the model quota** (APIs) or **GPU memory** (self-hosting). A hundred CPUs won't help if the provider gives you two million tokens per minute.

  The emphasis is arithmetic: convert 100k DAU into peak QPS, in-flight concurrency, and tokens per minute, then know where to queue, limit, and scale. Generic gateway and autoscaling topics get a quick pass.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Capacity math | How do QPS, concurrency, duration, and TPM relate? | 30 min |
  | 1 · Sync or queue | What should users wait on, and what goes to a queue? | 15 min |
  | 2 · Layered limits | Why limit users, tenants, and downstreams? | 20 min |
  | 3 · Statelessness and autoscaling | Where does state live? Why not scale on CPU? | 20 min |
  | 4 · Self-hosted GPUs | How does batch size trade throughput against latency? | 20 min |
  | 5 · Proving capacity | How do you load test? | 15 min |

  **Level 0 is the core** — be able to do it live. About 2 hours.

  ## Must know

  * Little's Law: concurrency = arrival rate × time in system; peak factors
  * DAU → peak QPS → in-flight → TPM, compared against provider quota
  * user / tenant / downstream / global limits and their purposes
  * scale LLM gateways on in-flight requests or queue depth, not CPU
  * self-hosting: KV-cache memory caps concurrency; batch size trades throughput for TPOT; slow cold starts
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Capacity math

  ### How do QPS, concurrency, and duration relate?

  **Little's Law**: `L = λ × W` — in-flight requests equal arrival rate times time in system, independent of distribution. LLM requests have large W, so 30 QPS × 8 s = 240 in flight versus 1.5 for a 50 ms API.

  ### From 100k DAU to provider quota

  300k requests/day → 3.5 average QPS → ~28 peak QPS at an 8× peak factor → ~224 in flight → ~8.4M input tokens/min and ~1.7M output tokens/min. If your tier allows 2M ITPM, peak traffic will 429. Fixes: prefix caching (some providers don't count cache reads toward ITPM), higher tiers or provisioned throughput, multi-region/multi-provider routing, and shifting non-real-time work to off-peak or Batch.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview signal">
    Going past QPS to "peak needs 8.4M ITPM, above quota, so caching + quota + multi-region" shows real experience.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. State Little's Law and why LLM concurrency is so high.
    2. Compute peak in-flight and ITPM for 50k DAU, 4 requests each, 6× peak, 10 s, 4k input.
    3. Three remedies when peak TPM exceeds quota?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Sync or queue

  ### What do users wait on?

  If a user is watching the screen, it's synchronous: chat answers, live order lookups, voice. Ingestion, embeddings, nightly evals, long reports, coding-agent tasks, and notifications go to queues for peak smoothing, decoupling, and redelivery. Keep queues bounded with priorities, make consumers idempotent (at-least-once delivery), and send repeated failures to a dead-letter queue.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Name three sync and three async steps in the support system.
    2. Why must queue consumers be idempotent?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Layered rate limits

  ### Why limit users, tenants, and downstreams?

  Users: abuse and scripts. Tenants: fairness and plan entitlements — otherwise one tenant's batch job drains the global quota and everyone gets 429s (noisy neighbor). Downstream: stay under provider RPM/TPM and protect internal APIs. Global: spend caps and a kill switch. Keep counters in shared storage like Redis, and limit by tokens, not just requests — a 100k-token call and a 100-token call aren't the same.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What does each layer protect?
    2. What goes wrong with only a global limit?
    3. Why count tokens?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Statelessness and autoscaling

  ### Where does state live with many replicas?

  Instances are stateless: conversation history in a database with a Redis hot cache, task state and checkpoints in a database ([Agent State](/docs/ai-native/agent-state)), rate-limit counters in Redis, files in object storage. SSE streams pin to one instance for their lifetime, so scale-down needs graceful draining.

  ### Why not scale an LLM gateway on CPU?

  It spends its time waiting; CPU stays low while connection pools and concurrency slots are full. Scale on in-flight requests, queue depth or wait time, and pool utilization. If the bottleneck is provider quota, more instances just hit 429 faster.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Where do history and task state live?
    2. How do you handle streams during scale-down?
    3. Why is CPU the wrong signal, and what's right?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Self-hosted GPU scaling

  ### How many requests can one GPU serve?

  Usually capped by **KV-cache memory**, not compute: every in-flight request stores K/V for all its tokens (order of 0.1 MB per token for an 8B model, so ~1 GB for 8k tokens). Longer contexts mean fewer concurrent requests; PagedAttention improves utilization ([Inference](/docs/llm/inference) Level 3).

  ### How does batch size trade throughput for latency?

  Larger batches raise tokens/s/GPU and lower cost per token but slow per-request TPOT and can queue prefills. Pick the largest batch that meets the TPOT SLO; run real-time and offline workloads on separately tuned pools.

  ### What else is different?

  Cold starts take minutes to load weights, so keep headroom or warm pools; route by shared prefix to raise cache hits; some stacks disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What caps per-GPU concurrency, and why do long contexts reduce it?
    2. How do throughput, TPOT, and TTFT move with batch size?
    3. Why can't GPU autoscaling absorb bursts?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 5 · Proving capacity

  ### How do you prove it holds at peak and under failure?

  Replay realistic traffic: production input/output length distributions, a ramp to 1.5–2× forecast peak plus spikes, cold and warm caches, and faults injected at peak. Look for the QPS where P95 knees upward, which layer saturates first, and whether shedding protects priority traffic.

  <Note type="warning" title="Load tests cost money">
    Test your gateway against a mock model server with realistic latency and token distributions; verify real provider quotas at small scale.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why not load test with one short prompt?
    2. Which three results matter most?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "Add machines." (Quota is often the bottleneck.)
    * "Autoscale on CPU."
    * Stopping at QPS without in-flight concurrency and TPM.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Same section: [Latency](/docs/production/latency), [API Engineering](/docs/production/api-engineering), [Reliability](/docs/production/reliability), [Cost](/docs/production/cost)
  * Mechanics: [Inference](/docs/llm/inference)
  * Applied: [AI System Design](/docs/system-design)

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do QPS, concurrency, and latency relate?
  2. Estimate peak concurrency and TPM from 100k DAU.
  3. What goes synchronous and what goes to a queue?
  4. Why layer user, tenant, and downstream limits?
  5. Why not autoscale an LLM gateway on CPU?
  6. How does batch size affect throughput and latency when self-hosting?
  7. How do you load test an LLM service?

  ## Sources

  * [Little's law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little%27s_law)
  * [Anthropic: Rate limits](https://docs.claude.com/en/api/rate-limits)
  * [vLLM documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/)
  * [Google SRE Book: Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## My answer
</Locale>
