title: Advanced RAG
description: 高级技巧要由具体失败驱动：查询改写 / 多查询 / 分解 / HyDE、层级摘要（RAPTOR）、GraphRAG 的建图与全局问题、agentic RAG 与 Self-RAG / CRAG，以及每种技巧的成本。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Listing names (HyDE, GraphRAG, Self-RAG) is the weakest answer to "which advanced RAG techniques do you know?" Better: identify the failure, choose the technique, state the cost. This page is organized failure → technique.

  Running examples: vague phrasing ("that thing never came, can I get money back"), multi-hop ("overseas order, delivered 10 days ago — who pays return shipping?"), and global ("what were last month's top complaint categories?").

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Failure-driven | Which technique for which failure? | 15 min |
  | 1 · Query side | Rewriting, multi-query, decomposition, HyDE? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Index side | How do RAPTOR and GraphRAG answer global questions? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Agentic RAG | Should the model decide what and when to retrieve? | 25 min |

  **Levels 0 and 2 are the core.** About 1.5 hours.

  ## Must know

  * the failure → technique map
  * rewriting, multi-query + fusion, decomposition, step-back, HyDE
  * RAPTOR trees; GraphRAG entity graphs, community summaries, local/global search, indexing cost
  * agentic RAG, Self-RAG, CRAG; when worth it
  * added latency and cost of each
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Failure-driven

  ### Which technique for which failure?

  Vague phrasing → rewriting or HyDE (+1 LLM call). Narrow single query → multi-query + RRF (more searches). Multi-hop → decomposition or iterative retrieval (multiple rounds). Context-poor chunks → parent-child or contextual retrieval. "Summarize everything" → RAPTOR or GraphRAG (expensive indexing). Varied strategies → agentic RAG (highest cost, least control). Get the baseline (parsing, chunking, hybrid, reranking, filters) right first.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why not start with GraphRAG?
    2. Techniques for vague queries and multi-hop questions?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Query side

  ### Rewriting, multi-query, decomposition?

  Rewriting normalizes vague phrasing and resolves references in multi-turn chats ("what about after delivery?" → "can in-transit orders be returned after delivery?"). Multi-query issues 3–5 paraphrases and fuses with RRF. Decomposition splits multi-condition questions into sub-queries. Step-back retrieves general principles first.

  ### HyDE?

  Hypothetical Document Embeddings (2022): have the LLM write a hypothetical answer and search with its embedding, which resembles real documents more than the question does. Its facts may be wrong — it's only used for search — but a misdirected draft steers retrieval astray.

  ### Cost?

  At least one extra LLM call (and more searches for multi-query). Use small fast models and trigger only when first-pass confidence is low.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why resolve references in multi-turn chats?
    2. Decomposition vs multi-query?
    3. How does HyDE work, and what if the draft is wrong?
    4. How do you limit added latency?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Index side

  ### Why does plain RAG fail global questions?

  "Top complaint categories last month" lives across thousands of tickets; top-10 sees ten. These are global (sensemaking) questions.

  ### RAPTOR?

  RAPTOR (2024) clusters chunks, summarizes each cluster with an LLM, repeats upward into a tree, and retrieves across all levels — details from leaves, overviews from upper nodes.

  ### GraphRAG?

  Microsoft (2024): an LLM extracts entities and relations per chunk, builds a graph, detects communities (e.g. Leiden), and summarizes each community. Local search follows specific entities and their neighborhoods; global search map-reduces over community summaries. Indexing can cost one to two orders of magnitude more than standard RAG and must track updates (LightRAG aims cheaper). Worth it for global, cross-document questions; not for clause lookups.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What's a global question, and why does plain RAG fail?
    2. How is a RAPTOR tree built and used?
    3. GraphRAG's four indexing steps; local vs global search?
    4. GraphRAG's main cost, and when it's not worth it?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Agentic RAG

  ### What is it?

  Retrieval becomes an agent tool: the model decides whether to retrieve, which source, whether results suffice (retrying with new queries), and when to stop — ideal for multi-hop questions like the overseas return case.

  ### Self-RAG and CRAG?

  Self-RAG (2023) trains reflection tokens judging retrieval need, passage relevance, and support. CRAG (2024) grades retrieval quality — use, discard and web-search, or combine. Shared idea: judge retrieval before using it. A light CRAG: reranker thresholds plus rewrite-and-retry on low confidence.

  ### Worth it?

  It handles multi-hop and multi-source questions and skips needless retrieval, but multiplies latency and cost, is harder to evaluate, and can under- or over-retrieve. Route only complex questions into agentic mode with a retrieval-round cap.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "Fixed pipeline first; enable iterative retrieval only for questions routed as complex, with a round limit."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Four decisions the model makes in agentic RAG?
    2. Self-RAG and CRAG's shared idea, and a light CRAG?
    3. Why enable agentic RAG for only some questions?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * Listing technique names without failure types.
    * "GraphRAG beats plain RAG." (Only for global questions, at much higher cost.)
    * "Show users the HyDE draft."
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Prereqs: [Failure Diagnosis](/docs/rag/debugging), [Hybrid Search](/docs/rag/hybrid-search), [Reranking](/docs/rag/reranking)
  * Agents: [Agent Loop](/docs/agent/loop), [Workflow vs Agent](/docs/agent/workflow-vs-agent)
  * Cost: [Cost](/docs/production/cost), [Latency](/docs/production/latency)

  ## Interview questions

  1. How do you choose advanced RAG techniques?
  2. What do rewriting, multi-query, and decomposition each solve?
  3. What is HyDE, and its risks?
  4. How does GraphRAG work, and when is it worth it?
  5. What is agentic RAG? What are Self-RAG and CRAG?
  6. What changes for RAG in multi-turn conversations?

  ## Sources

  * [HyDE (Gao et al., 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496)
  * [RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.18059)
  * [GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130), [Microsoft GraphRAG](https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/)
  * [Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511)
  * [CRAG (Yan et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884)
</Locale>

title: RAG Architecture
description: RAG 解决什么、不解决什么；离线索引与在线回答两条流水线；从证据到答案的四道关口与七个经典失败点；RAG / 长上下文 / 微调的取舍；五分钟白板设计企业级 RAG。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  "Design an enterprise knowledge-base Q\&A system" is one of the most common AI system design questions. Interviewers want to see where RAG breaks, why each component exists, how permissions and versions are enforced, and how you prove answers are right.

  This page is the map for the RAG section; every later page is one box on it.

  Running example: "Order 20240915 hasn't arrived — can I get a refund?" The policy store has current `P-17 v3`, expired `P-17 v2`, and unrelated FAQs; order status comes from the order API. "Not arrived" isn't "not shipped."

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · What RAG solves | Why not just ask the model? What can't RAG fix? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Two pipelines | What happens offline and online? Which fields does each chunk carry? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Evidence to answer | Why can answers fail after retrieval succeeds? What are the seven failure points? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Tradeoffs | RAG vs long context vs fine-tuning? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Whiteboard | How do you draw enterprise RAG in five minutes? | 25 min |

  **Levels 2 and 4 are the core.** About 2 hours.

  ## Must know

  * RAG's value (updatable, traceable, permissioned knowledge) and limit (bad retrieval breaks everything)
  * the offline and online pipelines
  * chunk metadata: `doc_id`, version, effective date, section, source, tenant, ACL
  * four gates and seven classic failure points
  * the RAG / long-context / fine-tuning decision
  * the whiteboard: constraints, baseline, evaluation and operations
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · What RAG solves

  ### Why not just ask the model?

  Parametric knowledge is stale, lacks private data, and isn't traceable. RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) retrieves relevant material before generation and asks the model to answer from it, decoupling knowledge updates from training.

  ### What can't RAG fix?

  Live business state (query the order API — a separate evidence chain), retrieval errors (an expired `P-17 v2` gets cited confidently), and reasoning errors over correct evidence.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Three problems with parametric knowledge?
    2. Why is order status an API call, not retrieval?
    3. Which two error types remain with RAG?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Two pipelines

  ### What happens offline and online?

  Offline: discover → parse → clean, dedupe, version → chunk → embed and build lexical index → validate and publish. Online: authenticate → understand/rewrite query → filter by tenant, ACL, effective version → retrieve dense and BM25 in parallel → fuse → rerank → assemble context → generate with citations → trace.

  ### Which fields does each chunk carry?

  `chunk_id`, `doc_id`, `version`, `effective_from/to`, `section`, `source_url`, `tenant`, `acl`, `content_hash`, `text`. Version and dates filter expired policy even when it's more similar; tenant and ACL filter at retrieval time; section and URL support citations; the hash drives incremental updates; the chunk ID keys fusion, traces, and labels.

  <Note type="warning" title="Permissions can't live in the prompt">
    Once text enters the model input it can leak. Filter at retrieval.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. List both pipelines.
    2. Which step stops `P-17 v2` ranked first?
    3. What is `content_hash` for?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Evidence to answer

  ### Why can answers fail after retrieval?

  Four gates: ① recall (is the right chunk in top-K?), ② selection (did it reach the final context?), ③ use (did the model read and cite it correctly?), ④ business (does the conclusion match live order state?).

  ### The seven failure points?

  From Barnett et al. (2024), based on three real projects: missing content, missed top-ranked documents, not in context, not extracted, wrong format, incorrect specificity, incomplete. Missing content matters most: the system must say "I don't know" instead of answering from the nearest irrelevant chunk.

  ### What is grounded?

  Every key claim maps to a specific chunk that supports it — citing a document name isn't enough. Cite by `chunk_id` and audit support (faithfulness).

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. The four gates, with a gate-② example?
    2. Five of the seven failure points?
    3. Why answer "I don't know" for missing content?
    4. Why isn't a document citation grounding?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Tradeoffs

  ### RAG, long context, or fine-tuning?

  RAG: any scale, cheap updates, strong citations and per-user filtering, low per-request cost. Long context: few documents that need reading in full (one contract), costly per request, effective length shorter than claimed. Fine-tuning: stable format, style, and task behavior — not facts; it can't update, cite, or isolate per user. Combine them: retrieve, then place a few full documents in context; fine-tune a small model for query rewriting or reranking.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. When is long context better?
    2. Why not fine-tune company knowledge in?
    3. A RAG + long-context combination?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Whiteboard

  ### How do you draw enterprise RAG in five minutes?

  Minute 1, ask constraints: corpus size and types, update frequency, permissions, latency and cost, cost of errors. Minutes 2–3, draw the baseline: parse → clean/version → chunk → embed + BM25 index with metadata offline; authenticate → rewrite → filtered dense and BM25 in parallel → RRF → rerank top-5 → cited context → generation with abstention → trace online. Minutes 4–5, evaluation and operations: layered offline metrics, online judged samples, feedback, no-answer rate, index freshness, permission negative tests, and a latency budget dominated by generation. Then go deep where the interviewer probes.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "That's the baseline. Advanced techniques come after error analysis shows which failures dominate."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. The five constraint questions?
    2. Draw both pipelines from memory.
    3. RAG-specific production metrics?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "RAG eliminates hallucination."
    * "Fine-tune company knowledge into the model."
    * "Tell the model to ignore unauthorized documents."
    * "The window is big enough; no RAG needed."
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * This section: [Ingestion](/docs/rag/ingestion), [Chunking](/docs/rag/chunking), [Hybrid Search](/docs/rag/hybrid-search), [Failure Diagnosis](/docs/rag/debugging)
  * Related: [Context Construction](/docs/context/construction), [RAG Eval](/docs/evaluation/rag-eval), [Context Window](/docs/context/window)

  ## Interview questions

  1. What does RAG solve, and what can't it?
  2. What are the offline and online pipeline steps?
  3. Which metadata should each chunk carry, and why?
  4. Why can answers fail after retrieval succeeds?
  5. What are the classic RAG failure points?
  6. RAG vs long context vs fine-tuning?
  7. Design an enterprise knowledge-base Q\&A system.

  ## Sources

  * [Lewis et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)
  * [Barnett et al., 2024: Seven Failure Points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05856)
  * [Anthropic: Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval)
</Locale>

  ## My answer
</Locale>

title: Chunking
description: 切分是在“定位精度”和“语义完整”之间取舍：固定 / 递归 / 结构切分，重叠与父子段，语义切分的实证，late chunking 与 contextual retrieval，以及怎样用实验选 chunk size。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Chunking is one of the most probed RAG topics because there's no standard answer — it separates "memorized 512" from understanding tradeoffs.

  Running example: `P-17 v3` has six clauses; clause 4 (~400 tokens) contains the key condition "in-transit orders are **not** eligible for the unshipped refund; returns allowed within 7 days of delivery."

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Why and how big | What goes wrong with chunks too large or too small? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Basic strategies | Fixed, recursive, or structural? | 25 min |
  | 2 · Overlap and parent-child | What do overlap, parent-child, and sentence windows solve? | 25 min |
  | 3 · Advanced methods | Is semantic chunking worth it? What are late chunking and contextual retrieval? | 30 min |
  | 4 · Choose by experiment | How do you pick a size without a magic number? | 20 min |

  **Levels 0 and 4 are the core.** About 2 hours.

  ## Must know

  * too large dilutes vectors and wastes tokens; too small loses conditions
  * recursive separator hierarchy; prefer structure
  * the cost of overlap; parent-child (search small, read large)
  * semantic chunking evidence
  * late chunking and contextual retrieval both fight context loss
  * controlled chunking experiments
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Why and how big

  ### What goes wrong at each extreme?

  Too large: one vector averages many topics and matches no specific question well; lots of noise in context; expensive top-K. Too small: precise but stripped of the condition and heading, so the model misapplies it. A chunk is an evidence unit — small enough to locate, large enough to understand alone; for policies, a full clause plus its heading.

  <Note type="warning" title="Embedding input limits">
    Inputs beyond the model's limit (often 512 or 8,192 tokens) are silently truncated.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why can large chunks match specific questions poorly?
    2. Why do tiny chunks cause misapplied rules?
    3. The two requirements of an evidence unit?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Basic strategies

  ### Fixed, recursive, or structural?

  Fixed-length cuts mid-sentence and mid-table. Recursive splitting tries paragraph breaks, then lines, then sentences, then characters — a common default. Structural splitting follows headings, sections, table rows, or code functions — best boundaries, dependent on parsing. For policies: split by clause, fall back to recursive for long clauses. Tables by row with headers, code by function via the syntax tree, tickets by turn, FAQs one Q\&A per chunk.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. The recursive separator hierarchy and why?
    2. How should policies be split?
    3. Why not split code by line count?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Overlap and parent-child

  ### Overlap?

  Shared text between neighbors (600 size, 100 overlap → stride 500) prevents boundary truncation, at ~20% more index, duplicate hits, and no help for long-range dependencies. Typical: 10–20% of chunk size; less needed with structural splits.

  ### Parent-child and sentence windows?

  Search small, read large: match on child chunks (~130 tokens) and return the parent clause (~400 tokens), or match sentences and return a ±k window. Deduplicate when several children hit one parent.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Stride and index overhead for 800/160?
    2. Why can't overlap fix cross-clause dependencies?
    3. Why does parent-child get both precision and completeness?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Advanced methods

  ### Is semantic chunking worth it?

  It splits where adjacent-sentence embedding similarity drops. Evidence is mixed: *Is Semantic Chunking Worth the Computational Cost?* (2024) found gains over fixed-size splitting inconsistent and not worth the cost; Chroma's 2024 evaluation found chunk size often mattered more than method. Use structure when available; test semantic chunking against recursive on your eval.

  ### Late chunking?

  Jina AI (2024): encode the whole document with a long-context embedding model first, then pool token vectors within each chunk's span — chunk vectors carry document context without extra chunks; requires long-input models and token-level outputs.

  ### Contextual retrieval?

  Anthropic (2024): an LLM prepends a situating sentence to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing; reported 49% fewer retrieval failures, 67% with reranking; one LLM call per chunk (cheaper with caching). Unlike late chunking, it also helps BM25.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. How does semantic chunking work, and what does the evidence say?
    2. Why encode before chunking?
    3. What do late chunking and contextual retrieval both fix, and how do they differ?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Choose by experiment

  ### How do you pick a size?

  Typical starting points are 256–1,024 tokens, but run a controlled experiment: fix the embedding model, retriever, top-K, filters, reranker, and generator; vary only the chunking strategy; use an eval set covering exact clause lookups, cross-sentence conditions, table questions, and unanswerable questions; compare Recall@K, context coverage, duplication and tokens, and answer accuracy. High recall but wrong answers means missing conditions (try parent-child); consistent failures on IDs usually mean you need BM25, not new chunks.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "No magic number: start structural, vary only chunking on a mixed eval set, and read recall, coverage, and accuracy together."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Which variables stay fixed?
    2. Which question types belong in the eval set?
    3. What does high recall with wrong answers mean?
    4. Why are ID-lookup failures rarely chunking problems?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

title: Failure Diagnosis
description: “RAG 答错了，你查什么？”——先复现与定义错误，再沿 原文 → 解析 → 切分 → 过滤 → 召回 → 融合 → 重排 → 组装 → 生成 逐层定位；六个典型案例；把每次排错变成回归测试与线上监控。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  "The RAG answer is wrong — what do you check?" is the capstone RAG question. Weak answers: "use a better model," "tweak the prompt." Strong answers walk the pipeline layer by layer, naming the evidence, the judgment, and the fix.

  This page ties the section together; layered metrics live in [RAG Eval](/docs/evaluation/rag-eval).

  Running case: asked about order 20240915, the system says "Yes, unshipped orders get a full refund" — but the order is **in transit**; the correct answer is "not eligible for the unshipped refund; return within 7 days of delivery."

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Before debugging | How do you pin down the error? What must the trace hold? | 15 min |
  | 1 · Layer by layer | What do you check at each layer? | 35 min |
  | 2 · Six cases | What do common failures look like, where, and how to fix? | 35 min |
  | 3 · Closing the loop | How do you prevent recurrence? What do you monitor? | 15 min |

  **Levels 1 and 2 are the core.** About 1.5 hours.

  ## Must know

  * reproduce, define the expected answer, get the full trace
  * the nine-layer order and evidence per layer
  * six typical cases
  * eval additions, regression tests, monitoring signals
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Before debugging

  ### Pin down the error

  Reproduce with identical inputs (question, user, tenant, time, history), several times; write down the expected answer and its evidence (`P-17 v3` clause 4 + `in_transit` from the API) — the most-skipped step; get the full trace.

  ### What must the trace hold?

  Raw and rewritten queries, user/tenant; applied filters; per-branch top-K with ranks and scores; fused and reranked scores with drop reasons; final context chunks, order, tokens, truncation; tool requests and responses; model, prompt version, output, cited chunk IDs.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Three preparation steps; which is skipped most?
    2. Trace fields for retrieval, assembly, generation?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Layer by layer

  ### What do you check at each layer?

  Go upstream to downstream: (1) source — is the answer in the corpus? (2) parsing — does indexed text match the original? (3) chunking — is the chunk complete with condition and heading? (4) filters — correct chunk not wrongly filtered, wrong ones (old versions, other tenants) removed? (5) retrieval — rank in each branch? (6) fusion — still a candidate? (7) reranking — pushed down by a near-opposite? (8) assembly — actually in the final context, untruncated, not beside conflicting chunks? (9) generation — grounded in it and consistent with the order API?

  Shortcut: check layer 8 first. If the right chunk is in context, it's generation; if not, search layers 1–8 — the practical form of the four gates.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Name the nine layers in order.
    2. Why upstream first?
    3. How does checking layer 8 split the search?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Six cases

  1. **Expired policy cited**: BM25 branch lacked the version filter → filter both branches; add a version-switch regression case.
  2. **Table row without headers**: "delivered: no…" read as the answer → repeat headers in row chunks.
  3. **ID lookup fails**: dense-only retrieval plus a tokenizer splitting "P-17" → add BM25 and protect IDs.
  4. **Right chunk in context, wrong answer**: the opposite clause ranked first and the model didn't match on order state → rerank by condition, require "confirm status, pick clause, cite it," pass status as a structured field. This is the running error.
  5. **Answering without an answer**: overseas policy never ingested and no threshold → calibrated threshold with "no applicable policy" and escalation; ingest the policy.
  6. **Second turn off-topic**: retrieval used "what about after delivery?" verbatim → rewrite with conversation history.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    Walk one case end to end: reproduce, state the expected evidence, inspect the final context, localize the layer, fix, and add a regression case.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Where did the old policy enter in case 1?
    2. Why does case 4 span reranking and generation?
    3. Case 5's two root causes?
    4. Tell one case as symptom → investigation → fix → regression.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Closing the loop

  ### Prevent recurrence

  Add the redacted conversation to the eval set with the expected answer and chunk; fix; regress on the full set; add automatic rule checks (e.g. cited chunks must be the current version); roll out gradually.

  ### What to monitor?

  No-answer rate (spikes = index trouble or new topics; dropping to zero = thresholds failing and the system bluffing), citation coverage, top reranker score distribution, expired-version citations (should be 0), index freshness, and sampled online faithfulness.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. The five closing steps?
    2. What might a no-answer rate of zero mean?
    3. Four RAG-specific monitoring signals?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "Switch to a stronger model."
    * "Tweak the prompt." (Fixing before localizing.)
    * Debugging without a written expected answer and evidence.
    * Inferring a root cause from the final answer without traces.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Every page in this section; metrics in [RAG Eval](/docs/evaluation/rag-eval); traces in [Observability](/docs/production/observability)

  ## Interview questions

  1. The RAG answer is wrong — how do you investigate?
  2. What do you prepare, and what does the trace record?
  3. How do you quickly tell retrieval from generation problems?
  4. The right chunk is in context but the answer is wrong — why?
  5. How do you stop RAG from bluffing when there's no answer?
  6. Which RAG-specific signals do you monitor?

  ## Sources

  * [Barnett et al., 2024: Seven Failure Points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05856)
  * [Anthropic: Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval)
</Locale>

title: Embedding
description: 稠密向量怎样表示语义：双塔编码与对比学习训练、cosine 与点积、维度与存储手算、Matryoshka 与量化、查询与文档的不对称、MTEB 怎么看、换模型为什么要全量重建、什么时候微调。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Embeddings are the foundation of vector search. Typical follow-ups: how are they trained, cosine vs dot product, storage for 10M chunks, what changing models requires, why "still on the way" finds "in transit" but order numbers fail.

  Running example: "My cat food is still on the way — can I get my money back?" should match clause 4, "shipped (including in-transit) orders aren't eligible for the unshipped refund" — little word overlap, related meaning.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Vectors for meaning | What is an embedding? How is similarity computed? | 20 min |
  | 1 · Training | Bi-encoders, contrastive learning, hard negatives? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Dimensions, storage, compression | Memory for 10M chunks? Matryoshka and quantization? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Selection and use | Reading MTEB; why treat queries and docs differently? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Operations and fine-tuning | What does a model swap require? When to fine-tune? | 20 min |

  **Levels 1 and 2 are the core.** About 2 hours.

  ## Must know

  * similar meaning → similar direction
  * cosine, dot product, Euclidean: equivalent ranking after normalization
  * bi-encoder vs cross-encoder
  * InfoNCE, in-batch and hard negatives
  * storage math, Matryoshka truncation, int8/binary quantization
  * dense weaknesses: IDs, rare terms, out-of-domain
  * query prefixes, MTEB and its limits
  * full reindex on model change; fine-tuning data and gains
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Vectors for meaning

  ### What is an embedding?

  A model maps text to a fixed-length vector so similar meanings point in similar directions; queries are embedded too and matched to the nearest chunk vectors — that's how "still on the way" finds "in transit."

  ### How is similarity computed?

  Dot product (direction and length), cosine (direction only), Euclidean distance. With unit-normalized vectors all three rank identically (cosine = dot; squared distance = 2 − 2·cosine). Use the metric the model documents.

  ### Dense weaknesses?

  Exact identifiers (order numbers, `P-17`, SKUs, error codes), rare or new terms, and out-of-domain jargon — BM25's strengths, hence hybrid search.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why does "on the way" match "in transit"?
    2. How do the metrics relate after normalization?
    3. Three query types dense retrieval handles poorly?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Training

  ### Why bi-encoders for retrieval?

  Query and document are encoded separately, so document vectors are precomputed and search takes milliseconds. Cross-encoders read the pair jointly — more accurate, but one model run per pair, so they only rerank a few candidates.

  ### How does contrastive learning work?

  Pull positives together, push negatives apart (InfoNCE). In a batch, other pairs' documents act as in-batch negatives, so larger batches help. **Hard negatives** — same topic, wrong answer ("unshipped orders get full refunds" for an in-transit question) — teach fine distinctions; they're mined with BM25 or a previous model. Modern models pretrain on huge weakly supervised pairs, then fine-tune on curated or LLM-generated data.

  <Note type="tip" title="Connection">
    The same contrastive idea underlies CLIP, ColPali, and reranker training.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why bi-encoders at scale, and what do they lose?
    2. What are in-batch negatives, and why big batches?
    3. A hard negative for the in-transit question, and why it matters?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Dimensions, storage, compression

  ### How much memory for 10M chunks?

  `chunks × dims × bytes`: 10M × 1,536 × 4 B ≈ 61.4 GB; at 1,024 dims ≈ 41 GB — before index overhead, usually held in RAM.

  ### Matryoshka embeddings?

  MRL (2022) trains nested prefixes so the first 256, 512, or 1,024 dims are each usable; OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models expose this via `dimensions`. Use short vectors to shortlist, full vectors to rescore.

  ### Quantization?

  float16 2× (near lossless), int8 4× (small loss), binary 32× (noticeable; Hamming distance; rescore top candidates with full-precision vectors). Combining 512-dim MRL with int8 brings 61.4 GB to ~5 GB — measure recall.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Storage for 5M × 1,024 float32, and in int8?
    2. Why can Matryoshka vectors be truncated, and how do two-stage searches use them?
    3. Binary compression ratio, and why rescore?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Selection and use

  ### Reading MTEB?

  MTEB (multilingual MMTEB since 2025) spans retrieval, classification, clustering, and similarity. For RAG read the Retrieval columns in your language, beware leaderboard overfitting, and weigh max input length, dimensions, Matryoshka support, cost, license, and self-hosting. Decide on your own data.

  ### Common models?

  APIs (OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere, Voyage, Gemini), open models (BGE incl. BGE-M3, E5, Qwen3-Embedding, Jina), and multi-vector ColBERT. BGE-M3 emits dense, sparse, and multi-vector outputs from one model.

  ### Why treat queries and documents differently?

  Asymmetric retrieval: short questions vs longer declarative chunks. Models expect prefixes (`query:` / `passage:`), task instructions, or `input_type` parameters; missing them silently lowers recall.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Which MTEB columns matter, and what else?
    2. What's special about BGE-M3?
    3. Why prefixes, and what happens without them?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Operations and fine-tuning

  ### What does swapping models require?

  A full reindex — vector spaces aren't comparable across models. Evaluate, build a new index alongside the old, shadow traffic, switch with rollback, and record the model version per index. 10M chunks × 300 tokens = 3B tokens of re-embedding cost.

  ### When to fine-tune?

  When a general model misses domain terms or confuses business-opposite phrases. Build query–chunk pairs (logs, labels, LLM-generated questions), mine hard negatives with the current model, fine-tune contrastively (thousands to tens of thousands of pairs), and check held-out recall for regressions. Try prefixes, hybrid search, reranking, and contextual retrieval first.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why reindex fully, and the five migration steps?
    2. Tokens to re-embed 20M chunks at 250 tokens?
    3. Signals for fine-tuning, and what to try first?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "New docs get the new model; old vectors stay."
    * "Top MTEB average is best."
    * "Vector search handles order numbers."
    * Missing prefixes or mismatched metrics.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Previous: [Chunking](/docs/rag/chunking); next: [Vector Search](/docs/rag/vector-search)
  * Mechanics: [Tokenization](/docs/llm/tokenization), [Transformer](/docs/llm/transformer)

  1. Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder?

  3. Cosine vs dot product?
  4. How much storage for 10M vectors, and how do you compress it?

  6. Why does dense retrieval struggle with IDs?
  7. What does changing embedding models require?
  8. When should you fine-tune embeddings?

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Vectors for meaning

  ### What is an embedding?

  A model maps text to a fixed-length vector so similar meanings point in similar directions; queries are embedded too and matched to the nearest chunk vectors — that's how "still on the way" finds "in transit."

  ### How is similarity computed?

  Dot product (direction and length), cosine (direction only), Euclidean distance. With unit-normalized vectors all three rank identically (cosine = dot; squared distance = 2 − 2·cosine). Use the metric the model documents.

  ### Dense weaknesses?

  Exact identifiers (order numbers, `P-17`, SKUs, error codes), rare or new terms, and out-of-domain jargon — BM25's strengths, hence hybrid search.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why does "on the way" match "in transit"?
    2. How do the metrics relate after normalization?
    3. Three query types dense retrieval handles poorly?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Training

  ### Why bi-encoders for retrieval?

  Query and document are encoded separately, so document vectors are precomputed and search takes milliseconds. Cross-encoders read the pair jointly — more accurate, but one model run per pair, so they only rerank a few candidates.

  ### How does contrastive learning work?

  Pull positives together, push negatives apart (InfoNCE). In a batch, other pairs' documents act as in-batch negatives, so larger batches help.

title: Hybrid Search
description: BM25 与向量检索为什么互补；RRF 用 k = 60 手算、k 的作用；分数归一化加权融合与它的校准问题；按查询类型分桶评估；融合后排错与延迟拆账。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Hybrid search is the production default: BM25 for exact matches, dense for semantics, fused. Expect to compute RRF by hand and explain why raw scores can't be added, what k is, and when to use weighted fusion.

  Running example: "`P-17` — can in-transit orders be refunded?"

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Why two branches | What does each miss? | 15 min |
  | 1 · RRF by hand | How is RRF computed, and what does k = 60 mean? | 30 min |
  | 2 · Weighted fusion | Normalized weighted sums vs RRF? | 25 min |
  | 3 · Evaluation and debugging | How do you prove hybrid helps? Debug a bad fused result? | 20 min |

  **Level 1 is the core.** About 1.5 hours.

  ## Must know

  * complementarity; unify IDs and filters before fusing
  * the RRF formula, k (commonly 60), hand calculation
  * why raw scores don't add; min-max / z-score normalization and convex combination
  * RRF drops magnitude; weighted fusion needs calibration
  * per-query-type evaluation; layered debugging
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Why two branches

  ### What does each miss?

  Dense handles paraphrase ("still on the way" ≈ "in transit") but blurs IDs; BM25 nails `P-17` and error codes but misses paraphrases. Their errors are uncorrelated — the reason fusion works. Prerequisites: shared `chunk_id`s across indexes, and tenant/version/ACL filters applied in **both** branches, or expired or foreign data leaks in through one.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why does fusion raise recall?
    2. Two prerequisites, and what happens if a filter is missing?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · RRF by hand

  ### Why not add raw scores?

  Cosine sits in a narrow range; BM25 is unbounded and varies with query length and term rarity. Summing lets BM25 dominate.

  ### How does RRF work?

  `RRF(d) = Σ 1/(k + rank_i(d))`, absent branches contribute 0, k commonly 60 (from the 2009 RRF paper). With k = 60: A (dense 1, BM25 3) = 1/61 + 1/63 ≈ 0.03226; B (2, 1) ≈ 0.03252; C (dense 3 only) ≈ 0.01587; D (BM25 2 only) ≈ 0.01613 — order B > A > D > C. Candidates in both lists score roughly double.

  ### What does k do?

  Large k flattens rank differences (rank 1 ≈ 0.0164 vs rank 10 ≈ 0.0143), favoring agreement; small k (k = 1: 0.50 vs 0.091) favors one branch's top hit. k isn't top-K. RRF needs no tuning or calibration and is built into Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Weaviate, Qdrant, and others.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why not add cosine 0.82 and BM25 12.4?
    2. E is dense 1, BM25 5 — compare to B.
    3. How does k = 1 change behavior?
    4. k vs top-K?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Weighted fusion

  ### How does normalized weighted fusion work?

  Normalize each branch to 0–1 (min-max, or z-score for robustness) and combine `α·dense + (1−α)·BM25`. With α = 0.5 and the example scores: A 0.50, B 0.91, C 0.00, D 0.28.

  ### RRF or weighted?

  RRF: rank-only, no tuning, robust, but loses magnitude (0.95 vs 0.40 becomes one rank). Weighted: keeps confidence and lets you favor a branch, but min-max is sensitive to per-query extremes (the lowest score always becomes 0) and α must be re-tuned when models or data shift. Default to RRF; move to weighted or per-branch-weighted RRF when evaluation shows query types lean on one branch.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Min-max and convex-combination formulas?
    2. What does RRF lose, with an example?
    3. Why re-tune α after changing embedding models?
    4. Side effect of min-max?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Evaluation and debugging

  ### How do you prove hybrid helps?

  Bucket by query type — paraphrase, identifiers, mixed, unanswerable — because hybrid's value is avoiding one branch's severe failures, which averages hide.

  ### Fused top result still wrong?

  Trace per-branch ranks, fused score, filter reasons, and rerank position, then walk the layers: neither branch recalled it (embedding/chunking/tokenization/index), recalled but dropped at fusion (top-K too small or fusion choice), dropped at rerank, or present in context but misused (generation).

  ### Latency?

  Run branches in parallel; the critical path is the slower one plus fusion and reranking (≈ 40 + 2 + 120 ms). Degrading to one branch hurts IDs (dense only) or paraphrases (BM25 only).

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "BM25 + dense with RRF at k = 60, identical filters in both, evaluated per query type."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why bucket by query type?
    2. Correct chunk was BM25 #2 but missing after fusion — what do you check?
    3. Latency math and which queries suffer under single-branch degradation?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "Add the BM25 and cosine scores."
    * "RRF's k is the top-K."
    * Filtering only the dense branch.
    * Proving hybrid with averages alone.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Previous: [Sparse Retrieval](/docs/rag/sparse-retrieval); next: [Reranking](/docs/rag/reranking)
  * Related: [Vector Search](/docs/rag/vector-search), [Failure Diagnosis](/docs/rag/debugging), [RAG Eval](/docs/evaluation/rag-eval)

  ## Interview questions

  1. Why combine BM25 and dense retrieval?
  2. Compute RRF by hand and explain k.
  3. Why not add raw scores?
  4. RRF or normalized weighted fusion?
  5. How do you show hybrid search is better?
  6. How do you debug a bad top hybrid result?

  ## Sources

  * [Cormack et al., 2009: Reciprocal Rank Fusion](https://plg.uwaterloo.ca/~gvcormac/cormacksigir09-rrf.pdf)
  * [Elasticsearch: RRF](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/rrf.html)
  * [Azure AI Search: Hybrid ranking](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/hybrid-search-ranking)
</Locale>

</Locale>

content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Garbage in, garbage out is literal in RAG: two-column PDFs parsed into interleaved sentences, tables flattened into rows of numbers, headers mixed into body text — nothing downstream recovers. Much of the real work in RAG projects is ingestion.

  Typical questions: tables in PDFs? Scans? Policy updates? Deleting user data from a vector index?

  Running example: `P-17` exists as a PDF (with an order-status × action table), an HTML help page, and a scanned legacy attachment.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Why ingestion caps quality | How do parsing errors reach the answer? | 15 min |
  | 1 · Parsing | What's hard about PDFs, scans, tables? Which tools? | 35 min |
  | 2 · Metadata and versions | What do you record? How do versions coexist? | 25 min |
  | 3 · Updates and deletion | How does the index keep up with edits and deletes? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Quality checks | How do you know ingestion is right? | 15 min |

  **Levels 1 and 3 are the core.** About 2 hours.

  ## Must know

  * parsing errors are a major source of "missing content"
  * PDF pain points (columns, headers/footers, tables) and OCR for scans
  * the tool spectrum: rule-based → layout models (Docling) → VLM parsing → page-image retrieval (ColPali)
  * table handling
  * metadata, versions, conflicts
  * content hashes, change detection, tombstones, ACL sync
  * an ingestion QA checklist
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Why ingestion caps quality

  ### How do parsing errors propagate?

  Naive extraction of a two-column PDF interleaves the columns into a sentence with the wrong meaning. It is then chunked, embedded, retrieved, and faithfully quoted — every downstream step "correct," the answer wrong, and faithfulness scores high. Debugging always starts with what the indexed text actually looks like.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why are parsing errors hard to detect downstream?
    2. How can high faithfulness coexist with a parsing-caused error?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Parsing

  ### What's hard about each format?

  Digital PDFs store glyphs at coordinates — no paragraphs, headings, or reading order — so you need layout analysis to order blocks and drop headers and footers. Scans need OCR (watch digit errors). Tables lose row/column structure unless detected and converted to Markdown or HTML. HTML needs main-content extraction and heading structure. Office files have text boxes, comments, and tracked changes.

  ### Which tools?

  Text-layer extraction (PyMuPDF, pdfplumber: fast, weak on layout); layout models (Docling, Unstructured, Azure Document Intelligence, Textract: the workhorse); VLM parsing of page images into Markdown (great on complex layouts and charts, expensive, occasionally invents text); and **ColPali** (2024), which skips parsing entirely and embeds page screenshots as multi-vectors for late-interaction retrieval — layout preserved, but heavy storage and a multimodal reader still needed.

  ### Tables?

  Small tables as one Markdown chunk; otherwise row-wise chunks that repeat the header; optionally a generated table description. Never let a chunk lose its header.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why do PDFs lack reading order, and what does layout analysis add?
    2. When does each tool class fit?
    3. ColPali's idea and cost?
    4. Why repeat headers in row chunks?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Metadata and versions

  ### What do you record?

  `doc_id`, `version`, effective dates, source URL/system, tenant and ACL, type/language/region, `content_hash`, and parser name/version with timestamp (so parser upgrades know what to reprocess).

  ### How do versions coexist?

  Delete old versions (simple, but can't answer "which policy applied when I ordered?") or keep all with effective-date filtering (auditable, but filtering must never fail). Support refunds usually need the latter: filter `effective_from ≤ applicable date < effective_to`.

  ### Duplicate sources?

  Duplicates waste top-K slots. Exact dedup via normalized hashes, near-dup via MinHash, and a recorded authoritative source for conflicts.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Why record parser and parse time?
    2. The filter when all versions are kept?
    3. Why do duplicates hurt, and how do you dedupe?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Updates and deletion

  ### How does the index keep up with edits?

  Detect changes (scans or CDC/webhooks), reparse and rechunk changed documents, compare per-chunk hashes (skip unchanged, embed new, delete vanished), publish atomically so queries never see half-old/half-new versions, and track **index freshness** — the delay from document update to retrievability.

  Stale ACLs are a security issue, not a quality issue — propagate them with higher priority than content changes.

title: Reranking
description: 为什么检索与重排分两阶段：双塔 vs 交叉编码器、ColBERT 的后期交互折中、LLM 当重排器、重排的延迟与成本手算、候选数量与阈值怎么定。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Hybrid retrieval returns 100 candidates; only 5 fit in context. Retrieval scores aren't precise enough to pick them — hence reranking. Common questions: why two stages, why cross-encoders can't search the whole corpus, latency, candidate counts.

  Running example: for "can in-transit orders be refunded?", "unshipped orders get full refunds" (same topic, opposite condition) ranks #2 at retrieval while the correct clause ranks #7.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Why two stages | What does each stage optimize? | 15 min |
  | 1 · Cross-encoders | Why more accurate? Why not search with them? | 25 min |
  | 2 · Other rerankers | ColBERT and LLM reranking? | 25 min |
  | 3 · Cost and parameters | How many candidates, how much latency, thresholds? | 20 min |

  **Level 1 is the core.** About 1.5 hours.

  ## Must know

  * recall-oriented retrieval vs precision-oriented reranking
  * cross-encoder joint encoding and O(K) cost
  * ColBERT multi-vector MaxSim
  * LLM reranking (pointwise/listwise) and cost
  * candidate count, latency, relevance thresholds
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Why two stages

  ### What does each stage optimize?

  Retrieval (10M → 100) must be fast and not miss the answer (recall), so it uses coarse bi-encoders and BM25 that can't separate near-opposites like "unshipped: refundable" vs "in transit: not eligible." Reranking (100 → 5) can afford a slower, sharper model to push the wrong one down — the classic cheap-wide-then-expensive-precise funnel.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Which metric does each stage optimize?
    2. Why can't retrieval separate the two refund clauses?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Cross-encoders

  ### Why are they more accurate?

  A cross-encoder reads `[query] [sep] [document]` in one transformer, so "in transit" attends directly to "not eligible" and "unshipped." A bi-encoder must compress each document into one vector beforehand, losing those fine correspondences.

  ### Why not search the corpus with them?

  Every pair needs a full model run and nothing can be precomputed: 10M pairs × ~10 ms is ~100,000 seconds per query, versus 100–200 ms for 100 batched candidates. Examples: Cohere Rerank, Voyage, Jina (APIs); BGE-reranker, mxbai-rerank (open).

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Explain the accuracy gain via attention.
    2. Why not use them for full search? Show the order of magnitude.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Other rerankers

  ### ColBERT?

  Late interaction (2020): encode query and document separately (documents precomputable) but keep one vector per token; score by summing, over query tokens, the maximum similarity to any document token (MaxSim). More accurate than bi-encoders, faster than cross-encoders, but stores hundreds of vectors per chunk (ColBERTv2 compresses them). ColPali applies the same idea to page images.

  ### LLMs as rerankers?

  Pointwise (score each candidate; simple, parallel, poorly calibrated) or listwise (rank a set at once, as in RankGPT with sliding windows; captures relations, long outputs, position bias). They understand complex business conditions and custom criteria but are slow and costly — 20 candidates × 300 tokens is a 6K-token call. Common compromise: cross-encoder 100 → 20, then LLM or the generator itself picks.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. How is MaxSim computed, and why the accuracy/speed middle ground?
    2. ColBERT's main cost?
    3. Pointwise vs listwise LLM reranking, and when is it worth it?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Cost and parameters

  ### How many candidates?

  Too few retrieved and reranking can't recover the answer; too many and latency grows linearly. Too few kept loses multi-part evidence; too many adds cost and noise. Start around 50–100 → 3–10 and increase retrieval depth until recall stops improving on your eval set.

  ### Latency and cost?

  A GPU cross-encoder over 100 × 300-token candidates takes roughly 50–200 ms batched; APIs bill per search or token; listwise LLM reranking of 20 is a 6K-token call at 1–3 s. It sits on the critical path before generation.

  ### Relevance thresholds?

  Drop candidates below a calibrated score and, when nothing passes, say no policy was found or escalate — a key defense against the "missing content" failure. Calibrate on answerable and unanswerable questions; scales differ by model.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "Reranking is one of the best-value RAG upgrades: retrieve 100, keep 5, ~100–200 ms; plus a calibrated threshold so the system can say 'I don't know.'"
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Problems with too few and too many candidates, and how to choose?
    2. Where does reranking sit in the latency budget?
    3. What do thresholds solve, and why calibrate locally?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "Use a cross-encoder to search the whole corpus."
    * "Reranking recovers documents retrieval missed."
    * No threshold — always stuffing the top 5.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Previous: [Hybrid Search](/docs/rag/hybrid-search); next: [Failure Diagnosis](/docs/rag/debugging)
  * Related: [Embedding](/docs/rag/embedding), [Latency](/docs/production/latency), [Context Construction](/docs/context/construction)

  ## Interview questions

  1. Why separate retrieval and reranking?
  2. Why are cross-encoders more accurate, and why not search with them?
  3. What is ColBERT?
  4. Can LLMs rerank, and at what cost?
  5. How many candidates do you rerank?
  6. How do you make RAG say "I don't know"?

  ## Sources

  * [Nogueira & Cho, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04085)
  * [ColBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832)
  * [RankGPT (Sun et al., 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.09542)
  * [Sentence Transformers: Cross-Encoders](https://www.sbert.net/examples/applications/cross-encoder/README.html)
</Locale>

title: Sparse Retrieval
description: 倒排索引与 BM25：IDF 和词频饱和手算、长度归一化、中文分词问题、BM25 为什么在 BEIR 上仍是强基线、SPLADE 等学习型稀疏检索。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Why BM25 alongside vectors? Users ask about "`P-17` clause 4," order numbers, error codes — dense retrieval's weak spot and keyword retrieval's strength. Expect to write the BM25 formula and explain `k1` and `b`.

  Running example: 1,000 policy documents; query "`P-17` in transit refund."

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Inverted index | Why is keyword search fast? | 15 min |
  | 1 · BM25 by hand | What do IDF, saturation, and length normalization do? | 35 min |
  | 2 · Chinese and engineering | No spaces? Synonyms? | 20 min |
  | 3 · Why it still matters | When does BM25 beat vectors? What is learned sparse retrieval? | 20 min |

  **Level 1 is the core.** About 1.5 hours.

  ## Must know

  * inverted index: term → posting list
  * the BM25 formula, `k1`, `b`; hand-compute IDF and saturation
  * Chinese segmentation vs n-grams
  * BM25 as a strong zero-shot baseline on BEIR; SPLADE
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Inverted index

  ### Why is keyword search fast?

  An inverted index maps each term to the documents containing it (with counts); a query merges the posting lists of its terms instead of scanning everything. It's "sparse" because a document is a vocabulary-sized vector that's almost all zeros.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What does an inverted index store, and why is it fast?
    2. Why "sparse"?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · BM25 by hand

  ### The formula

  `BM25(q,d) = Σ IDF(t) × tf(k1+1) / (tf + k1(1 − b + b·|d|/avgdl))`, with `IDF(t) = ln((N − n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5) + 1)`, typically k1 ≈ 1.2 (1.2–2.0), b ≈ 0.75.

  ### ① IDF

  N = 1,000: "P-17" in 5 docs → ≈ 5.20; "in transit" in 40 → ≈ 3.21; "refund" in 400 → ≈ 0.92. Rare terms like IDs carry the signal — why BM25 excels at identifiers.

  ### ② Term-frequency saturation

  At average length with k1 = 1.2: tf 1 → 1.00, 3 → 1.57, 10 → 1.96, capped at 2.2. Keyword stuffing can't dominate; larger k1 saturates later.

  ### ③ Length normalization

  At twice average length and tf = 1: 2.2 / (1 + 1.2 × 1.75) ≈ 0.71 vs 1.00. b = 0 ignores length; b = 1 normalizes fully.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Write BM25 and explain its three parts.
    2. IDF for a term in 10 of 1,000 docs?
    3. Frequency term for tf = 5 at average length, and its cap?
    4. What happens with b = 0?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Chinese and engineering

  ### Tokenizing Chinese?

  Dictionary segmentation (jieba, IK: meaningful terms, but new names get split; maintain a custom dictionary) or character n-grams (no dictionary, bigger noisier index). Usually segmentation plus a business dictionary; make sure IDs like `P-17` aren't broken into "P" and "17."

  ### Synonyms?

  Synonym lists, LLM query rewriting, or leave semantics to dense retrieval — the hybrid division of labor.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Pros and cons of segmentation vs n-grams?
    2. Why protect IDs from splitting?
    3. Three ways to handle synonyms?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Why it still matters

  ### When does BM25 win?

  BEIR (2021), zero-shot across 18 datasets, found BM25 a very strong baseline that many in-domain dense models failed to beat out of domain. It still often wins on exact identifiers, unseen jargon, verbatim quotes, and explainability — with no GPU, training, or costly updates. Hence hybrid by default.

  ### Learned sparse retrieval?

  SPLADE (2021) has a language model emit weighted terms, including related terms absent from the text, still served from an inverted index — semantic expansion with exact matching. BGE-M3's sparse output and Elasticsearch's ELSER are similar; they need model inference at index and query time.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "BM25 is a strong zero-shot baseline per BEIR; I default to hybrid, and consider SPLADE-style sparse retrieval when budget allows."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. BEIR's conclusion about BM25?
    2. Three scenarios where BM25 still wins?
    3. SPLADE vs BM25 — still an inverted index?
  </Note>

  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "Vectors make BM25 unnecessary."
    * "BM25 is just term frequency."
    * Splitting Chinese on spaces.
  </Note>

title: Vector Search
description: 从暴力搜索到近似最近邻：HNSW 的分层图与三个参数、IVF 的聚类与 nprobe、PQ 压缩手算、DiskANN；元数据过滤的三种方式与陷阱；召回率与延迟的权衡；向量数据库怎么选。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Next: find the 10 most similar of 10M vectors in milliseconds. Common questions: how HNSW works, what raising `efSearch` does, IVF vs HNSW, why tenant filtering shrinks results, pgvector vs a dedicated vector DB.

  Running example: 10M multi-tenant chunks; "can in-transit orders be refunded?" may only search tenant `miaomiao`'s valid versions.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Why approximate | How slow is brute force? What does approximation cost? | 15 min |
  | 1 · HNSW | How does the layered graph search? What do M, efConstruction, efSearch control? | 35 min |
  | 2 · IVF and PQ | How do cluster indexes search? How does PQ shrink 6 KB to 96 bytes? | 30 min |
  | 3 · Metadata filtering | Pre-, post-, and filter-aware search? | 25 min |
  | 4 · Selection and tuning | Which vector DB? How do you measure recall? | 20 min |

  **Levels 1 and 3 are the core.** About 2 hours.

  ## Must know

  * brute-force cost; ANN trades recall for speed
  * HNSW structure, greedy search, parameters, memory
  * IVF (`nlist`, `nprobe`), PQ compression, DiskANN
  * three filtering approaches and the post-filter shortfall
  * recall measured against exact search; parameter vs latency tradeoffs
  * pgvector vs search engines vs dedicated stores; multi-tenant isolation
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Why approximate

  ### How slow is brute force?

  Exact kNN costs about N × d multiply-adds: 10M × 1,024 ≈ 10 billion per query — seconds on a CPU core. ANN indexes inspect a fraction of vectors for millisecond latency at the risk of missing true neighbors, measured as recall against exact search (production often targets Recall@10 ≥ 0.95) — not the same as RAG's "was the right chunk retrieved."

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Brute-force cost for 5M × 768?
    2. ANN recall vs RAG Recall@K?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · HNSW

  ### How does HNSW search?

  A layered proximity graph: every vector is in layer 0; a random few also appear in sparser upper layers (highways). Search greedily from the top entry point toward closer neighbors, descend a layer when stuck, and refine at layer 0 — visiting hundreds to thousands of nodes instead of millions.

  ### What do the parameters control?

  `M` (neighbors per node: recall up, memory and build time up), `efConstruction` (candidate breadth at build: better graph, slower build), `efSearch` (candidate list at query: recall up, latency up — the only query-time knob). Typical: M 16–64, efConstruction 100–500, efSearch 50–500 and above k.

  ### Drawbacks?

  Memory (≈ 2M neighbor IDs per node at layer 0 — M = 32 adds ~2.5 GB for 10M nodes, all in RAM), awkward deletes (tombstones, periodic rebuilds), slow builds.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Explain HNSW search with the highway analogy.
    2. Which knob first for low recall, and its cost?
    3. Layer-0 neighbor memory for M = 16, 10M nodes, 4-byte IDs?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · IVF and PQ

  ### How does IVF search?

  k-means into `nlist` clusters (e.g. 4,096); at query time compare against centroids and search only the nearest `nprobe` clusters (e.g. 16 → ~0.4% of data). `nprobe` is the recall knob; true neighbors across cluster boundaries are missed when it's too small. IVF uses less memory and builds faster; HNSW is usually faster at equal recall.

  ### How does PQ compress?

  Split a 1,536-dim float32 vector (6,144 B) into 96 sub-vectors, learn 256 centroids per subspace, store one byte per subspace: 96 B (64×). Distances become table lookups — fast but approximate, so rescore top candidates with full vectors. IVF-PQ (e.g. Faiss) is the classic billion-scale combo.

  ### Data larger than RAM?

  DiskANN keeps the graph on SSD with compressed vectors in memory — billion-scale on one machine at somewhat higher latency.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. `nlist` vs `nprobe`, and why small `nprobe` misses results?
    2. Compression ratio for 1,024-dim float32 into 64 one-byte codes?
    3. Why rescore after PQ?
    4. When DiskANN?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Metadata filtering

  ### Pre-, post-, or filter-aware?

  Post-filtering (ANN then drop) can return almost nothing under strict filters — a tenant with 1% of data leaves ~0.1 of the top-10, and even top-1,000 leaves ~10 that may not be the tenant's best. Pre-filtering (filter, then brute force) is slow for large sets. Filter-aware ANN skips disallowed nodes during search but loses recall when the filter is extremely selective.

  ### In practice?

  Few large tenants: one index or namespace per tenant — no filter, strongest isolation. Many small tenants: shared index with filter-aware ANN; most vector DBs switch to pre-filter + brute force for very selective filters. Index the filter fields.

  <Note type="warning" title="Filters are a security boundary">
    Never relax tenant or ACL filters to get more results; tune retrieval instead.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Show the post-filter shortfall numerically.
    2. Per-tenant index vs shared index with filters?
    3. Why not relax ACL filters when results are sparse?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Selection and tuning

  ### Which vector database?

  pgvector for millions to tens of millions of chunks when you already run Postgres and want joins and transactions; Elasticsearch/OpenSearch when you need BM25 + vector hybrid and rich filters; Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, Pinecone for scale, QPS, quantization, disk indexes, multi-tenancy; LanceDB, Chroma, Faiss for prototypes and offline work. Start from scale and existing infrastructure.

  ### How do you measure recall and tune?

  Take ~1,000 real queries, compute exact top-10 by brute force, sweep ANN parameters, plot recall vs P95 latency, and choose the cheapest config meeting the target. `efSearch`/`nprobe` raise recall and latency; `M` raises recall and memory; heavier quantization cuts memory and latency at some recall (recoverable by rescoring). ANN-Benchmarks offers reference curves.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "ANN recall is relative to exact search; 99% there doesn't mean RAG found the right chunk — that's embeddings and chunking, measured separately."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. When is pgvector the best choice?
    2. Four steps to measure ANN recall?
    3. 99% ANN recall but RAG still misses — where's the problem?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * "Vector search returns the most similar results." (It's approximate.)
    * "Skip the filter and backfill when results are sparse."
    * "You obviously need a dedicated vector DB."
    * Conflating ANN recall with RAG recall.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Previous: [Embedding](/docs/rag/embedding); next: [Sparse Retrieval](/docs/rag/sparse-retrieval)
  * Related: [Hybrid Search](/docs/rag/hybrid-search), [Isolation](/docs/context/isolation), [Scaling](/docs/production/scaling)

  ## Interview questions

  1. Why approximate nearest neighbors, and what's sacrificed?
  2. How does HNSW work, and what do its parameters control?
  3. IVF or HNSW?
  4. How does product quantization compress vectors?
  5. How do you filter by metadata, and what's wrong with post-filtering?
  6. How do you design multi-tenant vector search?
  7. pgvector or a dedicated vector database?

  ## Sources

  * [HNSW (Malkov & Yashunin)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320)
  * [Product Quantization (Jégou et al., 2011)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5432202)
  * [DiskANN (Microsoft, NeurIPS 2019)](https://github.com/microsoft/DiskANN)
  * [Faiss](https://faiss.ai/), [ANN-Benchmarks](https://ann-benchmarks.com/)
  * [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector)
</Locale>

title: L4 · Agent Platform
description: 企业级 agent 平台：让几十个团队自助构建和上线 agent。agent 定义与运行时、MCP 工具注册与治理、身份与权限委托、沙箱与审批策略、agent 的评估与发布流水线、追踪与成本归因。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  > Design an internal agent platform where dozens of teams (support, finance, HR, engineering) configure and ship agents connected to internal systems, with the platform owning safety, reliability, observability, and cost.

  Not "design an agent" but "design a platform for others to build agents." What's shared vs team-owned? How do you stop one team's agent from reaching other systems? How do you assure quality before launch? Related: [Agent Harness](/docs/ai-native/harness), [MCP](/docs/ai-native/mcp).

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Interview time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Clarify | Platform vs team boundary? | 5 min |
  | 1 · High-level design | Which components? | 10 min |
  | 2 · Deep dive: tool governance and identity | Tool registration; whose identity? | 12 min |
  | 3 · Deep dive: quality and release | Evaluating, launching, rolling back agents? | 10 min |
  | 4 · Operations and cost | Tracing, quotas, attribution | 5 min |

  ## Must know

  * shared capabilities vs team responsibilities
  * declarative agent definitions and a managed runtime
  * an MCP tool registry with review, versions, scopes
  * delegated user authorization (OAuth, token exchange), no passthrough
  * risk policies for approvals and sandboxes
  * eval pipelines, canaries, rollback; tracing and attribution
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Clarify

  The platform owns the runtime (loop, state, retries, timeouts, budgets), a model gateway, the tool registry and permission framework, identity delegation, approvals, sandboxes, eval and release pipelines, tracing, attribution, and guardrails. Teams own goals, instructions, workflows, model tier choices, their MCP servers and tools, declared permissions, eval sets, success criteria, and business validation. Assume 50 teams, 200 agents, 1M tasks/day, full auditability, human approval for sensitive actions, data in the company cloud. The platform turns the parts every harness rebuilds into services and makes safety the default.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Five platform and five team responsibilities?
    2. Why make safety a platform default?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · High-level design

  Control plane: versioned declarative agent definitions (model tier, prompt, tools, scopes, budgets, approval policy, eval set), a tool registry of MCP servers with review status, versions, and scopes, a policy engine, eval and release pipelines, cost and quota management. Data plane: a managed runtime with durable execution, context management, and caps; a model gateway to external APIs or the internal inference platform; a tool gateway to MCP servers that checks identity, scopes, and policy and audits each call; sandbox and approval services. Cross-cutting: OpenTelemetry GenAI tracing, audit logs, attribution, guardrails. A single tool gateway centralizes enforcement and audit.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Contents of control and data planes?
    2. Why route tool calls through a gateway?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Deep dive: tool governance and identity

  Teams register MCP servers declaring names, descriptions, schemas, risk tier, and scopes; security reviews writes and irreversible actions and rejects instruction-like descriptions (tool poisoning); definition changes require re-review, with approved hashes checked at runtime (rug pulls); agent definitions reference only reviewed tools. User-triggered tasks act on the user's behalf via token exchange for short-lived, scope-limited, audience-bound tokens; background jobs use per-agent service identities. Never pass tokens through; effective permission = user rights ∩ declared agent scopes ∩ platform policy; the gateway triggers approvals for payments, outbound sends, deletions.

  <Note type="tip" title="Interview move">
    "Permissions are an intersection; delegated tokens are exchanged, not passed through; tool definition changes are re-reviewed and hash-checked."
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. What does registration declare, and why hash checks?
    2. Whose identity for user-triggered vs background tasks?
    3. Why intersect three permission sets?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Deep dive: quality and release

  Treat every agent-definition change (prompt, tools, model version) as a release: run the team's state-based business evals plus platform suites (injection, privilege escalation, budget), compare with production (success, pass^k, cost, steps), block on any security failure or regressions beyond thresholds, canary 1% → 10% → 100%, and auto-roll back on error, escalation, or cost anomalies. When the model gateway upgrades a model, rerun every dependent agent's evals — something individual teams would rarely catch.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. The five release steps?
    2. Why rerun evals on model upgrades?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Operations and cost

  One trace per task across model calls, tool calls (with identity and scope), approvals, and cost, propagated through MCP servers; tamper-proof audit logs; per-team and per-agent token, concurrency, and daily cost limits with chargeback; runtime-level stall detection and kill switches; durable execution for long and approval-waiting tasks; MCP server failures isolated to dependent agents.

  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * Leaving permissions and safety to each team.
    * Passing user tokens through.
    * Shipping prompt changes without evals.
    * Unreviewed tool definition changes.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Mechanics: [Agent Harness](/docs/ai-native/harness), [MCP](/docs/ai-native/mcp), [Agent Security](/docs/agent/security), [Agent Eval](/docs/evaluation/agent-eval)
  * Related: [AI Agent](/docs/system-design/ai-agent), [Long-running Agent](/docs/system-design/long-running-agent), [Inference Platform](/docs/system-design/inference-platform)

  ## Interview questions

  1. Design an enterprise agent platform.
  2. Where's the boundary between platform and teams?
  3. Whose identity does an agent use?
  4. How are tools registered, reviewed, and protected from tampering?
  5. How are agent changes evaluated and released?
</Locale>

  ## My answer
</Locale>
