title: L1 · RAG Chatbot
description: 最基础的 RAG 白板题：澄清需求与容量估算、离线 / 在线两条流水线、检索与 context 组装深挖、无答案与引用、评测与成本。45 分钟讲完一个可上线的设计。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  > Design a customer-facing help-center chatbot for an e-commerce company that answers return, shipping, and payment policy questions.

  This is the first AI system design problem; knowledge assistants, support bots, and AI search build on it. It tests whether you can present a shippable system in 45 minutes: ask the right questions, size it, draw both pipelines, go deep on two areas, and explain evaluation and fallbacks.

  Prereqs: [RAG Architecture](/docs/rag/architecture) and the RAG section. This page practices organizing an answer.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Interview time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Clarify and estimate | What to ask first? How big? | 5 min |
  | 1 · High-level design | How do the pipelines and a request flow? | 10 min |
  | 2 · Deep dive: retrieval | How do you find the right evidence? | 10 min |
  | 3 · Deep dive: answers | Citations, no-answer, multi-turn? | 8 min |
  | 4 · Eval, reliability, cost | How do you prove it, survive failures, and pay for it? | 7 min |

  ## Must know

  * opening questions and assumptions; capacity estimates
  * both pipelines and chunk metadata
  * hybrid + rerank; citations and abstention; multi-turn rewriting
  * layered evaluation, degradation, cost structure
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Clarify and estimate

  ### What do you ask first?

  Spend 3–5 minutes and write assumptions down: users (public and logged-in; public policy only, no personal orders), corpus (~2,000 HTML/PDF articles, dozens updated weekly), languages (Chinese and English), traffic and latency (50K DAU, first useful content within 1.5 s), cost of errors (complaints and payouts — citations required, escalate when unsure), success metrics (auto-resolution, escalation, accuracy). Conclude: read-only, public knowledge, citations, moderate scale — order actions belong to [Customer Support](/docs/system-design/customer-support).

  ### Sizing

  \~6M tokens → ~15K chunks → ~60 MB of vectors (pgvector is plenty); 100K requests/day ≈ 1.2 average and ~10 peak QPS; ~40 in flight. Say it: the hard part is quality, not scale.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Five opening questions and the decisions they drive?
    2. Estimate vector storage and peak concurrency.
    3. Why isn't scaling the deep dive here?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · High-level design

  ### Two pipelines

  Offline: CMS change events → parse (HTML main content, PDF layout analysis) → clean, dedupe, version → chunk by section with headings → embeddings into pgvector and a BM25 index, each chunk carrying `chunk_id`, `doc_id`, version, effective date, section, URL, language, hash. Online: gateway (auth, rate limits) → query rewriting with history → dense ∥ BM25 with identical filters → RRF top-50 → cross-encoder top-5 (below threshold → no-answer branch) → cited context → streamed generation → citation check → answer with links → trace.

  ### Latency walk

  Rewrite 300 ms + retrieval 50 ms + rerank 120 ms + first token 600 ms ≈ 1.07 s; full answer in ~5 s. Trim rewriting to multi-turn only if needed.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Draw both pipelines with metadata.
    2. Estimate time to first token and the first thing to cut.
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Deep dive: retrieval

  Prepare four points: chunk by section with headings (FAQs one pair per chunk, table rows with headers), compared on an eval set; hybrid search because users ask both paraphrases and clause IDs (RRF; Chinese BM25 needs segmentation and a business dictionary); reranking to separate near-opposite clauses at ~100–200 ms; policy updates via change events, hash-based incremental reindexing, atomic publish, version filters, and freshness monitoring.

  <Note type="tip" title="Deep-dive rhythm">
    Problem → solution → cost → validation, one sentence each.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Explain reranking in that four-sentence rhythm.
    2. How fast do updates become searchable, and how do you monitor it?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Deep dive: answers

  Citations: the model tags claims with `chunk_id`s, the server verifies IDs exist in this context, the UI links them, and sampled judges check support. No answer: a calibrated reranker threshold skips generation, the prompt and an `answerable` field forbid guessing, and the product offers a human handoff while logging the question — frequent no-answer questions are your missing-content backlog. Multi-turn: rewrite follow-ups like "what about international orders?" with recent history before retrieval; keep recent turns plus a summary.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Three layers of no-answer handling, and why log them?
    2. How are citations verified?
    3. Why not retrieve with the raw follow-up?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Evaluation, reliability, security, cost

  Evaluation: ~300 labeled questions across common, ID, multi-turn, no-answer, and bilingual cases, measured by Recall@5, faithfulness, accuracy, and abstention; shadow and canary; online resolution, escalation, feedback, judged samples, no-answer rate, citation coverage. Reliability: backup model → retrieved passages with links only → human; if retrieval is down, say so rather than answering from memory. Security: treat documents as data, protect the system prompt, rate-limit, don't promise beyond policy. Cost: 100K requests × ($0.012 + $0.0045) ≈ $1,650/day ≈ $50K/month at illustrative prices; prefix caching and small-model routing cut it substantially.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Five question types for the offline set?
    2. Why not answer from memory when retrieval fails?
    3. Monthly cost and two levers?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## 14-dimension cheat sheet

  Requirements: read-only cited policy Q\&A with escalation. Constraints: 2K docs, weekly updates, bilingual, 1.5 s. Architecture: offline ingestion + online RAG in one service. Data flow: change events → incremental index; request → rewrite → hybrid → rerank → generate. Model: mid-tier generator, small rewriter, cross-encoder. Retrieval: structural chunks, dense + BM25 + RRF, rerank + threshold. Agent: none — a workflow. Evaluation: 300-question layered set; online resolution and judged samples. Scaling: single-node pgvector. Latency: ~1.1 s first token, streamed. Cost: ~$50K/month order; caching and routing. Reliability: backup model → passages only → human. Security: documents as data, rate limits, no over-promising. Observability: candidates, ranks, citations, tokens, latency per request.

  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * Drawing before clarifying.
    * "Use an agent." (The flow is fixed.)
    * No unanswerable handling.
    * Kafka and distributed vector DBs for 15K chunks.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Mechanics: [RAG Architecture](/docs/rag/architecture), [Hybrid Search](/docs/rag/hybrid-search), [Reranking](/docs/rag/reranking), [Failure Diagnosis](/docs/rag/debugging)
  * Next: [Knowledge Assistant](/docs/system-design/knowledge-assistant), [Customer Support](/docs/system-design/customer-support)

  ## Interview questions

  1. Design a customer-facing RAG chatbot.
  2. How do you choose chunk size?
  3. Why hybrid search?
  4. How do you handle unanswerable questions?
  5. How would you reduce latency?
  6. The answer is wrong — what do you investigate?
  7. How do you stop citing outdated policy?
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## My answer
</Locale>

* 5 分钟白板版:

</Locale>

description: 多租户 RAG 平台（几千家客户、几十亿块）：存储与索引规模手算、按租户分片与冷热分层、入库流水线吞吐与 embedding 成本、新鲜度 SLA、换 embedding 模型的双索引迁移、租户隔离与 noisy neighbor、按租户评估与成本。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  > Design a RAG-as-a-Service platform: 5,000 business customers upload or sync documents and query via API — ~2B chunks total, millions of new documents a day.

  The mechanics are in [RAG](/docs/rag); the difficulty here is scale and multi-tenancy: where billions of vectors live, how big and small tenants coexist, how millions of daily documents get ingested, and how to re-embed billions of vectors when changing models.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Level | Question it answers | Interview time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0 · Clarify and estimate | Storage, ingestion, query volume? | 8 min |
  | 1 · High-level design | Ingestion, query, control planes | 8 min |
  | 2 · Deep dive: sharding and tiers | Storing and querying 2B vectors? | 12 min |
  | 3 · Deep dive: ingestion and migration | Throughput, freshness, model changes | 10 min |
  | 4 · Isolation, eval, cost | Tenant independence; per-tenant accounting | 5 min |

  ## Must know

  * storage, index memory, embedding cost math
  * tenant sharding, hot/cold tiers, disk indexes
  * ingestion queues, batched embedding, freshness SLAs
  * dual-index migration for embedding changes
  * isolation, quotas, noisy neighbors; per-tenant quality and cost
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Clarify and estimate

  Long-tail tenants (top 50 hold 60% of data; 4,000 have under 100K chunks), 2B chunks of ~400 tokens, 3M changed documents (~30M chunks) per day, 1,000 average and 3,000 peak QPS with retrieval P95 under 200 ms, 10-minute freshness, strict isolation with dedicated deployments for some. Vectors at 1,024 dims: 8 TB float32, 2 TB int8, 256 GB binary (shortlist only); HNSW links ~256 GB more — tiering is mandatory. Daily embedding ~12B tokens; a full re-embed ~800B tokens. Storage and embedding dominate, not QPS.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Storage in float32 and int8?
    2. Why is changing embedding models a major project?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · High-level design

  Control plane: tenants, quotas, index configs (embedding version, chunking), billing. Ingestion: connectors/uploads → tenant-partitioned priority queues → CPU/OCR parsing → chunking → batched GPU embedding → writes to vector, BM25, and metadata (doc ID, ACL, version) shards → publish and record freshness. Query: tenant auth → route to the tenant's shards → filtered dense ∥ BM25 → fusion → GPU reranking → chunks or answers. Partitioning queues by tenant prevents one tenant's bulk import from starving others.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Each plane's role?
    2. Why partition queues by tenant?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Deep dive: sharding and tiers

  Big tenants get dedicated shards (strong isolation, independent scaling, dedicated deployments, no tenant filter); small tenants share shards partitioned by tenant namespace with filtered search; a routing table maps tenants to shards and grown tenants migrate out. Tier by access: hot in-memory HNSW with int8, warm DiskANN-style SSD indexes for most tenants, cold in object storage loaded on demand; or binary shortlists rescored with int8/float. For P95 under 200 ms: fan-out across a big tenant's shards amplifies tails, so time-box shards and accept partial results, run dense and BM25 in parallel, and scale a dedicated GPU reranking pool on QPS.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Sharding for big vs small tenants?
    2. Storage per tier?
    3. Controlling tail latency under fan-out?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 3 · Deep dive: ingestion and migration

  Ingest through tenant-partitioned queues with quota-based backpressure (a 10M-document import can't starve others), batched GPU embedding (self-hosting usually beats per-token APIs at ~12B tokens/day), hash-based incremental updates, priority lanes so routine updates meet the 10-minute SLA while bulk imports run slow, and verifiable deletion across shards, BM25, and caches. Changing embedding models: prove gains per tenant, rebuild a new index in the background on idle GPUs (possibly weeks), dual-write during migration, switch tenant by tenant with shadow comparison, keep the old index for rollback. A tenant is entirely old or new, since query and document vectors must share a model.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should be able to answer">
    1. Preventing bulk imports from hurting others?
    2. The five migration steps?
    3. Why switch per tenant?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 4 · Isolation, eval, cost

  Isolate by shard or namespace, inject tenant conditions server-side, key caches by tenant, and run cross-tenant negative tests (zero violations). Enforce per-tenant quotas on storage, ingestion, and QPS. Offer per-tenant eval tooling, synthetic-question baselines for unlabeled tenants, and regression on representative tenants for any platform change. Costs are vector storage by tier, embedding GPUs, and reranking GPUs, attributed per tenant; tiering and quantization are the biggest levers.

  ## Pitfalls

  <Note type="danger" title="Claims that cost points">
    * All vectors in RAM as float32.
    * Treating all tenants alike (thousands of tiny indexes or one shared index).
    * Rebuilding with downtime.
    * Trusting client-supplied tenant IDs.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Mechanics: [Vector Search](/docs/rag/vector-search), [Embedding](/docs/rag/embedding), [Ingestion](/docs/rag/ingestion), [Scaling](/docs/production/scaling)
  * Related: [Knowledge Assistant](/docs/system-design/knowledge-assistant), [RAG Chatbot](/docs/system-design/rag-chatbot)

  ## Interview questions

  1. Design a large-scale multi-tenant RAG platform.
  2. How do you store 2B vectors, and how much memory?
  3. How do you shard big and small tenants?
  4. How do you ingest 30M chunks/day and stay fresh?
  5. How do you migrate embedding models without downtime?
